en: The Mahāyāna Ratnamegha Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Mandarasa of Funan together with Saṃghabara during the Liang Dynasty.
1. Introduction (I). Chapter One: The Introduction.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Gayāśīrṣa Hill in the kingdom of Gayā, together with a great assembly of seventy thousand monks. All of them were great arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions;
whose minds had attained mastery, being well-liberated in mind and well-liberated through wisdom.
Known and recognized by all, they are all great dragons and elephants;
having accomplished what was to be done, they do not undergo further existence; having laid down the heavy burden, they have attained their own benefit;
having exhausted the fetters of existence, they are well-liberated through both parts; possessing all mastery, they have reached the ultimate further shore.
They have thoroughly realized the nature of phenomena and are sons of the Dharma King;
their minds are disciplined, steadfast, and non-regressive, unshakable by the eight winds of the world;
they are endowed with all virtues, their aspirations are fully realized, and they abide in the path to Nirvana—with the sole exception of one person, namely the Elder Ānanda.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by a multitude of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, sixteen thousand in number—all of whom were in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). They were oriented toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), revering omniscience, advancing toward omniscience, and attaining omniscience. Having acquired the unimpeded *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi*, they dwelt in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
All of them sported freely, maturing sentient beings through their great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) without even a moment’s rest.

Free from all afflictions and hindrances, their great kindness and great compassion manifested throughout all lands in the ten directions; they were skillfully able to travel back and forth across immeasurable Buddha-fields.
Abiding in the realm of emptiness within the signless, they act for the benefit of all sentient beings in every movement, stillness, advance, and retreat;

they skillfully traverse the realms of all Buddhas. Their wisdom is boundless like space; their samādhi is subtle and profound as the ocean; their minds are unshakable like Mount Sumeru; they are pure and unsullied like the lotus flower; their minds are brilliantly clear like mani jewels; and their hearts are as bright and pure as refined gold. Their names were:
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnaketu, Ratnapāṇi, Ratnamudrāpāṇi, and Ratna...
Makuṭabodhisattva, Ratnaśikhara Bodhisattva, Ratnamukuṭa Bodhisattva, Ratnakūṭa Bodhisattva, Ratnacūḍa Bodhisattva,
Ratnadhvaja Bodhisattva, Suvarṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Ratnagarbha Bodhisattva,
Kṣemagarbha Bodhisattva, Vyūhagarbha Bodhisattva, and Tathāgatagarbha Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Saṃkusumitarājendra, Bodhisattva Jñānagarbha, Bodhisattva Candrasūryagarbha,
Bodhisattva Samādhi-garbha, Bodhisattva Padmagarbha, Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, Bodhisattva Samantacandra, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bodhisattva Vipaśyīśvara, and Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
...the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, the Bodhisattva Lotus Eye, the Bodhisattva Vast Eye,
the Bodhisattva Universal Dignified Manner, the Bodhisattva Universally Well-Ordered, the Bodhisattva Universal Pleasing, the Bodhisattva Universal Reverence,
the Bodhisattva Wisdom-Mind, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Mind, the Bodhisattva Supreme Mind, and the Bodhisattva Exalted Mind.
Bodhisattva Vajramati, Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita, Bodhisattva Mahāmeghasvararāja,
Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda, Bodhisattva Gambhīranirghoṣa, Bodhisattva Anupalipta, Bodhisattva Vimala,
Bodhisattva Vajraprabha, Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha, Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha, and Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī.
The Bodhisattvas— Candrasena, Puṇḍarīkasena, Ratnasena, and the youth Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta;
the sixteen Mahāsattvas, with Bhadrapāla as their leader;
As well as the great bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, with Maitreya Bodhisattva as their chief;
the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, with the Four Great Kings as their chiefs;
and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, with Śakra, Lord of Devas, as its chief.
The sons of the Yāma devas were headed by Suyāma;
the gods of Tuṣita were headed by the Lord of Tuṣita;
and the gods of Nirmāṇarati were headed by the Lord of Nirmāṇarati.
The gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, headed by the Lord of Mastery;
together with all the Brahmās, they assist the Brahma Kings and the entire assembly of Brahmās, headed by the Great Brahma King;
and all the gods of the Pure Abodes, headed by Maheśvara.
Led by the asura king Vemacitra, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of such asura kings;
led by the nāga kings Anavatapta, Mānasa, Sāgara, and Vāsuki, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of such nāga kings, including the nāga king Śrītejas;
as well as various nāga maidens, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
At that time, the great assembly surrounded him.
Gayāśīrṣa Mountain was four yojanas in extent; there was not a single spot on the ground nor a void in the air that was not filled with beings, even down to the size of a subtle atom (paramāṇu).
At that time, the great assembly gathered and, gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, sat down respectfully to one side.

Among them, the precious lion throne was one yojana high, while the precious thrones in the four directions were twenty li high; they were covered with countless silken brocades, and seven-jeweled bells, various jeweled nets, and hundreds of thousands of banners and flowers were suspended above them.

The ground surrounding the high seat on all four sides transformed into vajra, composed of the seven precious gems; it delighted the hearts of the assembly, being as level as the palm of a hand, swept and sprinkled until pure and clean, with various incenses burning and immeasurable celestial flowers scattered upon it.

Countless hundreds of thousands of lotuses, as large as chariot wheels, sprang forth from the earth; they were all golden in color, with pedestals of lapis lazuli and garlands made of indranīla jewels, emitting a fragrant scent and being lovely and soft, thereby making offerings to the World-Honored One.
Not too near and not too far from the four corners of the high seat, four jewel-trees emerged spontaneously, sixty *li* in height and fifteen *li* in width at each of the four cardinal points.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne; with a mind of equanimity, he skillfully turned the wheel of Dharma and subdued the demonic enemies. Unmoved by the eight winds of the world, free from fear, dread, or any sense of timidity, he was like a lion king. He was like the waters of the Anavatapta Lake—serene, clear, and overflowing with the eight virtues; like the great ocean—profound and bottomless; like Mount Sumeru—stable and immovable; like the sun—illuminating all worlds; like the moon—bringing joy to all living beings; like the Great Dragon King—showering the rain of Dharma everywhere; and like the Great Brahma King—transcending the three realms.

Surrounded by immeasurable, well-disciplined disciples, and respectfully saluted by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Śakras, Brahmās, and Lokapālas, his mind was free from pride or dejection, and his radiance illuminated the entire assembly.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance from the crown of his head—named "Universal Illumination"—which emerged accompanied by immeasurable rays of light, shining brilliantly throughout all the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions.
Having shone forth, they were withdrawn and circled three times to the right before all entering the Tathāgata’s face.
Having thus entered, there was neither increase nor decrease, just as when ghee, oil, or water are poured into sand, there is neither increase nor decrease;
the radiance of the Tathāgata is likewise.

At that time, to the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, there was a world named Lotus Flower. In it dwelt a Buddha named Lotus-Eye Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who was currently expounding the essentials of the Dharma for a multitude of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—namely, the single path of the Mahāyāna.

Within that Buddha-field, there are no names for the two vehicles of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; rather, all sentient beings in that world are at the stages of bodhisattvas, never regressing from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In that Buddha-world there are no other mixed foods; all bodhisattvas take only the savor of dhyāna as their food and drink, and only the joy of wholesome dharmas as their food and drink.
In this world-system, there is no longer any light from the sun, moon, or stars; it is illuminated solely by the radiance of the Tathāgata.
In this region of the world, there are no weeds, gravel, thorns, or any black mountains, and that world is as level as the palm of a hand.

Within this assembly, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin (in the language of the country of Qin, this means "The One Who Subdues All Obstacles"). If any sentient beings hear the name of this bodhisattva, they will be able to eliminate all obstacles by giving rise to a virtuous mind for even the duration of a single finger-snap.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, encountering the light emitted by the World-Honored One which shone upon his body, emerged from his dwelling and went to that Buddha. Having prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet in reverent salutation, he sat down to one side.

Likewise, immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas, touched by this light, each emerged from their respective dwellings and went to that Buddha. Having prostrated with their heads in salutation and completed their respectful homage, they withdrew and sat to one side.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground upon the lotus pedestal, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what cause and by what condition does this radiance shine everywhere, possessing various inconceivable colors, pure and stainless, bringing joy to the bodies and minds of all bodhisattvas?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva, saying: "Good son!

To the west of here, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a buddha-field named Sahā World. In it dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
If there are sentient beings who hear the name of Śākyamuni Buddha, those sentient beings shall never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This radiance is the light emitted by Śākyamuni Tathāgata; it is pure and stainless, most subtle and supreme, bringing joy to the bodies and minds of all bodhisattvas.
Having spoken these words, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason do there exist sentient beings who, upon hearing the name of Śākyamuni Buddha, do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Having asked this question, the Buddha Padmākṣa addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇavijaya,
saying: "Good son,
when Śākyamuni Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path in past lives, he had already made this vow:..."
"When I attain Buddhahood, may all sentient beings who hear my name be enabled to attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“World-Honored One!
Are all sentient beings in that world who hear the Buddha’s name necessarily non-retrogressive?
The Buddha said:
"Not so. "World-Honored One!
Do the sentient beings in that land not hear the name of Śākyamuni Buddha?"
The Buddha said: "Good son,
they all shall hear it."
“World-Honored One!
Since the sentient beings in that land are those who do not regress, in what sense are they ‘non-regressive’?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! These sentient beings have planted the causes for non-retrogression, arising through hearing the name of that Buddha.
Now, having perceived this matter, the Tathāgata declares that those sentient beings shall not retrogress; it is not merely by hearing the name that they do not retrogress.”
"Good son!
I shall now provide a parable for you in order to establish this meaning. Good son!"
Just as the seeds of a tree, whether large or small, will produce sprouts and continue to grow provided they encounter no obstacles and possess all external conditions,
so it is, O son of good family!
"In what way is this said to be the seed? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Because it is free from obstruction, it is called a seed.
The Buddha said, "So it is."
"Good son!
Upon hearing the name of the Tathāgata, one immediately plants the seed of non-retrogression; these sentient beings are then said to be non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to go to that Sahā world, desiring with joy to see Śākyamuni Buddha—the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—to draw near to him, to revere him, to pay homage to him, and to make offerings to him.”
At that time, the World-Honored One Padmanetra addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"O son of good family!
Excellent, most excellent! The time has arrived; you should know this."
Furthermore, there were immeasurable great bodhisattvas who all went to the presence of the Buddha Padmākṣa and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We also all wish to go to that Sahā world, desiring to see Śākyamuni Buddha and to draw near to, revere, respect, and make offerings to him.”
At that time, the Buddha Padmākṣa addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas:
"Sons of good family!
Go as you please; now is the very time."
Upon arriving in that world, you must remain vigilant and self-restrained; do not dwell in negligence. Why is this?

The sentient beings of that land have an abundance of greed, an abundance of hatred, and an abundance of delusion. They do not maintain the pure, holy life of a śramaṇa; they deeply delight in what is contrary to the Dharma; they are malicious, treacherous, and deceitful; they are cruel, poisonous, and coarse; they use slanderous and piercing speech, foul and perverse words that grate upon the ear, and abusive insults; they are dissolute and self-indulgent, arrogant and haughty, mocking and sycophantic; they are ugly in appearance, lazy and indolent, breaking the precepts and dull-witted; they diligently perform evil deeds and are envious, stingy, and greedy, bound by immeasurable afflictions.
"In this way, Śākyamuni Tathāgata is currently preaching the Dharma for the multitude of sentient beings in that land.
These bodhisattvas and the great assembly addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"It is most difficult, most difficult that the Tathāgata Śākyamuni should preach the Dharma for the sake of those sentient beings.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
"Good son!
For the sake of those sentient beings, Śākyamuni Tathāgata expounds the essentials of the Dharma; this is most difficult, most difficult.
Good son!"
The sentient beings in that land are so coarse and unruly that it is extremely difficult for them to give rise to even a single thought of goodness. Why is this?
In a pure world where sentient beings are themselves pure, it is not difficult to practice wholesome dharmas.

In this Sahā world, which is thus defiled and turbid, it is extremely rare for sentient beings to be able to give rise to a virtuous mind for even the duration of a finger-snap; it is extremely rare to take refuge in the Buddha, the True Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha for even the duration of a finger-snap; it is extremely rare to receive and uphold the pure precepts for even the duration of a finger-snap; it is extremely rare to give rise to a mind free from desire for even the duration of a finger-snap; and it is extremely rare to give rise to a mind of great compassion and the resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for even the duration of a finger-snap.
These bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous,
World-Honored One!”
"How rare!
Well-gone One!
At that time, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas said:
“Excellent,
World-Honored One!
We shall follow the True Dharma as you have instructed and practice according to your teachings.”
Having heard this from the Buddha, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; having completed his prostration, he departed.
He then manifested for Śākyamuni Tathāgata various articles of offering:
there were manifested jewel-trees, adorned with flowers and fruits, their features and marks perfectly complete.
There were manifested trees of *vaiḍūrya*, manifested trees of *vaidūrya* jewel, manifested trees of gold and silver, as well as wish-fulfilling trees and trees of flowers and fruits;

furthermore, there were manifested clouds of garments, clouds of ornaments, clouds of incense, clouds of garlands, clouds of parasols, and clouds of music—all such transformations combined to form a single cloud.
These bodhisattvas, together with the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, proceeded to the Sahā world.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed those bodhisattvas, saying:
"O noble ones!
"The sentient beings of this Sahā world are constantly oppressed and afflicted by manifold sufferings.
Excellent, O virtuous one!
We ought to exercise great supernormal powers for the sake of all sentient beings, using those powers to cause them to be far removed from all suffering and to experience happiness."
Those bodhisattvas replied:
“Excellent, excellent,
O worthy one!”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin manifested supernatural powers; from his body he emitted various kinds of light—cool, subtle, and wondrous, free from all defilement, bringing joy to both body and mind—which illuminated the entire trichiliocosm with its radiance.

Within this realm, all those in the various hells, as well as the classes of animals, hungry ghosts, and King Yama, upon encountering this light, were all freed from their manifold sufferings and experienced great joy; they no longer harbored thoughts of killing one another, nor thoughts of resentment, nor thoughts of malice, but instead treated each other with mutual respect, regarding one another as parents.

In the midst of the trichiliocosm, in places where there is no light—where the radiance of the sun and moon, nor the power of the divine paths and spiritual penetrations can reach—the light of this bodhisattva illuminates them all, so that the sentient beings therein are able to see one another.

Furthermore, all the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mucilinda mountains, the Mahāmucilinda mountains, and other immeasurable Black Mountains within the trichiliocosm are illuminated and made manifest by the light of the Bodhisattva.

Above, reaching all the Brahma heavens up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and below, reaching down to the hells—namely the Reviving Hell, the Black Rope Hell, the Crushing Hell, the Howling Hell, the Great Howling Hell, the Burning Hell, the Great Burning Hell, and the Avīci Hell—including the one hundred and thirty-six great earth hells and the various cold ice hells, which have no fixed location and where the light of the sun cannot reach—upon encountering this radiance, they all obtain happiness and their various sufferings are stilled.

By means of these supernormal powers, there are sentient beings who, seeking food, obtain food; seeking drink, obtain drink; and they obtain clothing, vehicles, wealth, silks, gold, silver, and precious jewels according to their thoughts. Those without eyes obtain eyes; the deaf obtain hearing; the mute are able to speak; those who have lost their minds or are deranged regain right mindfulness; the suffering obtain happiness; and pregnant women give birth in peace and security, free from pain and distress.
At that time, the assembly of all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas went to Mount Gayāśīrṣa; these great beings were not far from the mountain.
This trichiliocosm was completely covered above by nets of the seven precious jewels, and great lotus flowers rained down from the midst of space.

Clouds of celestial flowers, clouds of fruits, clouds of garlands, clouds of incense, clouds of robes, clouds of various scattered perfumes, and clouds of diverse silks, banners, and parasols—all appeared spontaneously in the air; all sentient beings who were touched by these clouds and rains attained happiness.

On Mount Gayāśīrṣa, all defiled trees no longer appeared; the entire realm of earth became utterly pure, filled only with jewel-trees, wish-fulfilling trees, flower-trees, fruit-trees, sandalwood trees, and aloeswood trees.
Immeasurable celestial maidens performed divine music in the void to make offerings to the Buddha, and through this music, they uttered these verses to sing the praises of the Buddha’s virtues:
“Born in the groves and gardens, you are a marvel in the world;
Pure, unstained, and peerless— We have come to this land because we wish to pay homage to him whose marks are equal to space.”
Having attained perfect enlightenment beneath the tree of the Way, you shattered all the hosts of Māra’s enemies;
we have come to this land to pay homage to you, who possess peerless and majestic spiritual power.
Turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma amidst the assembly, you preach the Dharma as being like an illusion or the moon reflected in water.
We pray to worship the subtle and wondrous wish-fulfilling tree; for this reason, we have come to this land.

Having realized that the world is like a dream, and that its various forms and appearances are like a whirling firebrand, we pray to worship the Immovable One, the mass of merit and wisdom; for this reason, we have come to this land.

Having practiced the two accumulations for immeasurable eons, And having perfected merit and wisdom through great compassion, We pray to bow before your face, pure as the full moon; It is for our sake that we have come to this land.
Immeasurable hosts of humans, devas, and bodhisattvas Pay their respects, make offerings, and prostrate in worship.
We have come to this land to pay homage to the one who dispels darkness beyond the light of the sun;
To the one who, through austerities over countless eons, attained the treasure of the Dharma, And out of compassion, bestows it upon all beings without stinting;
To the one who benefits both self and others, we have come to this land to pay homage.
With a mind pure, tranquil, and perfumed by compassion, Unstained by worldly afflictions like a lotus flower,
We come to this land to pay homage to the one who is a mass of immeasurable merit;
The unconditioned nature of reality is neither born nor extinguished, Yet through the power of spiritual penetration, it manifests the three marks.
We have come to this land to pay homage to the Sovereign of Inconceivable Virtue;
To him whose body is adorned with distinct marks and signs, The protector of the world, the one to whom all look up for refuge.
We pray to pay homage to the jewel tree with its infinite branches; We have each brought offerings to present.

At that time, not long after the verses had been uttered, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and having paid homage with reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"By whom were these auspicious signs produced now?
They have never existed before, nor have they ever been seen or heard of.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the Elder Maudgalyāyana, saying:
“Maudgalyāyana!

To the east, passing from here through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a world named Puṇḍarīka (Lotus Flower). Therein dwells a Buddha named Puṇḍarīkākṣa (Lotus Eye) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently exists and is correctly preaching the essentials of the Dharma.”

From that buddha-field, the Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇavijaya, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great beings, came to this Sahā world to manifest these auspicious signs.

Not long after the Buddha had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, together with hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, arrived at the place where the Buddha was by means of great supernormal powers. Together with those great beings, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet in respectful salutation. Having circumambulated him a thousand times, they all stood before the Buddha and simultaneously praised the Buddha in unison with these verses:
“O Greatly Famous One!”
O Great Hero! O Great Wisdom!
O Great Sage and Honored One!
Having transcended all perils, you take refuge in those who have crossed to the other shore.
With light that shines everywhere, you fully know the nature of all sentient beings;
universally compassionate and universally rescuing, I pay homage to the Most Supreme Honored One.
Immovable like Mount Sumeru, as deep and bottomless as the ocean, you subdue the hosts of non-Buddhists;
I bow my head in homage to the Dharma King.
Primordially free from arising and ceasing, the essence of the dharma-nature is spontaneous.
Lion’s Roar among the Assembly, I pay homage to the One who Turns the Wheel of Dharma;
at times he expounds the Right Path, at times he leads others to realize True Suchness,
at times he causes them to enter Nirvana, and at times he bestows individual prophecies of enlightenment.
Thoroughly realizing the nature of the three aggregates, you understand all times and circumstances without exception;
for all sentient beings to be converted, the net of Dharma is fulfilled according to their wishes.
The stains of lust, anger, and delusion, as well as other immeasurable afflictions—
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he consumed [all defilements] with the fire of wisdom.
Having crossed over himself, he delivers others; having liberated himself, he liberates the world.
For those long lost in the perils of the three realms of existence, only the Buddha can rescue and extricate them.
The long prison of the three realms of existence, where the masses sleep in the deep slumber of ignorance—now the lamp of Dharma has awakened them; I prostrate to the Kinsman of all beings.
Such bodhisattvas as these are all born through transformation by the Buddha.
“We pray that we may joyfully hear the True Dharma; may the World-Honored One expound it for us.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, together with the other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, having finished praising the Buddha with these verses, the World-Honored One, out of compassion, granted them permission to return to their seats. They all sat upon the lotus pedestals. Then, rising from their seats as was appropriate, they bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees upon the lotus pedestals, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I now wish to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding a small portion of his various states.
I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will answer my question as it has been asked.
After he had spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"Great Being, ask whatever you wish; the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, always grants permission to listen."
"Ask whatever you wish, and the Tathāgata shall explain it to you in detail.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇavijaya, having received the Buddha’s permission, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the dānapāramitā?
How does he fulfill the śīlapāramitā?
How does he fulfill the kṣāntipāramitā?
How does one fulfill the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā)?
How does one fulfill the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā)?
How does one fulfill the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā)?
How does one fulfill the *auṣadha-kauśalya-pāramitā*?
How does one fulfill the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā*?
How does one fulfill the *bala-pāramitā*?
"How does one fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā?
World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is equal to the earth?"
How is it that a bodhisattva is equal to water?
How is it that a bodhisattva is equal to fire?
How is it that a bodhisattva is equal to wind?
"How is it that a bodhisattva is equal to space?
World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva is like the moon and like the sun?"

“Good son! How does a bodhisattva fulfill the gift of Dharma? Good son!”

The Bodhisattva upholds the True Dharma with a mind free from expectation, not for the sake of gain or profit, nor for the sake of acquaintances, nor for the sake of various causes such as fame; rather, it is solely because he desires to extinguish the causes and conditions of the intense suffering of all sentient beings that he preaches the Dharma to them with a mind of non-attachment, being consistently impartial and free from dualistic thought.

Just as he preaches the Dharma in the presence of kings, princes, court ministers, and the wealthy and noble, so too does he preach the Dharma with equal impartiality toward *caṇḍālas* and those of low birth—because he is free from dualistic thought—let alone toward all sentient beings throughout the cities and towns of the myriad people.
Teaching the Dharma in this way, one does not give rise to arrogance.

“Good son! How does a bodhisattva fulfill the perfection of the gift of fearlessness? Good son!”

The Bodhisattva personally discards all weapons and does not cause any sentient beings to feel fear; he transmits and exhorts others through the Dharma he practices, regarding all sentient beings as his parents, his kinsmen and wives, and his spiritual friends.
Why is this? As the Buddha has taught:

"In birth after birth, the cycle of transmigration is beginningless; there is not a single sentient being who has not been your parents, relatives, wives, children, or friends in the past—even down to the smallest crawling creatures among all beings of the four modes of birth. "Good son! In this way, a bodhisattva is fully endowed with the gift of fearlessness. Good son!"

He provided all manner of requisites for life—clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and even warm or cold water—and in this way made offerings to the Saṃgha.

The Bodhisattva is intimate with the fourfold assembly and all the people of the nation; when such persons offer him gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, jade, and various other precious objects, the Bodhisattva alone does not give rise to greed.

Thus, the bodhisattva observes with a sense of shame and remorse:

Whatever mental karma is unwholesome—namely, greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth—is entirely abandoned; this is called the purity of the bodhisattva’s mental karma.
This is called the pure precepts of the three wheels.

“What is the bodhisattva’s perfection of external patience?

"What is the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*)?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva encounters the profound sūtras and teachings spoken by the Tathāgatas, they sever all doubts regarding the difficult-to-penetrate intentions of the Buddhas’ realm—namely, that all phenomena are primordially quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing, and by nature in *nirvāṇa*. Upon hearing such a teaching, they are not terrified, not afraid, not startled, and not intimidated; they then engage in this progressive reflection:
'Is there perhaps even a single person who, without hearing such a profound and subtle sublime Dharma of the Tathāgata, has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? "

For these reasons, one should with a sincere mind receive, uphold, recite, study, observe, and practice this true Dharma; this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).

Thus he observes, seeing no cause for anger, seeing no place of its arising, and seeing no source. For these reasons, he immediately endures it and does not give rise to afflictions; this is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of patience as certified by the Buddha.
“What is the perfection of patience that is without spatial limitation?

It is when a bodhisattva does not practice patience by day but not at night, nor practices patience at night but not by day; does not practice patience in this country but not in that country, nor practices patience in that country but not in this country; and does not practice patience toward those who are not acquaintances while practicing patience toward acquaintances, nor practices patience toward those who are not acquaintances while not practicing patience toward acquaintances.”

The Bodhisattva is not like that; at all times and in every place, they are entirely composed and able to endure everything. This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience that is without spatial limitation.

It is not the case that a bodhisattva practices forbearance only toward parents, elders, wives, children, and all kinsmen, while being unable to endure others; it is not so for the bodhisattva."

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva possesses endurance that is free from partiality toward kin or strangers; regardless of whether one is noble or lowly, even including a candāla, he endures them with an impartial mind. This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of impartial patience.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s fulfillment of patience that does not perceive objects?
A bodhisattva practices patience not because of external circumstances, not for the sake of fame, not for the sake of worldly renown, and not out of a sense of shame or dread of blame."
Wherever a bodhisattva constantly cultivates patience, this is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of patience that does not perceive objects.
What is the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of unshakable patience?
When a bodhisattva practices patience for a time before anger has even arisen, in order that evil does not occur, this is not called "patience.

However, if they encounter adverse conditions—whether by being struck with the hand, or with a blade or weapon, or being beaten, or killed, or being reviled with harsh words—the bodhisattva endures them all; this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of unshakable patience.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being fully endowed with compassion and patience?

If a bodhisattva becomes a king, a prince, a court minister, or a person of great wealth and power, possessing abundant treasures and sovereign authority, even if he is subjected to verbal abuse, disparagement, slander, or various forms of contempt and deception, he endures them all. He does not become angry, harbor resentment, or flaunt his wealth and status, but instead reflects:
‘These sentient beings are all those whom I must support and protect; therefore, I must not increase my anger toward those I am charged to protect and abandon them.’”

By these causes and conditions, one gives rise to great compassion and is able to endure it without conceiving anger or resentment; this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of compassionate patience.
“What is the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the vow of patience?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:
‘Before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, I utter this lion’s roar:’”

"I shall practice for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; seeing all sentient beings sinking in birth and death, submerged in the deep mire, I should rescue them and cause them to attain liberation."
Therefore, I must not now give rise to anger or resentment toward the many beings I am to deliver, nor harbor a heart of malice or impatience.
If I am not patient myself, I cannot even cross over; how much less can I ferry others across?
"Good son! It is like a king of physicians who, seeing various blind people, thinks to himself:
'I shall now, for the sake of such people as these, remove all darkness and cataracts from their eyes, as well as their various obstructing films.'"
"Although he thinks this, the physician is himself originally blind and ignorant.
Son of good family,
what do you think?"
"Can such a physician remove the cataracts from the eyes of sentient beings? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Good son!”
In this way, if a bodhisattva lacks the eye of wisdom themselves within this world of those born blind due to ignorance, how could they remove the ignorance of the world?
If one cannot even treat the cataracts of one's own eyes, how could one possibly treat others?
For this reason, a bodhisattva who wishes to eliminate the darkness of ignorance for all sentient beings should first personally eliminate all dark obstructions and only thereafter do so for others.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should endure this and not give rise to anger or resentment.
In this way, the bodhisattva vows for themselves to be fully endowed with patience. "Good son!
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s fulfillment of the ten dharmas, whereby the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is perfected.
*Mahāyāna-ratnamegha-sūtra*, Scroll One.
*Mahāyāna-ratnamegha-sūtra*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Mandarava of Funan during the Liang Dynasty, together with Saṃghavarman and others.
Chapter on the Ten Pāramitās, Part Two:
"O Son of Good Family!..."
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, their *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of vigor) is fulfilled.

What are these ten? First, indestructible adamantine vigor; second, courageous vigor; third, vigor free from the two extremes; fourth, expansive vigor; fifth, refined vigor; sixth, unceasing vigor; seventh, pure vigor; eighth, incomparable vigor; ninth, vigor free from contempt; and tenth, non-exhortatory vigor.
“Good son! How is it that the bodhisattva’s diligence is indestructible, like a vajra?

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva exerts courageous diligence and makes great vows for the sake of all sentient beings: to cause those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa; to cause those who have not been delivered to be delivered; to cause those who are not liberated to be liberated; to cause those who are not established in peace to be established in peace; and to cause those who have not awakened to attain awakening.”
When he thus courageously exercises such a vast mind, Māra Pāpīyān immediately goes to where this bodhisattva is and admonishes him, saying:
"O son of good family!
There is no need for such diligent effort and vigor. Why is this?
O son of good family!
"In the past, I was indeed as courageous as this, and I also made great vows for the sake of sentient beings, vowing that those who had not yet attained nirvana would do so.
Such vows were all false speech; they deceived the infants and ordinary worldlings of the world and possessed no reality."
"Good son!
I have never seen a single person who, through such diligence and the making of great vows, has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by the power of those vows."
"Good son!
I have only seen immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who, with such diligence, enter parinirvāṇa by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle."
"For this reason, you must urgently abandon such diligence that exhausts the body and mind and brings about extreme hardship and fatigue.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought: "Alas, Pāpīyān!"
"Is he not coming here intentionally to harass and disturb me?
Does he not wish to create obstacles and hindrances to my Dharma-work?
Having discerned that it was indeed Māra, he spoke these words:
“Pāpīyan! Well said.
You who maintain yourself with few desires—why trouble yourself to take pleasure in knowing worldly affairs?”
Pāpīyan! The Tathāgata has taught that all these worlds have karma as their master; they depend upon karma and are driven by the power of conditions. Pāpīyan!
"You should restrain yourself and return by the way you came.
Because of your current act of provoking me, you shall suffer for a long night in future lives, to no avail and without benefit."

"In this way, although the hosts of Māra and the celestial subjects of Māra intentionally create obstacles and come to harass and provoke him, this bodhisattva does not break, disperse, destroy, or retreat."
In this way, a bodhisattva is fully endowed with adamantine diligence.
"Good son, what is the courageous diligence of a bodhisattva?"

By means of this diligence, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to transcend and surpass the previous practices; all other bodhisattvas cannot equal even a single fraction of this bodhisattva’s merit, such that neither calculation nor analogy can reach it, let alone the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

From the first generation of the mind of awakening, by means of the power of diligence, one upholds the entire Dharma-treasury of all Tathāgatas and thereby becomes remote from all that is unwholesome.
In this way, the bodhisattva is fully endowed with courageous diligence.
"How does a bodhisattva fulfill diligence that is free from the two extremes?
Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva exerts such courageous diligence, they do not excessively torment their own body, nor do they become inferior through indolence or laziness."
In this way, the bodhisattva is fully endowed with diligence that is free from the two extremes.
How is it that the bodhisattva is fully endowed with ever-increasing and expanding diligence?
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva exerts such diligence as follows:
Just as the body of the Tathāgata is, so too is my body;

just as no one can see the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, his halo extends a fathom, his marks and signs are extraordinary, he is endowed with immeasurable, inconceivable, and unimpeded wisdom, the merits of all Buddhas, the constant lion’s roar, the powers, and the fearlessnesses—so too am I in every respect.
Such diligence is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of expanded diligence.
"How does a Bodhisattva fulfill the refinement of diligence? Good son!

Just as with mani-jewels, gold, silver, and the like, because they have been refined and treated, their impurities are removed and they are polished until they are pure, bright, and radiant; when people see them, they exclaim in praise:
"These mani-jewels, gold, silver, and so forth have attained such brilliance because they have been refined and treated."
"In this way, when a bodhisattva practices diligence, the cleansing of all defilements and impurities is likewise.
What are the stains and impurities of diligence?"

What are called indolence and laziness are the stains of diligence; lack of contentment regarding food and drink and ignorance of one's own body are the stains of diligence—all these the Bodhisattva completely eradicates.
Such valor is then stainless and undefiled, appearing as pure, clean, and radiant.
In this way, the bodhisattva fulfills the refinement of diligence.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being endowed with tireless diligence?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly cultivates diligence within the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), never resting for even a moment at any time or place; this is called a bodhisattva being endowed with tireless diligence."
"What is the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of pure diligence?

It is that such a bodhisattva constantly cultivates diligence, ensuring that any coarse or evil dharmas, causes and conditions that obstruct the path, or unbeneficial matters are all swept away. Furthermore, all wholesome dharmas that accord with nirvāṇa, do not oppose the right path, assist in the accomplishment of bodhi, and flow toward bodhi, he causes them to grow, flourish, and expand."
"In even a single moment of thought, one does not intentionally give rise to even subtle evils, let alone great evils;
this is called being fully endowed with pure diligence. Good son."
What is the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of incomparable diligence?
A bodhisattva forms this thought:

"Suppose that throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there were the fierce fires of the Avīci hell burning; within these worlds, one sees all sentient beings without rescue, without protection, without a place of refuge, suffering in distress with no way out."

The Bodhisattva immediately gave rise to a courageous and resolute mind; alone and without companion, even for the sake of delivering but a single person, he would be able to cross through such worlds of raging fire on foot to liberate them—how much more so when it concerns many?
In this way, a bodhisattva cannot be compared to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or any of the non-Buddhists.
Thus, the bodhisattva is endowed with incomparable diligence.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being endowed with diligence free from contempt?
A bodhisattva does not think:
'Awakening is not something that can be attained by ordinary worldly people, yet the diligence I am now practicing is insufficient to mention—lowly and meager.'"
I am now indolent, yet the Dharma of Bodhi is attained through courageous diligence as if one’s head were on fire, cultivated over immeasurable eons.
If I am now unable to bear such a heavy burden, how could this Dharma of Bodhi ever be attained?
The Bodhisattva should further contemplate and reflect with careful attention:

"In the past, there were already immeasurable Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—those who have now attained perfect enlightenment and those who shall attain it—who all employed such exertions, practiced in such ways, and applied such diligence, whereby all those Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, fully realized perfect enlightenment."

Yet, my current application of such strategies and my courageous diligence cannot be compared to that of all sentient beings; likewise, it is through the conditions provided by all sentient beings that I have attained Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
Therefore, I would rather undergo the sufferings of hell for the sake of all sentient beings than seek my own benefit alone by realizing liberation and entering nirvana.
"In this way, the bodhisattva is endowed with diligence that is free from contempt.
Son of good family,
how is it that the bodhisattva is endowed with diligence that is free from contrivance?"

When a bodhisattva practices such diligence, they are not incited by others, nor do they cling to its flavor; furthermore, because of this diligent exertion, they do not incite others to wonder at them, nor do they exalt themselves, reflecting:
"What wise person would attend to their own private affairs while waiting for others to incite them?"
"This is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of diligence through indefatigability. Good son,
in this way, a bodhisattva who possesses these ten dharmas fulfills the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā)."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, the dhyāna-pāramitā is fulfilled.
What are these ten?

First, assistance through merit; second, a great sense of weary detachment; third, courageous diligence; fourth, being fully endowed with extensive learning; fifth, a mind free from inversion; sixth, acting in accordance with instructions; seventh, practicing in accordance with the Dharma; eighth, possessing naturally sharp faculties; ninth, skillfully understanding the ground of the mind; and tenth, skillfully understanding the uninterrupted intent of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s assistance through merit?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva has planted roots of virtue within the Mahāyāna Dharma; as they transmigrate through birth and death in various places, they are sustained by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), taking birth according to their vows—whether among wealthy and noble clans, or among great households of lay devotees, or families of faith and joy.”

Having already formed the intention to go there and take birth, one immediately creates the karmic causes and conditions for that rebirth, thereby attaining birth there life after life and from age to age encountering and drawing near to true spiritual friends.
Who are those called true spiritual friends?
They are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Thus increasing the causes and conditions of wholesome karma cultivated in past lives, they constantly maintain this thought:
"Alas, the world! How painful is the world! There is no secure foundation;
the entire world has long been afflicted by a grave illness, by delusion and darkness, and by ignorance."
Why is this? Because of desire as a causal condition.
Therefore, I should not now seek to receive the five desires within such a world of hardship and distress.
Sexual desire is nothing but deluded thought and perversion; within the three types of suffering, one erroneously conceives the notion of pleasure.

Therefore, in various sūtras, the Tathāgata has fully explained through manifold causes and conditions that sexual desire possesses many faults and is truly to be dreaded and loathed. That is to say, sexual desire is like the method of roasting meat, where both the flesh and the skewer are scorched together;
it is like licking a blade, greedily craving the taste at the cost of the tongue.
Like the head of a venomous snake, which possesses four kinds of poison;
like a pig in a latrine, amidst stench, filth, and impurity;
like that foolish dog who gnaws on a dry bone, its mouth bleeding while it deems this to be pleasure.
"It is also like a monkey stuck in birdlime.

"Therefore, a bodhisattva should give rise to weary detachment, shave off hair and beard, don the dharma robes, and go forth from home according to the Dharma within the True Dharma. Going to the homeless state, they should aspire to diligence, so as to attain what has not been attained, realize what has not been realized, and reach what has not been reached."

By these causes and conditions, one attains the three types of wisdom; one skillfully understands the profound and subtle principles of the two truths—the teachings of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the teachings of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Acting in accordance with such instructions, one follows them, abandons all perversions, and practices in conformity with the Dharma.
"What is called practicing in accordance with the Dharma?
It refers to right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."

"Because he has attained thorough penetration of the Truth of the Path, he has perfected his sharp faculties and understands all faculties; he thus delights in tranquility and ultimately distances himself from all crowds, commingling, and clamor, as well as from haste, much speech, lust, anger, ignorance, and all such evil thoughts. He is utterly detached from kinsmen, acquaintances, gain, and fame; his body and mind are blissful, supple, and harmonious."
Furthermore, he further reflects upon and examines this mind:
"In what phenomena does it operate—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
If it operates in the wholesome, he immediately gives rise to joy.
If one gives rise to thoughts of desire, it is called unwholesome.
There are three kinds of desire: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
What is the superior?
Because desire pervades the body and dwells deeply within the mind, one becomes deluded and frantic, unable to cultivate the causes and conditions for seclusion due to this deep attachment.
What constitutes this deep attachment?

Because they are unable to give rise to a sense of shame and remorse to the ultimate degree, even when dwelling alone in seclusion, they constantly recollect [these things] without a moment’s forgetfulness; they give rise to evil thoughts and reflections, decisively declaring that sexual desire is truly exquisite, praising it through chanting and song, and becoming deluded by false imaginings and inversions, claiming it to be a desirable thing—just like a foolish monkey who, seeing the moon in the water, desires to seize it.

Failing to perceive their own evil, they lack a sense of shame or remorse; driven by the causes and conditions of desire, they are even capable of contending with their parents and elders, even to the point of killing one another, without regard for kinship or distance.

Ordinary people are foolish and stubborn; they are addicted to and attached to craving and defilement. Because they cannot relinquish the causes and conditions of desire, after death they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts to undergo various retributive sufferings; this is called "superior desire."
What is moderate desire?

If a person practices and associates with sexual desire, seeking it through preliminary means before actual union, yet upon accomplishing the act, they immediately feel revulsion and develop a sense of shame; knowing that desire is unwholesome, they reproach themselves and repent—this is called moderate desire.
What is inferior desire?

If one happens to encounter conditions for desire, such as merely extending the hand to grasp another’s, mutual rubbing and touching, conversing together, or gazing at one another with the eyes—this is called inferior desire.
Now, as for what is called "lust": whether it be the adornment of the body, or attachment to life and various means of subsistence, anything that can give rise to craving is termed lust.
"What is called 'anger'?"
Hatred is also of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.

As for superior hatred, it gives rise to fury, malice, resentment, indignation, wickedness, and envy; through these, one is capable of committing all five of the grave offenses of immediate retribution.

Or one may slander the True Dharma; the grave offense incurred by slandering the True Dharma does not equal even a fraction of the five heinous crimes mentioned previously, such that neither calculation nor analogy can reach it.

Due to these causes and conditions, after death they enter the great hells to undergo various bitter sufferings. After a vast duration of immeasurable kalpas, they may finally escape to be born as humans; yet their eyes will be bloodshot, they will be shameless and evil-natured, violent and roaring, and they will be born into the lowly families of caṇḍālas.
Due to these causes and conditions, one wanders through birth and death without any prospect of escape; this is called "superior anger.
What is "middling anger"?

Although one gives rise to anger and commits various evil deeds, one immediately conceives a mind of regret, confesses and apologizes for the offenses born of that anger, and swiftly cultivates the methods of its antidote; this is called "middling anger."
What is minor anger?

When anger arises, one may utter harsh words, unpleasant speech, or look with an evil eye; yet, although one performs such unwholesome acts, the anger is not constant. Because one swiftly cultivates and applies counteractive methods within a single moment of thought, this is called minor anger.
“Delusion is also of three kinds: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
What is superior delusion?
Regarding the aforementioned circumstances, one is deluded by such states and remains without sorrow or regret, failing to know how to reform or repent; this is called superior delusion.”
What is middling delusion?

If delusion arises momentarily and one commits an evil deed, but quickly reforms and repents, confessing and repenting before one's fellow students without daring to conceal it, and recognizing that the committed offense is not beneficial—this is called middling delusion.
What is inferior delusion?

Regarding the precepts one upholds, if two or three instances of transgression occur—these being all *prajñapti-āpatti* (proscribed offenses)—one never dares to violate the fundamental *prakṛti-sāvadya* (natural) prohibitions; this is called inferior delusion.
"In this regard, the bodhisattva employs skillful means to subdue the mind so that it does not commit transgressions.
Thus, by subduing the mind, the causes and conditions for bondage and attachment—such as sensual desire—are no longer produced."
Why is this? Because he skillfully subdues the mind in such a manner.
If the mind is neutral (*avyākṛta*), at that time he maintains mindfulness and single-mindedly contemplates, causing the nature of the mind to correspond with the wholesome.
"What is called the indeterminate mind?

It is when there is a state of mind that does not scatter outwardly, nor abide within; it does not abide in the wholesome, nor abide in the unwholesome; it is neither in śamatha nor in vipaśyanā; it cannot be gathered and brought to tranquility, but remains submerged, oppressed by sleep."
Just as when a person awakens from sleep, their mental faculties remain unclear because the influence of drowsiness has not yet subsided,
so too at that time the Bodhisattva, through skillful means, restrains the mind, causing it to give rise to joy and abide securely within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
In this way, the bodhisattva skillfully understands the mind.

Having thus understood the mind, the bodhisattva perceives all phenomena as being like illusions and like dreams, discerning: "This phenomenon is unwholesome; this phenomenon is wholesome; this phenomenon leads to transcendence; this phenomenon does not lead to transcendence."
One should understand this as follows:

all these phenomena depend upon the mind and arise from the mind; the mind is their foremost leader. If one can collect, tame, and restrain the mind, and if one realizes the nature of the mind, then one will be able to master all phenomena, tame all phenomena, and penetrate all phenomena.
If one views all phenomena in this way, one can cultivate the mind to attain tranquility, binding the mind to the mind;
if the mind is not tranquil, one restrains it to become tranquil, settling the mind within the mind.
"If the mind is thus associated with tranquility, it is called 'one-pointedness of mind';
having attained one-pointedness of mind, one enters into meditative absorption;
having entered into meditative absorption, there arises a singular joy born of tranquility."
With a joyful mind, he extinguishes sensual desire;

with the extinction of sensual desire, all unwholesome states are likewise stilled. With directed thought and sustained evaluation, born of seclusion, he attains the joy and happiness of the first dhyāna.
At that time, the bodhisattva, in order to extinguish applied and sustained thought, practices with diligent vigor, yet does not cling to the flavor of the joy and happiness [therein]. Why is this?
Because it is impermanent.

"Practicing the first dhyāna, he shifts his mind; becoming detached from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), his mind no longer clings to them. Without applied or sustained thought, born of samādhi, he attains the joy and happiness of the second dhyāna."
At that time, the bodhisattva perceives this pleasure as being definitively suffering.
Why is this? Because it is encompassed by the three types of suffering.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva dwells in a mind of equanimity;

having dwelt in equanimity, he dwells with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing pleasure with the body. Such pleasure as this is called 'equanimity' by all the Noble Ones; mindful and dwelling in pleasure, he enters the third dhyāna."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, realizing that the third dhyāna is definitively empty, sought the fourth dhyāna and caused his mind to enter it; consequently, all views of self were completely overturned, and both pleasure and suffering were extinguished.

With the cessation of suffering and pleasure, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy, he enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

“Furthermore, when one performs this contemplative practice, one sees one’s own body and the realm of empty space as a single characteristic. Having seen thus, all perceptions of form are ultimately transcended, and perceptions of obstruction no longer arise at all.”

Why is this? Because they have already attained transcendence by surpassing perceptions of form, they are no longer subject to obstruction; regarding all perceptions, they see only unobstructed, boundless space, and thus they enter and abide in the sphere of boundless space.

"At that time, one further perceives consciousness as being in correspondence with infinite space; because one considers this consciousness to be without limit, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Having transcended this consciousness, there is therein only a mind of signlessness, wherein all formations have ceased and there is no mental activity—this is called cessation."

"A Bodhisattva should understand that when the mind has thus ceased, they should again enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), cultivating therein without rest. In this state, their mind is associated with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), as fully described previously;

continuing until they attain mastery over the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they likewise do not cease their diligent effort, but should seek to cultivate and fulfill the practices of the Dharma for enlightenment."
“Good son! In this way, when a bodhisattva possesses these ten dharmas, they are fully endowed with the perfection of dhyāna. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they are fully perfected in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

What are these ten? First, skillfully understanding the truth of non-self; second, skillfully understanding the retribution of all karmic actions; third, skillfully understanding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); fourth, skillfully understanding the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); fifth, skillfully understanding the non-continuity of birth and death; sixth, skillfully understanding the path of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha; seventh, skillfully understanding the path of the Mahāyāna; eighth, skillfully understanding the distancing from the deeds of Māra; ninth, unerring wisdom; and tenth, incomparable wisdom.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the truth of non-self? Good son!”

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by means of skillful and correct wisdom, observes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), and likewise observes feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) with skillful observation.
Observing in this way, they do not see the arising of form, do not see its accumulation, and do not see its cessation;
likewise, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they do not see their arising, do not see their accumulation, and do not see their cessation.
Why is this? Because it is based on ultimate reality (*tattva*), not on conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
These two natures—ultimate reality and the conventional—are both natures that cannot be expressed by words or phrases.
For these reasons, one should exert diligence without ceasing, as if extinguishing a fire on one's head, and with courageous diligence benefit all sentient beings.
In this way, the bodhisattva skillfully understands the truth of non-self.
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the retribution of all karmas?
A bodhisattva should observe in this way:
'The so-called various retributions that exist in the world are all like actors or a city of the gandharvas; their intrinsic nature is itself empty.'"

What are called "sentient beings" are not actually sentient beings; yet they perversely grasp at signs and cling to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Due to these causes and conditions, they do not penetrate the true principle.
Because they cannot comprehend the true reality, they form such a view:

"If it is said that there is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-span, no individual (*puruṣa*), no nourisher, and no male or female, as well as no causes for good or evil karma and no retributive fruits, then who is born and who dies?"
At that time, although there are no sentient beings, the Bodhisattva fully knows that there are actions and their retributions;

he also knows that these are neither sentient beings nor the causes of various wholesome and unwholesome actions, nor their karmic fruits and retributions—this being due to his correct wisdom and because of reality as it truly is.
In this way, the bodhisattva is skillfully proficient in understanding the causes, effects, and retributions of karma.
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should, regarding all conditioned phenomena, thoroughly penetrate them through wise insight and contemplate them in this manner:

"These phenomena of conditioned formations are restless and unstable; they are like drops of morning dew that vanish as soon as the sun rises, or like mountain streams that flow away forever without returning."
"How could a wise person give rise to craving and attachment toward the practice of the Dharma, or have their heart yearn for it?
If one can contemplate such reality, seeing the true causes and conditions will give rise to a mind of weary detachment and tranquility.
In this way, the bodhisattva skillfully understands conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
How does the bodhisattva skillfully comprehend the circulation of birth and death (*saṃsāra*)?
By means of excellent wisdom, the bodhisattva penetrates all conditioned phenomena and reflects as follows:

"All throughout the worlds, beings are shrouded and obscured by the darkness of ignorance, which obstructs their eye of wisdom; like those born blind who cannot see the correct path, by what means could they possibly attain liberation from birth and death?"

Bound and fettered by the ropes of craving and attachment to birth and death, they grasp at the four types of clinging and head toward the three realms of existence, sinking and stagnating in saṃsāra;
through the conditions of clinging, they are able to perform wholesome and unwholesome karmas;
and because of the performance of these various wholesome and unwholesome karmas, they undergo birth within the three realms of existence, which arises from the causal conditions of becoming.
Due to birth as a causal condition, there is old age and death;
due to old age and death as causal conditions, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction arise in endless variety.
Thus the cycle revolves like a chariot wheel, and this saṃsāric transmigration continues without further interruption.
"In this way, a bodhisattva skillfully understands the circulation of birth and death. Good son,
how does a bodhisattva skillfully understand birth and death so as no longer to circulate within it?"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates in this way:
"Because ignorance ceases, one does not cling to birth and death;
because there is no clinging, craving does not arise."
Because craving does not arise, grasping does not arise;
because grasping does not arise, becoming is not continued;
because it is not continued, birth does not arise.
Because birth does not arise, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and all forms of suffering and affliction are completely extinguished, leaving nothing behind.
By means of this principle, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through his excellent wisdom, fully penetrates and understands it all.
In this way, the bodhisattva thoroughly understands birth and death and no longer wanders in saṃsāra.
How does the bodhisattva thoroughly understand the vehicles of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha?
He contemplates them in this manner:

"If one practices this Dharma, one may attain the fruit of Srotāpanna, or the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, or the fruit of Anāgāmin, or become an Arhat; with the outflow of defilements exhausted and the six supernormal powers attained, all fetters of existence are severed, and being free from further bondage, one proceeds toward the path of Nirvāṇa.
Or, if one practices this Dharma, one may become a Pratyekabuddha, attaining self-deliverance and self-liberation, equal to the rhinoceros horn."
"In this way, through his excellent wisdom, the bodhisattva attains thorough penetration of all these dharmas; yet, although he thus penetrates them, he does not realize them. Why is this? "
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this thought:
"I now bear the burden of all classes of sentient beings, making a lion’s roar to vow their deliverance.
Therefore, I must not now cross the perilous wilderness and dense forest of birth and death alone, without having first delivered all sentient beings from the dangers of saṃsāra."
"In this way, a bodhisattva well understands the paths of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles.
Good son, how does a bodhisattva well understand the Mahāyāna?"
The Bodhisattva studies all the precepts and various sūtras and dharmas established by all Buddhas to their ultimate conclusion without exception.
Yet, there is no one who learns, no path to be learned, and no phenomena of any kind to be learned; it is not on account of such causes and conditions that he falls into the view of annihilationism.
In this way, the bodhisattva well understands the correct path of the Mahāyāna. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva well understand the distancing of the works of Māra?"
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva remains ultimately distant from evil associates;

likewise, having recognized that he must remain far removed from and ultimately avoid unsuitable lands and villages, the memorization and recitation of worldly non-Buddhist texts and incantations, and the greedy pursuit of gain and offerings with earnest reverence, he does so.

Furthermore, he remains entirely distant from all fetters, bonds, afflictions, and delusions that can obstruct the pure path of a bodhisattva, cultivating the gates of remedial practice to ultimately sever them.
In this way, the bodhisattva skillfully knows how to remain far removed from the deeds of Māra. "Good son,
how is it that the wisdom of a bodhisattva is non-erroneous?"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas learn and master all the arts, crafts, and esoteric techniques of the world. Why is this?

It is because they desire to accomplish the benefit of sentient beings; it is not for the sake of seeking personal renown, but solely to glorify and manifest the supreme merit of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.
Regarding external dharmas, one does not give rise to the notion that they possess superior merit, but understands only this:
"The Tathāgata’s scriptural teachings are the most profound and ultimate; the merits of the various Vinaya rules are immeasurable."
Therefore, a bodhisattva does not adopt the rules of external paths or false views as a means of purification.
In this way, the wisdom of a bodhisattva is non-erroneous.
“Good son! What is the incomparable wisdom of a bodhisattva?

In this world, whether among Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, or devas—throughout all the ten directions—there is not a single person who is equal to the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
There is no wisdom capable of surpassing it—whether that of devas, Brahmā, humans, or Māras; among all the wisdoms existing in the entire world, none can equal it.
In this way, the wisdom of a bodhisattva is incomparable. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, the perfection of prajñāpāramitā is fulfilled."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they are well-versed in the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā).
What are these ten?

First, skillfully understanding the expedient means of dedicating merit to fulfill vows; second, skillfully understanding the expedient means of converting all non-Buddhists; third, skillfully understanding the expedient means of transforming the poisons of sensory dust; fourth, skillfully understanding the expedient means of subduing doubt and regret; fifth, skillfully understanding the expedient means of rescuing and delivering sentient beings; sixth, skillfully understanding the expedient means of prolonging the lives of sentient beings; seventh, skillfully understanding the expedient means of gathering and sustaining others; eighth, skillfully understanding the expedient means of discerning what is possible and what is impossible; ninth, skillfully understanding the expedient means of exhorting, transforming, benefiting, gladdening, instructing, and guiding; tenth, skillfully understanding the expedient means of making offerings and serving others.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the expedient means of dedicating merit to fulfill vows? Good son!”

If a bodhisattva sees flowers or fruits that have no owner and are not protected by non-human beings, he offers these flowers and fruits to the Buddhas and the various bodhisattvas during the three periods of the night and the three periods of the day. By this causal condition, he dedicates the merit obtained toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If he sees incense trees, jewel trees, or wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) that have no owner and are not protected by non-human beings, he makes offerings to them during the six periods of the day and night, dedicating [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, regarding the various kinds of sublime and extraordinary offerings heard of in the various sūtras, one should, with a profound inner mind, dedicate them all to the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, all Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
All wholesome deeds and practices for awakening, through the power of the profound resolve, he rejoices in them all and dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When making offerings of flowers or fruits at a Buddha-stūpa or an image, one should dedicate them all, vowing that all sentient beings may be free from the foul and stinking odors of broken precepts, and that all sentient beings may obtain the fragrant scents of the Tathāgata’s morality, concentration, and wisdom.
When sweeping and sprinkling water as an offering to the Buddha, one vows that all sentient beings may attain upright appearance and be fully endowed with dignified deportment.
When setting up banners and canopies as offerings to the Triple Gem, one dedicates them all, so that all sentient beings may be far removed from afflictions and all their burning fevers.
If entering a temple, may all sentient beings enter the temple of nirvana;
if exiting a temple, may all sentient beings escape the prison of the hardships of birth and death;
if opening doors, may all sentient beings open the gates to the wholesome paths.
When closing a door, may I vow that the gates to the evil realms be entirely sealed shut;
when sitting to rest, may I vow that all sentient beings sit upon the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
when bathing, may I vow that all sentient beings be freed from the defilements of affliction.
When receiving water, may all sentient beings be freed from all foulness and impurity;
when washing the feet, may all sentient beings be freed from the hindrance of afflictions;
when using a tooth-stick, may all sentient beings eliminate all that is unclean.
In going out, coming in, moving, or staying still, may this body of mine serve solely to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings of the six realms;
when prostrating to the Buddha, may all sentient beings swiftly attain the Buddha-body and be venerated by all humans and devas.
In this way, the bodhisattva is skilled in the dedication that fulfills all vows.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the expedient means for converting non-Buddhists?"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly manifests as a Daoist, a Brahmin, or a Nirgrantha among the various non-Buddhist teachings in order to bring sentient beings to maturity through skillful means. He approaches them to study their scriptures and doctrines, thinking:
"These sentient beings are full of arrogance; if I were to act as a Dharma teacher, they would not believe or accept my teachings."

For this reason, having previously been a disciple and scholar among the non-Buddhists, he shall leave the household life within their ranks; through his diligent vigor and subtle, meticulous deportment, he will surely cause them to be surpassed by his followers.

By virtue of extensive learning and through the practice of asceticism, one is then able to become a Dharma teacher among the non-Buddhists, becoming worthy of honor and respect, possessing effective speech, and endowed with perfect eloquence.
Once he knew they had gained faith, he then disparaged their path and pointed out its faults:
"O virtuous ones!
The path you study is not for the sake of purity, nor for the sake of detachment from desire, nor for the sake of renunciation; it cannot extinguish the hindrances."
Having turned them back from those false paths, he established them in the Buddha’s true Dharma, causing them to observe the holy life as five-attainment seers:
"Cultivate this holy life with courageous diligence, and you will surely be able to master the magical arts of the non-Buddhists."

Thus, through such heroic accomplishment of samādhi and samāpatti, he will certainly surpass all non-Buddhists and the five-attainment rishis, acting as a great Dharma teacher for those sages and becoming an object of veneration for the world.

Knowing that the time for their maturation had come, he disparaged these various teachings of the non-Buddhists, manifesting their faults and turning them away from their meditative concentrations, saying:
"O virtuous ones!..."
"This path does not lead to purification, nor to disenchantment, nor can it extinguish all hindrances.
Having thus turned them away from such teachings, he established them in the True Dharma of the Buddha.
In this way, a bodhisattva skillfully understands the expedient means for converting non-Buddhists. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva convert poisonous dust?"

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see sentient beings who are deeply attached to sensual desire, they merely cause those causes and conditions for greed to be extinguished by employing such skillful means: they manifest illusory female forms with upright features and endowed with the marks and signs of excellence, surpassing all other women.
When sentient beings see this, they give rise to profound greed, craving, and attachment.

While they are enjoying the pleasure of sleep and rest, they suddenly die; in the space of a single thought-moment, their bodies become putrid and rotten, loathsome and impure. Upon seeing them, they feel terror and give rise to great revulsion, becoming frantic and distressed, thinking:
"This is foul and filthy; who can remove it?"
