At that time, the Bodhisattva stood in attendance before him and immediately preached the Dharma for him, causing him to attain certainty and enter the stage of right determination, whereby he attained one of the three types of enlightenment.
In this way, a bodhisattva is skillfully adept in the expedient means for transforming poisonous defilements. "Good son,
how is it that a bodhisattva is skillfully adept in the expedient means for severing doubt and regret?"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees sentient beings committing the five heinous crimes and other various unwholesome karmic offenses, the bodhisattva approaches them and says:
"O worthy ones!..."
"Why are you so distressed and ill at ease?
Your mind has no peace or reliance; you are like one who lacks a spirit.
He replied:
“Good son! Because I have committed various karmas of immediate retribution, by reason of these causes and conditions, I have now lost my mind and am filled with fear, finding no peace.
Due to these sins, I shall undergo various sufferings and all manner of non-beneficial states in future lives.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva first causes them to believe and accept [the teaching] through these causes and conditions; he may employ supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or read their minds.

Those who witness the supernatural powers, having gained faith, experience great joy in the presence of the Bodhisattva, give rise to a mind of faith and understanding, and become capable of receiving the Dharma teachings.
Having thus gained faith, the Bodhisattva then manifests a transformation before that person, creating the forms of his parents, and speaks these words:
"O worthy one, do you see?"
"My own parents have also been slain.
Having killed his parents, he again manifested supernatural powers to appear before that person, causing him to rejoice:
"If even a person such as this, who possesses great supernatural powers, can still kill his own parents, how much more so could I?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva expounds the essentials of the Dharma for these sentient beings, causing their karmic offenses to become progressively lighter and more subtle, as thin as the wings of a fly.
In this way, the Bodhisattva employs skillful means to eliminate doubt and regret.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means for effectively rescuing and liberating sentient beings?

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees sentient beings who are capable of hearing the true Dharma yet are committing evil deeds, for the sake of teaching and transforming them, the bodhisattva then skillfully manifests supernormal powers (ṛddhi):”
If those who should be delivered by means of a king’s body, he manifests a king’s body;
if those who should be delivered by means of a minister’s body, he manifests a minister’s body;
and if those who should be delivered by means of the bodies of the wealthy, the subjects, or the kṣatriyas, he manifests those very forms.
If there are those who should be delivered by means of a celestial body, he manifests a celestial body;
if there are sentient beings who should be delivered through gentle speech, he employs gentle speech to teach and transform them;
if there are those who should be delivered by means of a vajra body, he manifests a vajra body.
If there are sentient beings who should be delivered through fear, he immediately manifests fear;
if there are those who should be delivered by being struck, scolded, reviled, or bound, he immediately manifests these things.

If there are sentient beings who wish to commit acts of rebellion, or who strike, beat, harm, or afflict others, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees such people, he immediately gives rise to compassion and thinks:
"These sentient beings wish to come and afflict me."
Seeing these sentient beings as clearly as one would observe an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of one's hand, he gives rise to great sorrow and distress, and thinks:
"I would rather this body of mine undergo the great suffering of the Avīci Hell than cause these sentient beings to immediately enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and attain liberation."

Seeing these sentient beings committing various sinful deeds, and knowing that by reason of these causes and conditions they will surely undergo the retribution of suffering in the Avīci Hell after casting off their present bodies, the Bodhisattva then gives rise to a heart of compassion. Out of loving-kindness and pity, he keeps those sentient beings in mind; for the sake of administering punishment and subduing them, he subsequently instructs them in repentance.
In this way, the bodhisattva employs skillful means to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the means for extending the lifespan of sentient beings?"

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees sentient beings who do not receive offerings or sustenance, who lack power, who are unable to understand the sublime Dharma of the noble ones, and who, despite seeking food and drink, cannot even maintain their bodies or speech—then at that time, the bodhisattva shall instruct such persons in literature, arts and crafts, mathematics, and various technical skills, so that those who are capable may thereby gain their livelihood.
In this way, a bodhisattva is skillfully proficient in the expedient means of extending the lifespan of sentient beings.
"Good son, how is it that a bodhisattva is skillfully proficient in the expedient means of gathering and sustaining [sentient beings]?"

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva obtains various heaps of precious jewels as high as Mount Sumeru, they accept them all; likewise, they accept even those that are subtle and minute according to their suitability.
Why is this so? At that time, the Bodhisattva reflects: "These sentient beings are stingy, greedy, and parsimonious;

they are addicted to their attachments without satiety, guarding them firmly and grasping them tightly. Due to the causes and conditions of such stinginess and greed, they wander and sink into the great ocean of birth and death."
"Just as all rivers and streams flow together into the great ocean, so too it is with these sentient beings who fall into the three evil realms.

For the sake of the benefit and peace of such beings, the Bodhisattva accepts what is offered not for his own profit, nor to satisfy himself, but receives and stores it without giving rise to greed. He does so solely for the benefit of all sentient beings so that they may share in its use; solely to make offerings to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; and solely to rescue and relieve destitute beings, thereby causing the donor to attain joy and benefit.
In this way, the bodhisattva masters skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the means regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*)?"

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees sentient beings who possess great power and are capable of accomplishing anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet who practice various conducts while seeking the paths of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas with courageous diligence;

At that time, the Bodhisattva employs skillful means from such a place to cause them to abandon [their attachments], demonstrating the Mahāyāna path so that they may practice it; or, if they do not believe or accept it, he even manifests great conflict and strife to bring them into subjection.
In this way, the bodhisattva develops skillful means through the correct understanding of what is possible and what is impossible.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva develop skillful means for exhorting, transforming, benefiting, and gladdening others?"

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cause those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta to generate that resolve; when they exhort those who have already generated the resolve but are indolent and lazy to practice diligence; when they cause those who do not observe the precepts to uphold them; and when they employ skillful means to inspire those who are content with minor virtues so that they may be endowed with all wholesome qualities;

or when they see sentient beings who, having transgressed the precepts, are capable of repentance—on account of these circumstances, they restrain their minds and remain therein, feeling neither joy nor delight.
At that time, the Bodhisattva extensively expounds the essential Dharma for these sentient beings, enabling them to perform repentance and extinguish such offenses.
In this way, the Bodhisattva exhorts, transforms, benefits, and gladdens others through skillful means.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the expedient means of making offerings and serving?

After a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has gone forth into homelessness, even if no one makes offerings to him, he remains content with whatever he obtains in accordance with the Dharma as circumstances allow; dwelling alone in a secluded place in tranquility, he reflects thus:”
"How may I now obtain the means to make offerings to and serve the Tathāgata?

Thinking thus, he maintained this contemplation without interruption, his mind constantly reflecting upon various articles of offering, vowing to make offerings to and serve the Triple Gem; by this, he is able to fulfill the practice of the six pāramitās:
in a single thought-moment, he directs a mind of offering and relinquishes what is most cherished—this is the dāna-pāramitā.
To cultivate the mind of making offerings by directing it toward all sentient beings is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā);
to abide in peace and happiness within this mind is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā);
and to be free from weariness within this mind is the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
In this state, when the mind is neither distracted nor moved, this is the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā);
in this state, when the mind contemplates various articles of offering, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this way, the bodhisattva makes offerings and serves with skillful mastery of means. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten skillful masteries of the perfection of making offerings, they are fully perfected."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they fulfill the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*). What are these ten?

First, the vow that is not inferior; second, the vow that is not timid; third, the vow to deliver, liberate, and benefit all sentient beings; fourth, the vow to praise the merits of all Buddhas; fifth, the vow to subdue all Māras and adversaries; sixth, the vow that does not depend on others for faith; seventh, the boundless vow; eighth, the vow free from fear; ninth, the vow free from weariness; tenth, the vow that is ultimately perfect and pure.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s vow that is not inferior?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take delight in receiving the pleasures of the three realms of existence when making a vow, this is called the bodhisattva’s vow that is not inferior.”
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s vow free from timidity?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes a great vow, he does not seek to escape the triple world by withdrawing from it to realize [nirvana] for himself; this is called the bodhisattva’s vow free from timidity.”
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s vow to rescue, protect, benefit, and bring happiness to all sentient beings?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes this vow:”

"May I first cause all realms of sentient beings, throughout the limits of the future, to attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder; only then shall I myself enter *parinirvāṇa* following the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*."
This is called the bodhisattva’s vow to rescue, benefit, and bring welfare to all sentient beings. "Good son,
what is the bodhisattva’s vow to praise the merits of all Buddhas?
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva makes this vow:

"If there are sentient beings who have not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta, may I teach and transform them so that they resolve to do so; for those who have already resolved their minds, may I lead them step by step to practice the various Bodhisattva deeds; and for those who have already practiced, may I cause them to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). I shall provide offerings and entreat them to turn the wheel of Dharma, and entreat them to remain in the world to benefit sentient beings, and not enter parinirvāṇa."
This is called the bodhisattva’s vow to praise the merits of all buddhas. "Good son,
what is the bodhisattva’s vow to subdue all māras and enemies?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva makes this vow:

"I shall now perform such deeds as these; once I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, in my buddha-field the very name of Māra shall not be heard, and none of Māra’s subjects shall be born in my land."
"This is called the bodhisattva’s vow to subdue all māras and adversaries.
'Good son, what is the bodhisattva’s vow that does not depend on the faith of others?'"
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not rely on others, he vows to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
It is because, by means of wisdom, he reflects as follows:

"Seeing that these realms of sentient beings are mired in the suffering of birth and death, without rescue or protection," one makes the vow for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of providing rescue and protection; this is called the bodhisattva’s vow that does not depend on the faith of others.
“Good son! What is the boundless vow of a bodhisattva?
A bodhisattva makes vows without limit, and their practice is free from attachment.”

Therefore, the Bodhisattva bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with a sincere mind made this exhortation: he beheld all worlds throughout the ten directions, seeing bodhisattvas seated at the site of enlightenment and bodhisattvas attaining perfect awakening within the realms of the ten directions; he requested them to turn the wheel of Dharma, and he recollected well their skillful adaptation to the differing faculties and natures of sentient beings.

To have faith and understanding in all the essential teachings spoken by the Buddhas, to rejoice in them with such faith and understanding, and having rejoiced, to dedicate this toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—this is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of boundless vows.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s vow of fearlessness?

From the first generation of the mind of awakening, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears that the various Buddha-dharmas are exceedingly profound, hears that the merits of the Buddhas are exceedingly profound, hears that the playful manifestations of the supernatural powers of the bodhisattvas are exceedingly profound, and hears that the skillful means of the bodhisattvas are exceedingly profound, he is not terrified, not afraid, not fearful, and not startled; rather, he forms this thought:”

"The enlightenment of all Buddhas is immeasurable and boundless; the realm of all Buddhas is immeasurable and boundless; the maturation of sentient beings is immeasurable and boundless. How could those such as ourselves ever be able to conceive of or calculate the realm of the Tathāgata?"
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, can know this for themselves, whereas I cannot.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the vow free from fear.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s vow of tirelessness?

If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who are stubborn and difficult to tame or subdue, who are negligent and self-indulgent, and who are unwilling to receive transformation—these are what such bodhisattvas find wearying and distressing. Yet, they do not abandon them.”

Regarding those who are thus stubborn, difficult to tame, and difficult to transform—those whom one grows weary of—for these reasons, one becomes fatigued and turns away from them, vowing instead to be reborn in the pure lands of the Buddhas within the world-systems of purity.
In this Pure Land, there are no such stubborn and unruly sentient beings, nor even the mention of their names; bodhisattvas do not wish to hear these names, much less behold them face to face.

If there are bodhisattvas who turn their backs on sentient beings, they will likewise be unable to attain birth in the pure lands of the Buddhas. Among them, the wise bodhisattvas conceive this thought:

"May all those sentient beings in every world who are stubborn, dull-witted, dark and obtuse, deaf, blind, mute, or speech-impaired—those who lack the nature for *nirvāṇa* and are abandoned by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of those worlds—may they all come to gather within the Buddha-land adorned by me."
May there be no such sentient beings left behind; I shall cause them all to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and sit at the site of enlightenment to realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reflects in this way, from the moment of first generating the mind of awakening, no realm of Māra remains unmoved; he is praised by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions. Furthermore, the Buddha-land adorned by this Bodhisattva is swiftly accomplished as ultimately pure, and he realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This is called the "vow of tirelessness" of a Bodhisattva.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva excellently fulfill his vows to the ultimate degree?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment and crushes the armies of Māra, and thereafter, upon attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, no longer form further vows—this is called attaining the fulfillment of the vow for enlightenment exactly as it was vowed.”
It is like a vessel filled to the brim with clarified butter; it cannot accommodate even a single atom-sized drop more. Therefore, it is said:
"This bowl is full, perfectly complete."

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has realized the path of the Buddha, they no longer form further vows; they are like an atom (*paramāṇu*), for all their vows have reached ultimate fulfillment. This is called being well-perfected in the complete fulfillment of all vows.
“Good son! By means of these ten dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of aspiration. Good son!”
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they are fully possessed of the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).

What are these ten? First, being endowed with the power that cannot be subdued; second, being endowed with the power that cannot be destroyed; third, being endowed with the power of merit; fourth, being endowed with the power of wisdom; fifth, being endowed with the power of retinue; sixth, being endowed with the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); seventh, being endowed with the power of mastery (*vaśitā*); eighth, being endowed with the power of dhāraṇī; ninth, being endowed with the power of unshakable stability; and tenth, being endowed with the power of transcendent non-intellection.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s possession of invincible power?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva cannot be subdued by any non-Buddhists; this is called the possession of invincible power.”
"What is the perfection of the indestructible power? Good son!

Among the multitudes of humans, devas, and sentient beings, there is not a single being whose power of their own path can destroy the power of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of the indestructible power."
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva become fully endowed with the power of merit?

There is not a single practice among all meritorious deeds—whether mundane or supramundane—that a bodhisattva does not traverse; this is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with the power of merit.”
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva fulfill the power of prajñā?

For a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all Buddha-dharmas, there is not a single dharma that—by virtue of his excellent wisdom—is not seen, not realized, or not thoroughly penetrated, with the sole exception of the profound wisdom of the Tathāgata; this is called a bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the power of prajñā.”
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the power of retinue?

The bodhisattva’s retinue consists of those who do not break the precepts, those who do not hold wrong views, those who do not lack dignified deportment, and those who do not maintain wrong livelihoods.”

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva’s retinue shares whatever means of subsistence they possess, thereby fulfilling the purpose of both self-benefit and the benefit of others; this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the power of his retinue.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva become fully endowed with the power of supernormal knowledges?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva completely transcends all worldly powers of supernormal knowledge, as well as the spheres of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
Why is this? Because the power of the bodhisattva’s supernormal knowledges is most supreme;
even if they were established within a single hair-pore inside Jambudvīpa, there would be no diminution.

In this way, whether it be the four continents, various worlds, a trichiliocosm, or worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he establishes them within a single minute particle (*paramāṇu*), yet there is neither increase nor decrease.

Whether it be two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten times the sands of the Ganges, or even worlds as numerous as expressible or inexpressible sands of the Ganges, he places them within a minute particle, and likewise there is neither increase nor decrease.
These worlds do not obstruct one another, and the sentient beings therein experience no crowding; this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s perfection of the power of mastery?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva transforms this trichiliocosm into the seven treasures and fills it with them; because of his power of mastery, there is no task that is not accomplished. This extends even to unspeakably many unspeakable worlds being filled with the seven treasures, wherein he possesses complete mastery. This is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of the power of mastery.”
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva become fully endowed with the power of dhāraṇī?

Regarding all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—whether they consist of various scripts, various phrases, or various underlying intentions—a bodhisattva, upon hearing them but once, is able to receive, maintain, penetrate, and explain them all within a single kṣaṇa, a single lava, or a single muhūrta. This is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with the power of dhāraṇī.”
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being endowed with the power of an unshakable stabilization?

Wherever a bodhisattva-mahāsattva establishes his stabilization, among the multitudes of humans, devas, and sentient beings, there is not a single sentient being capable of disturbing him, except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; this is called a bodhisattva being endowed with the power of an unshakable stabilization."
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s perfection of the power of transcendent wisdom?
A bodhisattva completely transcends all forms of knowledge; even all sentient beings cannot equal them, let alone surpass them.”
Except for the Tathāgata, who is skillfully proficient in expedient means, this is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the power of transcendent wisdom. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, he fulfills the perfection of power."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, the perfection of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā) is fulfilled. What are these ten?

First, the perfection of the wisdom of the selflessness of persons; second, the perfection of the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena; third, the perfection of the wisdom of boundlessness; fourth, the perfection of the wisdom of the objects of samādhi; fifth, the perfection of the wisdom of stability; sixth, the perfection of the wisdom of indestructibility; seventh, the perfection of the wisdom that observes the conduct of sentient beings; eighth, the perfection of the wisdom of effortlessness; ninth, the perfection of the wisdom of the characteristics of all phenomena; and tenth, the perfection of supramundane wisdom.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva fulfill the wisdom of the selflessness of persons?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the arising and the ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas):”
"When these aggregates arise, there is no real arising; they are unmoving and inactive, all being false and illusory.
Thus one observes them:
"When these aggregates cease, no disintegration is seen."
Again, he had this thought:

"These aggregates (skandhas) are without self, without person, without sentient being, without life-span, and without a nourishing man. Yet there are those who are deluded, stubborn, infants, and worldlings, who are deeply attached to the view of self and form such an understanding:
'These aggregates are not the self; the self does not exist within the aggregates.'"
They develop deep attachment toward the five aggregates and insist that they possess substantial reality;
thus, they do not penetrate the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because they do not penetrate the true principle, they wander through birth and death without rest, like a whirling firebrand.

The Bodhisattva thus attains ultimate and complete penetration into this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), leaving nothing further remaining; this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the wisdom of the non-self of persons (pudgala-nairātmya-jñāna).
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva fulfill the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows, as it truly is, the denial of diminution and likewise knows, as it truly is, the denial of exaggeration, and forms this thought:”

"Regarding phenomena that are merely conventional designations, one establishes and discriminates various names; yet although such discrimination is made, all phenomena that are discriminated are fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Those words and phrases that perform the discrimination likewise lack intrinsic nature. The essence of these phenomena does not conform to the discrimination, for the discrimination of names does not correspond to their actual substance."
Why is this so? All phenomena possess only names and signs; they are spoken of merely by way of provisional designations. Within these phenomena, one should not harbor attachment.

These dharmas of provisional designation are not ultimate; they are entirely non-existent. Rather, these various phenomena arise depending on other conditions and through the conjunction of those conditions; when causes and conditions disperse, they likewise perish accordingly.
“A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who knows such dharmas as these according to reality is said to be fully endowed with the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*).
‘Good son, how does a Bodhisattva become fully endowed with unconditioned wisdom (*apramāṇajñāna*)?
A bodhisattva does not produce wisdom in one moment and fail to produce it in the second moment. Why is this?
Because for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, wisdom is produced in every single moment—boundless, unimpeded, and without limitation; this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of unlimited wisdom.
“Good son! What is the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the wisdom regarding the spheres of samādhi?

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thoroughly knows all the samādhis of the śrāvakas, thoroughly knows all the samādhis of the pratyekabuddhas, thoroughly knows all the samādhis of the bodhisattvas, and thoroughly knows all the samādhis of the Tathāgatas. Within these samādhis, the Bodhisattva thoroughly knows the sphere of practice of the śrāvakas; within these samādhis, the Bodhisattva also knows the sphere of practice of the pratyekabuddhas; within these samādhis, the Bodhisattva also knows the sphere of practice of the bodhisattvas; and within these samādhis, the Bodhisattva also knows the samādhis practiced by the Tathāgatas, which are the samādhis of the Buddhas. Furthermore, he thoroughly knows the fruits and rewards that are accomplished therein, as well as the wisdom attained of its own accord. This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the wisdom regarding the spheres of samādhi.”
“Good son! What is meant by a bodhisattva being fully endowed with the power of suppression?

If a bodhisattva is suppressed by a śrāvaka, or suppressed by a pratyekabuddha, or even suppressed by another bodhisattva, the bodhisattva does not even know it; how much less so by all other sentient beings?”
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of steadfast wisdom. "Good son,
what is the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of indestructible wisdom?

The all-encompassing wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is indestructible; neither the various non-Buddhists, nor the armies of Māra, nor the Śrāvakas, nor the Pratyekabuddhas can ever destroy it. This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of indestructible wisdom.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva fulfill the wisdom that contemplates the conduct of sentient beings?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with pure wisdom, clearly and lucidly contemplates the realm of sentient beings; this is...”
Within [this state], he perceives that there are sentient beings who have already resolved upon bodhicitta and those who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta;
there are sentient beings who have already cultivated the practices of bodhi and those who have not yet cultivated the practices of bodhi;
and there are those dwelling in the first bhūmi up to the tenth bhūmi, attaining equal enlightenment, and having attained equal enlightenment...
When the wheel of Dharma has been correctly turned and the Buddha’s work is complete,
he enters parinirvāṇa; some sentient beings enter parinirvāṇa by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle, some enter parinirvāṇa by means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
some sentient beings are born in the heavens, and some sentient beings are born in the three miserable realms— the Bodhisattva understands all of this with perfect clarity.
To thus attain such vision is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the wisdom that observes the conduct of sentient beings. "Good son,
how does a Bodhisattva perfect effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*)?"
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, going out, or coming in, this wisdom constantly arises for the bodhisattva mahāsattva without the application of effort.
Just as the breath continues to arise constantly while a person is in deep sleep, so too does the wisdom of a bodhisattva arise.
Such wisdom pervades everywhere without exception; this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*).
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva fulfill the wisdom that comprehends the characteristics of all phenomena?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva thoroughly knows all phenomena—whether their general characteristics, their specific characteristics, or their immeasurable characteristics—and knows them as having the characteristic of being like an illusion or the characteristic of being false. This is called a bodhisattva fulfilling the wisdom that comprehends the characteristics of all phenomena.”
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva fulfill supramundane wisdom?

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains fulfillment through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), he transcends all worldly humans and devas; this is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of supramundane wisdom.”
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they are fully perfected in the perfection of wisdom.
*Mahāyāna-ratnamegha-sūtra*, Fascicle 2.
The Mahāyāna Ratnamegha Sūtra, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mandarasa from Funan, together with Saṃghavarman and others, during the Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Three: On Equanimity (3). Chapter Three: On Equanimity.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvāvaraṇavijaya,
saying: “Good son,
when a bodhisattva possesses ten dharmas, they are equal to the earth.”

What are these ten? First, they are vast and immeasurable; second, they nurture and sustain sentient beings; third, they harbor no distinction between those who have been kind and those who have not; fourth, they are able to receive the great rain-clouds of the Dharma; fifth, they are the place upon which all sentient beings rely; sixth, they are the ground for planting roots of goodness; seventh, they are vessels for rare jewels; eighth, they are vessels for wondrous medicines; ninth, they are unshakable; and tenth, they are free from all fear.
“Good son! How is it that a bodhisattva is vast and immeasurable?
It is like the great earth, which pervades the ten directions, being vast and immeasurable.”

The Bodhisattva is likewise: pervading all places, vast and immeasurable, because he practices the two together, endowed with both merit and wisdom; therefore, this is called the "vast and immeasurable" Bodhisattva.
"How does a bodhisattva nurture all sentient beings? Good son!
It is like the great earth, upon which all sentient beings depend for their existence, and by means of which they obtain various necessities of life according to their wishes."

The Bodhisattva is likewise: he nurtures sentient beings by planting all the pure practices of a Bodhisattva—such as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—as well as providing other immeasurable necessities of life that bring them benefit. This is called the Bodhisattva’s nurturing of all sentient beings.
“How is it that a bodhisattva has no discriminatory thought regarding those who have been kind and those who have not? Good son!

It is like the great earth: even if it is harmed or insulted, it does not give rise to anger; even if it is honored or offered to, it does not give rise to joy; within this, it does not form two distinct conceptions.”

The Bodhisattva is likewise: when harmed or afflicted, he does not become angry; when benefited, he does not rejoice. Toward those sentient beings, he gives rise to neither hatred nor attachment, and he does not expect any recompense. This is called the Bodhisattva’s equanimity toward both those who have been kind and those who have not.
"How can a bodhisattva receive all the great clouds and rains of the Dharma? Good son!
It is like the great earth, which can fully contain and receive all heavy rains as well as all other great masses of water."

The Bodhisattva is likewise; they fully receive and accept all the great rain-clouds of the Dharma showered by the Tathāgata. This is called the Bodhisattva’s ability to receive the great rain-clouds of the Dharma.
"What is the Bodhisattva as the place of reliance for all sentient beings?"
"Good son!
Just as all sentient beings—whether emerging from or entering into it—rely upon the great earth;
so too is the Bodhisattva, for all sentient beings who travel through the six realms of existence or the path to Nirvana rely upon him as their support."
In this way, the Bodhisattva is the place of reliance for all sentient beings.
"What is the place where the Bodhisattva plants roots of goodness?
Son of Good Family!
Just as the great earth serves as the cause for all seeds to grow, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:

all the seeds of wholesome qualities within sentient beings depend upon the Bodhisattva to attain growth. Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called the locus where the seeds of all wholesome dharmas are sown.
“How is it that a bodhisattva is a vessel for precious jewels? Good son!
It is like the great earth, which serves as a vessel for precious jewels; depending upon the earth, immeasurable precious jewels all appear.”

The Bodhisattva is likewise; various merits, radiances, and precious ornaments appear by depending upon the Bodhisattva as their cause and condition; thus, the Bodhisattva is called a vessel for rare treasures.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being a vessel for sublime medicine? Good son!
It is like the great earth, which produces all kinds of sublime medicines capable of curing the sickness and suffering of all sentient beings."

The Bodhisattva is likewise; as the medicinal herbs of all dharmas appear because of him, he is able to extinguish the various grave illnesses of affliction within all worlds. This is called the Bodhisattva being a vessel for medicine.
"How is it that a bodhisattva is unshakable?

Good son, it is like the great earth, which cannot be disturbed by any instruments of suffering; though touched by the cold and heat of the seasons, or by mosquitoes, ants, and venomous insects, it remains unmoved."

The Bodhisattva is likewise; he cannot be disturbed or vexed. All the various internal and external instruments of suffering raised by sentient beings are entirely unable to disturb him; this is called the Bodhisattva being unshakable.
"How does a bodhisattva have no fear? Good son!
It is like the great earth, which hears the sounds produced by all the dragon kings, elephant kings, lion kings, and so forth, yet remains unafraid."

The bodhisattva is likewise: hearing the voices of various māras and the voices of non-Buddhists, they do not feel alarm, do not feel terror, do not feel timidity, and do not feel fear; this is called the bodhisattva being without fear.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he is equal to the earth. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they are equal to water. What are these ten? First, their merit becomes gradually deeper;

second, they give rise to pure and white dharmas; third, they are moistened by the joy of joyful praise; fourth, they soak and rot the roots and sprouts of all afflictions; fifth, they are pure and free from turbidity; sixth, they extinguish the heat of afflictions; seventh, they eliminate all thirst and craving; eighth, they are profoundly deep and difficult to fathom; ninth, they can float away both the beautiful and the ugly; and tenth, they cleanse the dust of afflictions.
“Good son! How does the merit of a bodhisattva mahāsattva gradually deepen? Good son!”
Just as various waters flow in succession, gradually entering deeper;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva, who flows toward the wholesome dharmas, progressively moving toward the profound. This is called the gradual deepening of the Bodhisattva’s merit.
“How does a bodhisattva give rise to pure and white dharmas?
Son of good family!
It is like a collection of water that can produce all grasses, trees, forests, and various kinds of wonderful medicinal herbs.”

The Bodhisattva is likewise: by means of samādhi, they cause all factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣadharma) to grow; those already grown, they further increase and expand, until they form a forest of trees of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Within the Buddha-fields, they cause the fruits of the Dharma to arise and establish sentient beings—this is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation and growth of wholesome dharmas.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s moistening through joyful praise?
Son of good family!
It is like clear water, which is moist by its very nature and further moistens other things.”
The Bodhisattva is likewise: by nature joyful, praising, and moistening, they further moisten others.
What is called "joy" refers to supramundane dharmas;
what is called "praising" refers to relying upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
What is called "moistening" is the purity of the mind.
This is termed the Bodhisattva’s joyous exultation and moistening.
How does a Bodhisattva soak and rot the roots and sprouts of the afflictions?
Good son! It is like clear water, which can soak and rot away grass, wood, roots, or leaves; so it is with the Bodhisattva.

By practicing samādhi, they soak and rot away the continuity of all the root-seeds of afflictions, until even names and signs are completely extinguished and their whereabouts unknown. The foul-smelling habitual tendencies of the afflictions are also exhausted; this is called the Bodhisattva soaking and rotting away all the root-seeds of afflictions.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being pure and free from turbidity? Good son!
It is like pure water, whose essential nature is clear and pure, without any defilement or impurity.”
The Bodhisattva is likewise: by nature pure, stainless, and undefiled.
It is called "pure" because all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth, have been completely extinguished.
When the faculties are unstained, stainless, and undefiled, this is called the bodhisattva’s purity and lack of turbidity.
How does a bodhisattva extinguish the heat of the afflictions?
Good son! It is like the nature of water: when the summer months bring scorching heat, it provides coolness for all the earth and for all sentient beings upon the earth.

So too is it with the Bodhisattva: when the realms of sentient beings are scorched by the heat of afflictions (*kleśa*), he causes them all to become cool and extinguishes their burning fever with the pure water of the Dharma. This is called the Bodhisattva’s extinguishing of the heat of afflictions.
“How does a bodhisattva eliminate all thirst and craving? Good son,
it is like cool water that relieves the thirst and exhaustion of those who are parched.”

The Bodhisattva is likewise: all sentient beings thirst for the six sense-objects, which are difficult to disregard and difficult to endure. For these beings, the Bodhisattva brings down the rain of Dharma; by means of this rain of Dharma, he causes all sentient beings to turn away from their thirst for the six sense-objects. This is called the Bodhisattva’s removal of all thirst and craving.
"What is the profound depth that is difficult to fathom for a bodhisattva? Good son,
it is like a mass of water that is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom."

The Bodhisattva is also like this: he cultivates various wisdoms that are extremely profound and difficult to assail—meaning they cannot be easily overcome by any devas, māras, or non-Buddhists—and this is called the Bodhisattva’s profundity and invulnerability to assault.
"How does a bodhisattva float away both the beautiful and the ugly? Good son!
It is like flowing water, which can wash away all things upon the earth—whether beautiful or ugly."
The Bodhisattva is likewise; by means of the flow of the Dharma, they can carry away all realms of sentient beings, whether they be good or foul.
Although they carry them away in this manner, they do not afflict the sentient beings, and the flow of the water is likewise.

In this way, the bodhisattva moistens sentient beings with great compassion and descends the great rain of Dharma without causing any harm or affliction; this is called the bodhisattva’s ability to wash away both the beautiful and the ugly.
"How does a bodhisattva purify the dust of afflictions? Good son!
It is like the element of water, which moistens all impurities, dust, coarse grit, and filth upon the earth until they are completely purified without remainder."

The Bodhisattva is likewise: when there are sentient beings whose mental natures are coarse and unruly, and who possess the adventitious dust of afflictions, the Bodhisattva, by relying on concentration and wisdom, purifies them until nothing remains; this is called the Bodhisattva’s purification of the dust of afflictions.
“Good son! Possessing these ten dharmas, all bodhisattvas are equal to water. Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they are equal to fire. What are these ten? First, they can burn away the filth of afflictions;

second, they bring all Buddha-dharmas to maturity; third, they dry up the mud of afflictions; fourth, they are like a mass of fire; fifth, they are able to produce light; sixth, they are able to cause [the unawakened] to feel awe; seventh, they are well able to provide consolation; eighth, they are impartial toward all sentient beings; ninth, they are honored by the world; and tenth, they cannot be treated with contempt.
“Good son! How is it that a bodhisattva can burn away the filth of afflictions? Good son!”
Just as the nature of fire is able to burn all refuse, filth, grass, wood, thickets, and various medicinal trees;

so too is the Bodhisattva, who with the fire of wisdom can burn away all latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), all fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the refuse of afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the tools for kindling the fire—the remedial paths—until they are all utterly consumed. This is called the Bodhisattva’s ability to burn away all the refuse of affliction.
"How does a bodhisattva bring all Buddha-dharmas to maturity? Good son!
It is like the nature of fire, which brings all crops, seedlings, medicinal herbs, and grasses to maturity."

The Bodhisattva is likewise; by means of the fire of wisdom, they bring to maturity all internal Buddha-dharmas. Such maturation is never subject to loss; this is called the Bodhisattva’s maturation of all Buddha-dharmas.
“How does a bodhisattva dry up the mire of afflictions?
Son of good family!
It is like the nature of fire, which parches and dries all the mud of the earth.”

The Bodhisattva is also like this: by means of the fire of wisdom, he parches and dries all phenomena associated with the outflows (*āsrava*); this is called the Bodhisattva drying up the mire of afflictions (*kleśa*).
"In what way is the Bodhisattva likened to a mass of fire?"
"Good son! Just as various masses of fire dispel the cold and frost for those in freezing ice, so too is the Bodhisattva:
the feverish chills of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings are dispelled by the fire of wisdom. This is called the Bodhisattva being like a mass of fire."
“How does a bodhisattva produce light?

Good son, it is like a great mass of fire, blazing with intense flames, which produces light over a snow mountain, or the peak of Mount Vinataka, for one yojana, or two yojanas, or three, or four yojanas.”

The Bodhisattva is likewise; with the light of wisdom, he is able to illuminate and perceive from afar—whether across a thousand yojanas, ten thousand yojanas, or even immeasurable asaṃkhyeya realms—acting as a great light for all sentient beings, illuminating them with penetrating clarity. With the light of wisdom, he is able to completely dispel all dharmas of ignorant blindness and darkness; this is called the Bodhisattva’s ability to produce light.
"How does a bodhisattva produce fear?
Son of good family!
It is like birds, beasts, or even a lion king who, upon seeing a great mass of fire, gives rise to fear—namely, the fear that it will harm their bodies—and thus avoids that place from afar."

In this way, when Māra and his hosts of demons see a bodhisattva, they become terrified; because the bodhisattva lacks [their] majestic power, they immediately flee far away, to the point that they cannot even hear the bodhisattva’s name, let alone behold him.
This is called a bodhisattva being able to inspire fear.
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully provide consolation? Good son!

For example, suppose a person becomes lost in a dense forest or a vast wilderness and loses their way; suddenly seeing a great mass of fire, they approach it and are able to see a village within it, or perhaps see a herd of cattle. Having seen this, they feel reassured and are freed from all fear.

In this way, when all immeasurable sentient beings encounter the dense forest and vast wilderness of birth and death, if they see a bodhisattva, they obtain consolation and are freed from all fears; this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful ability to console.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equality toward all sentient beings?
Good son, it is like the nature of fire, which is entirely equal toward all sentient beings; as it is toward a king and a caṇḍāla, it is equal and without distinction."

The Bodhisattva is likewise; he is entirely impartial toward all sentient beings, providing benefit to kings as well as to butchers—this is called the Bodhisattva’s impartiality toward all sentient beings.
"How does a bodhisattva become one who is honored by the world?
Good son, it is like the nature of fire, which is honored by kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others."

The Bodhisattva is likewise; he is honored by all the worlds—gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—and is regarded as a teacher and model. This is called the Bodhisattva being honored by the world.
"How is it that a bodhisattva is not to be despised?
Good son, it is because, although fire may be small, it must not be touched lightly, for it is free from arrogance; likewise, a bodhisattva is free from arrogance."

The Bodhisattva is likewise; abiding in the stage of practice through faith, one should not disparage the Mahāyāna Dharma even though they have not yet attained power since first generating the mind of enlightenment.
Whether gods or humans, or all those in the world—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth—they shall know and recognize this, saying:
"This Bodhisattva will, before long, sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)."
"This is what is called a bodhisattva who is not to be despised. Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas is equal to fire."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they are equal to space.
What are these ten?

First, vastness; second, non-obstruction; third, tranquility; fourth, boundless wisdom; fifth, boundless knowledge; sixth, conformity with the dharma-realm; seventh, faith that all phenomena share the nature of empty space; eighth, having no fixed location; ninth, transcending the sphere of conceptualization; tenth, surpassing discursive thought.
“Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas attains equality with empty space.
Furthermore, good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that are equal to space.
What are these ten?
First, regarding the beautiful and the ugly in form, they are neither greedy nor angry.
Second, regarding pleasant and unpleasant sounds, one neither loves nor hates them;
third, regarding pleasant and unpleasant odors, one neither desires nor resents them;
fourth, regarding pleasant and unpleasant tastes, one neither indulges in nor rejects them.
Fifth, regarding pleasant or unpleasant tactile sensations, one is neither lustful nor angry;
sixth, regarding pleasant or unpleasant mental phenomena, one neither clings nor resents;
seventh, regarding gain or loss, one neither rejoices nor harbors bitterness.
Eighth, one is neither dejected by suffering nor elated by pleasure;
ninth, one neither craves fame nor recoils from ill repute;
tenth, one is neither drawn to praise nor alienated by slander.
These ten dharmas are equal to space. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, he is likened to the moon."
What are the ten? First, they bring coolness to sentient beings;

second, those who see them rejoice; third, they increase pure dharmas (*śukladharma*); fourth, they eliminate dark dharmas (*kṛṣṇadharma*); fifth, they are praised by the world; sixth, their physical appearance is pure; seventh, they ride upon the most supreme vehicle; eighth, they are constantly adorned; ninth, they sport within the True Dharma (*saddharma*); and tenth, they possess great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), with majestic virtue so lofty and sublime.
“How does a bodhisattva bring coolness to sentient beings, and even possess great supernormal powers and majestic virtue? “Good son!
It is like when the moon rises, all sentient beings obtain coolness because it is lovely to behold.”

The Bodhisattva is also like this: he can eliminate the feverish heat of the afflictions of sentient beings, causing them to attain joy, delight, and exultation, and bringing them refreshing coolness. "Good son!
Just as when the moon rises, people see it with joy and their hearts are gladdened by its coolness;
so too is the Bodhisattva: having extinguished the heat of afflictions, his faculties are pure, and he is fully endowed with dignified deportment, every movement, and meritorious virtues.
“Good son! Just as the waxing moon, from its first appearance, gradually increases until it becomes fully complete on the fifteenth day;

so too is the Bodhisattva: from the initial generation of the mind of awakening until sitting at the site of enlightenment, the white dharmas increase day and night, becoming perfect and complete in every respect.”
“Good son! Just as during the waning phase of the moon, its color, form, radiance, and lovely appearance gradually diminish until, at the end of the month, it no longer manifests;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva: having attained supramundane wisdom, all delusive appearances are entirely diminished and ultimately do not manifest when he sits at the site of enlightenment.”
“Good son! Just as when the moon rises, all those in the world—whether great or small, monastics or laypeople, ministers or subjects, men or women—all praise it;
so too is the Bodhisattva, whom all people in the world—humans, devas, and asuras—extol and glorify.”
“Good son! Just as the Deva Candrātmaja has a body and mind that are pure and radiate brilliant light, born from the retribution of karma;

so too is the Bodhisattva: his body and mind are pure and his light shines everywhere, emerging from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) through spontaneous transformation. He is not produced by parents, nor is he defiled by the five stages of impurity, such as the kalala and so forth.”
“Good son! Just as the Moon Deva-putra rides upon a pure vehicle to illuminate the four quarters;
so too does the Bodhisattva ride upon the most supreme vehicle to universally illuminate immeasurable and boundless worlds.”
“Good son! Just as the Moon Deva is always adorned and never obscured at any time,
so too is the Bodhisattva, for he is always adorned by his merits.”
“Good son! Just as the Moon Deva-putra is constantly possessed of natural joy and happiness, so too is the Bodhisattva:
he always abides in the bliss of the Dharma and does not abide in the pleasures of desire.”
“Good son! Just as the Moon Deva possesses great supernormal powers and great majestic virtue;
so too does the Bodhisattva, being endowed with all merits, mastery, wisdom, and the transformations of supernormal powers, acting according to his will without obstruction.”
“Good son! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he is likened to the moon. Good son!”
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, he is like the sun. What are these ten? First, the extinction of the darkness of ignorance;

second, the ability to bring about awakening; third, the ability to illuminate the ten directions; fourth, the arising of the causes of wholesome dharmas; fifth, the ability to extinguish all outflows (*āsrava*); sixth, the ability to produce radiance; seventh, the ability to obscure the false views of non-Buddhists; eighth, the manifestation of the beautiful and the ugly; ninth, the performance of various karmic actions of wholesome dharmas; and tenth, being revered by virtuous people.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva extinguish the darkness of ignorance, and so forth, up to how are they honored by virtuous people? Good son!”
Just as when the sun rises it extinguishes all darkness,
so too does the rising of the Bodhisattva-sun extinguish the darkness of ignorance.
"O son of good family!
Just as the lotus blossoms when the sun rises,
so too do all sentient beings who are ready for transformation awaken when the Bodhisattva-sun rises.
"O Son of Good Family!..."
Just as when the sun rises it illuminates the ten directions;
so too, when the Bodhisattva-sun rises, the radiance of its wisdom shines universally throughout the ten directions without causing harm or distress to any sentient being.
“Good son! Just as when the sun rises and emits a thousand rays of light to illuminate Jambudvīpa, people of the world only then know that the sun has risen;
so too, when the Bodhisattva-sun rises and its light of wisdom shines, it is only then that one knows the existence of all wholesome dharmas.”
“Good son! In Jambudvīpa, when the sunlight fades, one knows that the sun has set;

likewise, when the Bodhisattva-sun rises, it produces the light of wisdom for all sentient beings, able to extinguish all the darkness of ignorance, the heavy gloom, and the blinding obscurity of beings. Because this darkness of ignorance is extinguished, the Bodhisattva who has exhausted the outflows (āsravakṣaya) is said to ‘not appear.’”
"Good son! When the sun rises, all other lights are eclipsed and cannot shine; yet at that time, the sun does not form this thought:
'I shall cause these other lights to be eclipsed so that they do not shine.'"
By the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), they naturally disappear.
When the Bodhisattva-sun rises, all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), wrong views, and the blindness of darkness naturally recede and perish; yet at that time, the Bodhisattva does not form the thought:
"I have caused these to recede, perish, and disappear."
“Good son! Just as when the sun rises, it reveals to all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa what is beautiful and ugly, high and low, and right and wrong;
so too is the rising of the Bodhisattva-sun, for it manifests to all sentient beings what is beautiful and ugly, high and low, and right and wrong.”
That which is called "good" refers to the Noble Path;
that which is called "ugly" refers to all heterodox paths. "Good son!
Just as when the sun rises, activities such as planting and cultivation can be accomplished;
so too, when the Bodhisattva-sun rises, wholesome dharmas are born.
"O Son of Good Family!
Just as when the sun rises, virtuous people rejoice, make offerings, and offer praise, while the wicked feel sorrow, bitterness, and displeasure;

so too, when the Bodhisattva-sun rises, those who possess wisdom, who are sagacious and of sharp faculties, rejoice and offer praise, whereas those who follow deviant paths, the spiritually infantile, ordinary worldlings, those of dull faculties and wickedness, those lacking the eye of wisdom, and those who long for birth and death while turning their backs on the path to Nirvāṇa, do not show reverence.
"This is called the bodhisattva’s extinguishing of the darkness of ignorance, up to being honored by virtuous people.
In this way, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he is like the sun."
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas is like a lion king.
What are these ten?

First, fearlessness; second, absence of timidity; third, not looking back in retreat; fourth, being able to roar the lion’s roar; fifth, being unstartled; sixth, wandering through mountain forests; seventh, dwelling in mountain caves; eighth, having no stores or possessions; ninth, walking alone without companions; tenth, residing in an araṇya.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva, being without fear, even dwell in an araṇya? Good son!”
Just as the lion king travels everywhere without fear or alarm, always seeing himself as walking alone and without rival;
so too is the Bodhisattva, who comes and goes through all places without fear or alarm, always seeing that he has no adversary.
“Good son! Just as the lion king has no thought of timidity, so too is the bodhisattva:
when engaging in contests of strength with various non-Buddhists, or in debates and disputes, he has no thought of timidity; he is neither arrogant nor inferior.”
“Good son! Just as the lion king does not look back even when he has been insulted, so it is with the bodhisattva:
if he is harmed or insulted by followers of external paths, he neither turns back nor remains silent.”
“Good son! Just as when the lion king lets out a lion’s roar, all birds and beasts, as well as jackals and wolves, flee far away and disperse;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva, who lets out a lion’s roar by preaching the dharma of non-self. The jackals and wolves of the non-Buddhists who cling to the view of self scatter and vanish throughout the ten directions. Yet this Bodhisattva does not let out this lion’s roar of the dharma of non-self to afflict them; rather, he does so solely to transform those sentient beings who are to be converted.”
“Good son! Just as the lion king has no fear and gazes everywhere throughout the ten directions, so too is the bodhisattva:
by nature delighting in tranquility, he dwells in mountain forests.”
“Good son! Just as the lion king dwells in a mountain cave,
so too does the bodhisattva dwell securely in the mountain cave of the tranquility of wisdom.”
“Good son! Just as the lion king has no store of provisions;
so too is the bodhisattva, having cast off the heavy burden of all afflictions, possesses no store of provisions.”
“Good son! Just as the lion king strides alone without companion to subdue the herds of birds and beasts;
so too is the Bodhisattva, who sits at the site of enlightenment, alone and without companion, to shatter the armies of Māra.”
“Good son! Just as in the dwelling place of the lion king, no birds or beasts can damage any of the crops; so it is with the Bodhisattva:
in whatever land or village he resides, the birds and beasts of the heterodox cannot harm or invade the sprouts of the wholesome Dharma.”
"In this way, the bodhisattva is neither terrified nor afraid, and is even able to protect the roots of goodness in sentient beings.
Thus, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he is like a lion king."
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas is well able to subdue.
What are these ten?

First, firmness in the bodhicitta; second, mastery over the bodhicitta; third, guarding the six sense faculties; fourth, practicing the noble path; fifth, bearing the heavy burden; sixth, benefiting sentient beings with a mind free from weariness; seventh, right livelihood; eighth, being truly without arrogance; ninth, being without flattery, crookedness, or deception; and tenth, being upright and sincere.
"Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas is well able to tame [the mind]. Good son!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they become renowned and known throughout the world. What are these ten?
First, sitting in meditation to collect and concentrate the mind;
Second, they extensively cultivate the practice of emptiness;
third, they study the Dharma without ceasing;

fourth, they do not rely on sensory objects and remain free from the latent afflictions, upholding all the Tathāgata’s scriptural teachings without ever transgressing them, and they accord with the equality of all dharma-principles because they penetrate the principle of the Dharma-realm.
Fifth, they conduct themselves in the world like the lowly offspring of a *caṇḍāla*, because they distance themselves from self-exaltation, arrogance, and intoxication through a humble and base mind;
sixth, they subsist constantly on alms-food, because they proceed with sequential equanimity;
seventh, they dwell in the world with minds free from doubt, because they possess knowledge and vision according to reality within the Buddha-dharma.
Eighth, the mind is free from hesitation because one has internally realized the Dharma;
ninth, one no longer relies on the faith of others and cannot be led astray because one perceives the principles for oneself;
tenth, one is a field of merit for the world because of the excellence of one’s practice.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas is known by the world. "Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas is like a lotus flower."

What are the ten? First, the body is free from defilement; second, one does not dwell together with subtle evils; third, the fragrance of morality is pervasive; fourth, rebirth is pure; fifth, the countenance is harmonious and joyful; sixth, one is supple and subtle; seventh, what one beholds is auspicious; eighth, the mind is awakened; ninth, the mind is matured; tenth, one is well able to gather and sustain [virtue].
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s body become free from defilement, up to being fully capable of gathering and sustaining [virtue]? Good son!”
Just as a lotus flower, when emerging from the water, is naturally free from defilement, so too is it by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) that there is no defilement;
likewise, the bodhisattva emerges from the waters of birth and death yet remains undefiled.

Why is this? Because they have attained the wisdom of skillful means; all bodhisattvas are well-versed in the practice of skillful means within saṃsāra, and thus the faults and afflictions of saṃsāra cannot defile them, for they are sustained by the bodhisattva’s skillful means and wisdom.
“Good son! Just as a single drop of water cannot remain within a lotus flower,
so too, even the most subtle transgressions of a bodhisattva find no place to abide.”
“Good son! Just as the earth element where lotuses grow fills that location with a fragrant scent,
so too, wherever a bodhisattva dwells— in a village, a town, a city, or a settlement— the fragrance of their precepts pervades every place without exception.”
“Good son! Just as there may be lotus flowers growing in a place within the earth-element that are pure, clean, and lovely, such that kings, royal subjects, and all the common people go to them;

so it is with the Bodhisattva, who takes birth in various places with a naturally pure nature, fully endowed with the virtue of precepts and dignified deportment, and is thus revered, cherished, and prostrated to by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, while being praised and extolled by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.”
“Good son! Just as when a lotus flower is in full bloom, one feels joy upon seeing it, for its appearance is lovely and can delight the hearts of all;
so too is the Bodhisattva: when he smiles subtly, his face is free from frowning, and his faculties are pure.”
“Good son! Just as a lotus flower is supple and lacks any coarseness or roughness,
so too is the bodhisattva naturally supple, fundamentally free from any harshness or brutality.”
“Good son! Just as seeing a lotus flower during a dream is auspicious because it brings praise and benefit, so too is seeing the benefit of a bodhisattva;
it is most auspicious in every dwelling place for the sake of attaining all-knowledge.”
“Good son! Just as a lotus flower gradually unfolds, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:
when the lotus flower of the factors of enlightenment through wisdom unfolds, that moment is called the Buddha’s awakening.”
“Good son! Just as when a lotus flower blooms, it delights the eye-faculty when seen, the nose-faculty when smelled, the body-faculty when touched, and the mind-faculty when the heart rejoices;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva. When the light of mature wisdom appears, the eye-faculty is purified upon seeing it; the ear-faculty is purified upon hearing it; the nose-faculty is delighted by the fragrance of the merit of their precepts; the body-faculty is delighted by making offerings and showing reverence upon contact; and the mind-faculty is purified when one can contemplate and praise their merits.”
“Good son! Just as the lotus flower, when it arises, is cherished by humans and devas;
so too is the bodhisattva: having emerged into the world, he is revered and honored by all buddhas and bodhisattvas, as well as by all devas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World Protectors.”
"This is called the bodhisattva being free from defilement and so forth, up to the gathering [of virtues].
Good son, in this way,
when a bodhisattva possesses these ten dharmas, he is like a lotus flower."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, his mind and intentions are vast and great.
What are these ten?
First, one generates an expansive mind because one shall practice all the pāramitās;
second, one generates an expansive mind because one shall bring all Buddha-dharmas to maturity;
third, one generates an expansive mind because one shall teach and transform all sentient beings.

Fourth, he generates an expansive mind, thinking: "I shall sit at the site of enlightenment and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; having attained perfect awakening, I shall turn the wheel of Dharma, which neither Brahmā, nor the devas, nor any being in the entire world can turn.
Fifth, he generates an expansive mind, thinking: "I shall benefit all sentient beings throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Sixth, he generates an expansive mind, thinking: "I shall construct the vessel of wisdom to ferry all sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death."

Seventh, because all sentient beings are without rescue, without protection, without a place of refuge, and have no kinsmen or acquaintances capable of delivering them, I shall generate an expansive mind in order to act as their relative;

eighth, I shall manifest the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, utter the lion’s roar, and sport in the supernatural powers and path of all Buddhas, and furthermore, I shall look upon the Mahānāgas and generate an expansive mind;
ninth, I shall generate an expansive mind because I am incomparable and peerless with respect to the entire world—whether devas or humans.

Tenth, by means of the Buddha’s true Dharma, I shall transform and guide all sentient beings; for this reason—not because of base conduct, nor asceticism, nor inferior practices—I give rise to an expansive mind.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he gives rise to an expansive mind. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, their mind attains purity.
What are these ten?

First, the mind is full of faith and joy; the mind is internally unmoving; the mind dwells in firmness; the mind is free from artifice; and it remains far removed from all unwholesome thoughts—namely, not generating the aspiration to seek the path of the śrāvaka or the path of the pratyekabuddha.
"By means of having few desires and being content, one remains far removed from all defilements and impurities:
one is free from bodily arrogance, which means not adopting artificial deportment;
one is free from verbal arrogance, which means not speaking words that are untrue."

They are free from mental arrogance because they are without deceit or crookedness; their bodies are not intermingled with others; their speech is characterized by few desires; and their minds are free from greedy seeking.
They recognize kindness and repay it, never forgetting even the most subtle acts of benevolence, let alone those that are great.

"In the truth of speech, one does not disparage others regarding their actions; one says nothing that is not beneficial; one praises only those who possess virtue; and one encourages and extols them with benefit and joy. Within this, one perceives only merit and acts according to what has been said."
“A bodhisattva must not offer words of consolation while harboring resentment in the heart;
when the bodhisattva offers words of praise and encouragement, the mind must not incite contention;
and when speaking loving words with the mouth, the heart must be free from anger and hatred.”
“A bodhisattva does not manifest goodness with the body while practicing evil with the mind; a bodhisattva does not show respect with the body while harboring contempt in the mind.

A bodhisattva is without arrogance and without indolence; they are not stingy and not envious. Since a bodhisattva is without arrogance and without indolence, they are neither miserly nor jealous, nor are they delusive or deceitful.”
“A bodhisattva does not engage in conflict to cause the two sides to destroy and disperse one another. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva honors others with his body, speaks truthfully with his speech, and thus brings the three karmas into correspondence.”
"One does not slander the Tathāgata’s pure and true Dharma; a bodhisattva does not dare to slander the Dharma.
How does one not slander the true Dharma of the Buddhas?
A bodhisattva resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, shaves off hair and beard, dons dyed robes, and goes forth into homelessness within the true Dharma of the Buddha."

Thus, one leaves the home life not out of fear of kings, nor out of fear of being plundered by bandits, nor because of debt, nor out of terror, nor for the sake of a livelihood; rather, one leaves the home life to study the Path out of faith and joy, seeking only the Dharma, drawing near to virtuous friends, serving them with a profound mind, approaching spiritual mentors, and listening to the Dharma with a deep heart.

Practicing in accordance with the Dharma, one’s mind is free from arrogance; though free from arrogance, one may still grasp things erroneously. If there is no erroneous grasping, one can penetrate the Buddha’s true path; by virtue of this penetration, one attains the True Dharma; and by attaining the Dharma, one becomes certain of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In this way, the student does not slander the Tathāgata’s true teaching and true Dharma. "Good son!
Thus, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, their mind attains purity."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they are free from doubt and confusion.
What are these ten?

They believe that the Tathāgata’s body possesses secrets; they believe that the Tathāgata’s speech possesses secrets; they believe that the Tathāgata’s mind possesses secrets; they believe in the bodhisattva practices; they believe in the possession of supernormal powers; they believe in the fulfillment of original vows; they believe in the path of the One Vehicle; they believe in the various teachings; they believe in the wondrous resonance and profound depth of the Buddha’s voice; and they believe in the transformation of sentient beings according to their respective capacities.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva believe that the Tathāgata possesses the secret of the body, and so forth, up to believing in the teaching and transformation of sentient beings? Good son!”
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"That which I have heard regarding the Tathāgata’s possession of this Dharma-body—
the tranquil body, the unequaled body, the peerless body, the immeasurable body, the unshared body, and the vajra body— is entirely true, not false, and not deceptive."
"In this matter, the Bodhisattva gives rise to no doubt or confusion and possesses no dualistic mind.
Thus, he places his faith in the secret of the Tathāgata’s body.
Furthermore, he reflects as follows:"

"Whatever secret oral teachings of the Tathāgata they have heard, whether prophecies bestowed directly from the Tathāgata’s own mouth or prophecies indicated through physical signs, and whatever sūtras and instructions he has spoken that are of provisional meaning—they believe in them all."
The Tathāgata is free from error and does not speak without meaning; for these reasons, his words are never false.

All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have extinguished all evils and are pure and stainless. They no longer possess afflictions or the burning heat of fetters and latent tendencies; they are sovereign and complete, without expectation, without turbidity, and without defilement.
"If one were to say that the Tathāgata has faults or that the Tathāgata speaks words without meaning, such a thing is impossible; he is most true and most real, without any deception.
Having no doubt or confusion regarding this point, one thus places faith in the Buddha’s secret oral teachings.
He further thought:

"Whatever is secret within the Tathāgata’s mind, cherished in his heart, and dependent upon his mind—this is unknown to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as to all bodhisattvas and sentient beings, except for those who possess the supernatural power of the Tathāgata."

Why is this? The Tathāgata is profoundly deep, difficult to assail and difficult to measure; his realm is vast and expansive, boundless and immeasurable, equal to space and inconceivable. It is solely true and real, devoid of any falsehood or deception.
"In this matter, one should have no doubt; such is the secret of faithful confidence.
Furthermore, one should think:

'Whatever all bodhisattvas have heard regarding their diligent benefit of sentient beings and their accomplishment of all sentient beings—in these undertakings, they experience no weariness whatsoever, nor do they feel any fear.'"

Bearing the great burden with firm and steadfast power, they practice all the Buddha-dharmas of the ten perfections, possessing unimpeded wisdom, boundless wisdom, incomparable wisdom, and unique wisdom.
With firm courage, firm adornment, and firm vows, one sequentially fulfills them for the sake of bodhi; these are only true and real, not deceptive.
"Having no doubt in this matter, the bodhisattva thus has faith in the practice.
Furthermore, they think:

'When a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they attain the pure supernormal power of the eye that is unimpeded, unobstructed, and unhindered, as well as the supernormal powers of the ear, the knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the miraculous powers, and the exhaustion of outflows—all of which are unattached, unimpeded, unobstructed, and unhindered.'"

Within the three periods of time, he attains the wisdom corresponding to a single kṣaṇa and views the realm of sentient beings as it truly is: "These sentient beings are fully engaged in evil physical karma, fully engaged in evil verbal karma, and fully engaged in evil mental karma; they slander the noble ones, hold perverted wrong views, and practice false dharmas. Due to these karmic causes and conditions, after they cast off their bodies and die, they are born in the various evil realms and undergo the sufferings of hell.

There are other sentient beings who, by virtue of good physical karma and good verbal and mental karma, are fully endowed with right view; because they do not slander the noble ones and practice right view, their three types of karma are purified through that right view. By these causes and conditions, after they cast off their bodies and die, they are born in the good realms and experience happiness in the heavens."
Thus, by observing the realm of sentient beings with such reality, one sees the wholesome and unwholesome karma of sentient beings.
Again, one reflects:
"In the past, when I was practicing the path of bodhi as a bodhisattva, I made this vow:..."
"To first attain perfect enlightenment for oneself and then cause others to awaken" was my former vow;
now that it has been fulfilled and realized exactly as wished, all of it is true and free from any falsehood.
"In this matter, there is neither doubt nor delusion; therefore, a bodhisattva is called 'Equally Awakened' (Samyaksaṃbuddha), and having already awakened by oneself, is named a 'Buddha' (Saṃbuddha).
Good son!..."
