In this way, the bodhisattva has faith in bodhi and faith in the appearance of Buddhas in the world.
He further reflects:
"The One Vehicle that I have heard—the sole Buddha Vehicle—is entirely true; it is not deceptive, nor is it false or erroneous."
Why is this so? Because all vehicles emerge from within the Mahāyāna.

It is like the continent of Jambudvīpa, which is surrounded by various other continents; although each has its own name, they are all subsumed under the name of Jambudvīpa when spoken of collectively.
"All other vehicles are likewise thus; they emerge from the Mahāyāna, and there is neither a second nor a third.
Having no doubt regarding this point, one thus places faith in the path of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
Again, he thought:
"I have heard the various teachings spoken by the Tathāgatas, and within all those sūtras, everything is entirely true. Why is this so?
"For the sake of transforming sentient beings, the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma according to their capacities.
One should not doubt this point, nor give rise to confusion, nor entertain a dualistic mind; in this way, one has faith that there are distinctions among the three vehicles.
Again, he thought:
"I have heard that the resonant voices of all Tathāgatas are profoundly deep; their sublime Brahma-voices are entirely true. Why is this so?

If even the Brahma-sons, with their meager roots of goodness, possess voices that are subtle and resonant, supple and clear, elegant and lovely, how much more so for the Tathāgata, who has cultivated and perfected the adornment of a hundred blessings and is endowed with ten thousand virtues over immeasurable eons?
"In this matter, one is without doubt or confusion; thus, one has faith in the Tathāgata’s profound resonance.
Furthermore, one reflects:

'I have heard that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, discerns the capacities and natures of beings, as well as the sharpness or dullness of their faculties. When he teaches the Dharma with a single voice to the sentient beings he transforms, they each understand it according to their own kind, and their doubts are severed. Those whose roots of goodness are matured, he approaches and transforms. "
Each and every sentient being forms this understanding:
"The Tathāgata is now preaching such a Dharma for me alone.
Yet, the Tathāgatas have no such discrimination nor any conceptual thought; all these [teachings] are entirely true, neither erroneous nor deceptive.
"In this matter, one should be free from doubt and confusion, giving rise to such faith:
that one teaches and transforms sentient beings according to their respective conditions and circumstances. Good son!
In this way, when these ten dharmas are fully possessed, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is free from doubt and hesitation. "Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas is like the great ocean."
"What are the ten? It is the gathering place of all precious jewels;

it is difficult to assail; it is vast; it gradually deepens; it does not harbor corpses; it is of a single uniform taste; it can receive all flowing streams; it does not exceed its boundaries; it is the refuge for all great beings; and it is without limit."
“Good son! How is it that the Bodhisattva is the gathering place for all manner of jewels, and so forth, up to how he is without limit? Good son!”
For example, just as the great ocean is where all precious treasures are gathered in immeasurable and boundless quantities, and all sentient beings go there to gather those treasures;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva, who is the gathering place for all the treasures of merit in immeasurable and boundless quantities, and all sentient beings seeking merit and virtue go to him.
“Good son! Just as the ocean is difficult to fathom, so too is the Bodhisattva;
he is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom.”
“Good son! Just as the ocean is vast and expansive,
so too is the bodhisattva, for their compassion and wisdom are exceedingly vast.”
“Good son! Just as the great ocean gradually becomes deeper, so too it is with the bodhisattva:
their cultivation of the path and the knowledge of all modes gradually become deeper.”
“Good son! Just as that great ocean does not dwell together with any corpses. Why is this? Because...”
It is the natural law of the great ocean that it does not harbor all afflictions or dwell together with evil associates. Why is this? Because...
This is the natural law of Bodhisattvas. "Good son!
Just as this great ocean receives all streams that flow into it until they become of one taste—namely, the salty taste;
The Bodhisattva is also like this: all the pure dharmas (śukla-dharma) that he cultivates become of one single flavor, namely, the flavor of omniscience (sarvajñatā). "Good son!
"Just as the ocean receives immeasurable streams of water without increasing or decreasing, so too is the Bodhisattva:
he receives immeasurable dharmas without increase or decrease. Good son!
Just as that great ocean does not exceed its boundaries, so too is the Bodhisattva:
in teaching and transforming sentient beings, he does not exceed his limits. "Good son!
Just as the waters of the great ocean provide a dwelling place for beings with massive bodies, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:
all sentient beings possess pure and white dharmas that dwell in dependence upon the Bodhisattva’s body.
“Good son! Just as the waters of the great ocean have no limit, and all sentient beings cannot know their quantity;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, who expounds the essential Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings—boundless and inexhaustible, such that none can measure it.”
"In this way, the Bodhisattva is a great ocean, a place where the jewels of merit accumulate, extending even to the limitless. 'Good son!
Thus, when a Bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they are like a great ocean.'"
The Mahāyāna Ratnamegha Sūtra, Volume Three;
The Mahāyāna Ratnamegha Sūtra, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mandarasa of Funan together with Saṃghavarman during the Liang Dynasty.
4. Chapter on Dhāraṇīs (IV). Chapter Four: On Dhāraṇīs.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"O son of good family!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they profoundly understand the subtle and minute.

What are these ten? They are: understanding and seeking liberation; understanding the ultimate nature of all phenomena; understanding the fulfillment of all phenomena; understanding compliance with the characteristics of all phenomena; understanding the analytical discernment of all phenomena; understanding that the twelve links of dependent origination are profound and difficult to fathom; understanding that the power of karma is inconceivable; understanding the profound meaning as it has been taught; understanding the penetration of the principle of suchness; and understanding the single absolute truth.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva seek liberation, and so forth, up to how does he understand the single ultimate truth?
A bodhisattva constantly reflects thus:”

"Alas, how painful it is for all the world! It is being consumed by the fierce fires of the eight sufferings: the blazing flames of lust burn its body and head; the thick smoke of hatred rises in profusion as delusive thoughts arise in chaos; and the dark gloom of ignorance and folly obstructs its eyes."
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva further thought:
"How can these sentient beings escape from this burning house of the triple world and be delivered from the peril of fire?"
"For the sake of providing these sentient beings with the causes and conditions for liberation, I therefore seek to understand all dharmas and attain accord with the equality of all dharmas;
having attained this equality, I realize the illusory nature of all dharmas as they truly are;
having realized their illusory nature, I then know them as they truly are."
Having known it as it truly is, one accordingly contemplates the profound and unfathomable twelvefold chain of dependent origination;
having attained this contemplation of conditions, one contemplates the inconceivable power of karma.
Having made this contemplation, he gives rise to a sense of great wonder and reflects:
"Although all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they are able to skillfully manifest various forms and images."
"In this way, by awakening to these subtle matters through the mind, the meanings of what has been taught will be clearly understood;
having understood the meaning, one penetrates suchness (tathatā);
having penetrated suchness, one attains the vision of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."
Having realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one is then able to deliver all sentient beings from the burning house of birth and death. "Good son!
In this way, the bodhisattva seeks liberation and even understands the single ultimate truth."
Endowed with these ten dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva deeply understands the subtle.
"Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, his eloquence accords with principle."
What are these ten? They are as follows:

all dharmas are merely provisional designations; they are without self, without person, without sentient being, without life-span, without nourisher, without creator, without experiencer, without knower, and without seer. They are fragile and subject to calamity, lacking autonomy, empty and non-existent, consisting of false discrimination, and a provisional confluence of causes and conditions—thus are they described through such provisional combinations and provisional names.

Good son! There is this principle that accords with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*): there is no person, no self, no sentient being, no life-span, no agent, no experiencer, no knower, and no seer; there is no independent sovereignty, no false discrimination, and only the provisional conjunction of causes and conditions.

Thus, this teaching of the Dharma possesses this principle; it accords with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena, and is consistent with reason. Observing the principles of actual phenomena in this way, one clearly manifests the characteristics of phenomena without any inversion.
In this way, eloquence that accords with principle is therefore called "eloquence that accords with principle.
Son of good family!
By being endowed with ten dharmas, a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s eloquence accords with principle.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, his eloquence will be clear and lucid.
What are these ten?

That is to say: the eloquence of resolving knots, inexhaustible eloquence, uninterrupted eloquence, non-arid eloquence, non-inferior eloquence, fearless eloquence, incomparable eloquence, indestructible eloquence, infinite eloquence, and the eloquence fully endowed with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
"Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas has clear and lucid eloquence. Good son!"
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, their eloquence is pure and refined. What are these ten? They are: eloquence that is not stammering;

eloquence that is without fear; eloquence that is not weak or inferior; eloquence that does not boast of itself; eloquence that does not impair the meaning; eloquence that does not impair the phrasing; eloquence that does not lose the method; eloquence that does not miss the proper time; eloquence that is not coarse or harsh; and eloquence that is not unclear.
“Good son! A bodhisattva’s eloquence is free from all stammering. Why is this?
Because he possesses fearlessness, the bodhisattva is like a lion king amidst the great assembly—neither afraid nor timid.
The bodhisattva’s eloquence is neither boastful nor sycophantic.
Why is this? Because they have distanced themselves from afflictions;
those who possess afflictions constantly indulge in self-display, whereas those without afflictions do not.
“The bodhisattva’s eloquence is without loss of meaning.
Why is this? Because he has attained the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).”
"A Bodhisattva possesses no eloquence that is without meaning. Why is this?
Because they have realized the Dharma."

“Good son! One who has not realized the Dharma may suffer a loss of meaning, yet they have not failed to attain the Dharma; however, for a Bodhisattva’s eloquence, there is no loss of phrasing. Why is this?
Because they master all sutras and śāstras, there is no deficiency in their literary composition if they do not study them;
yet, if they do study the sutras and śāstras, this deficiency does not occur.
"The Bodhisattva does not lose the correct method."
Why is this? Because they have already cultivated all methods.

The Bodhisattva has skillfully studied immeasurable scriptural teachings; because they do not miss the proper timing and are free from the error of sequence, the Bodhisattva possesses no harsh or coarse eloquence, no coarse or evil speech, and no words that are offensive to the ear.
Why is this? Because they have distanced themselves from harsh speech and all such faults.
"The eloquence of a bodhisattva is without anything that is not clear."
Why is this? Because they are endowed with sharp faculties. "Good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess these ten dharmas have pure and refined eloquence. "Good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are endowed with ten dharmas can bring about eloquence that causes all sentient beings to rejoice."

What are these ten? They are: affectionate speech; a countenance that is joyful and free from frowning; constantly explaining principles; constantly preaching the True Dharma; teaching the Dharma with impartiality; not boasting of one's own abilities; having no sense of contempt; a mind free from defilement; being neither frivolous nor restless; and possessing various forms of eloquence.
“Good son! A bodhisattva’s pleasant speech can cause the minds of sentient beings to attain joy.
With a countenance radiant and serene, free from frowning, and full of praise, they bring harmony and delight to sentient beings.”
"He constantly expounds upon principles and meanings, gladdening the minds of sentient beings through his measured speech.
He constantly preaches the Dharma, gladdening sentient beings through his beneficial words."
“They preach the Dharma with impartiality, causing all sentient beings to find joy in their minds.

These bodhisattvas do not display their own prowess; they remain far removed from arrogance, self-indulgence, and conceit, instructing beings according to their respective natures and ensuring that they invariably rejoice.”
“The Bodhisattva does not treat others with contempt, but diligently explains the Dharma for them so that they may attain joy.
The Bodhisattva is free from defilement; because he maintains pure precepts, he causes the assembly to rejoice.”
“The Bodhisattva is not frivolous or restless because he has extensively cultivated patience.
Through various forms of eloquence and pleasant speech, the Bodhisattva causes the assembly to rejoice.”
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, his eloquence is able to bring joy to all sentient beings. Good son!”

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is endowed with ten qualities, his speech and eloquence will be trusted and accepted by others. What are these ten? They are as follows: a Bodhisattva does not preach to sentient beings who are not vessels for the Dharma;

he does not preach to sentient beings who slander the Dharma; he does not preach to those who come to mock him; he does not preach to those with the false views of non-Buddhists; he does not preach to those who lack reverence; he does not preach to those who lack faith; he does not preach to those who are deceptive, crooked, or hypocritical; he does not preach for the sake of providing for his own lack of livelihood; he does not preach out of a desire for gain, profit, jealousy, or stinginess; and he does not preach to those with disheveled hair, those who go naked, or those who are mute.
Why is this so? Good son!

A bodhisattva has no stinginess toward sentient beings, nor does he withhold any secret Dharma; he has no lack of compassion and no failure to benefit them. It is only because sentient beings are not vessels for the Buddha-Dharma that the bodhisattva does not take them under his care.
The Bodhisattva Subduer of All Obstructions said:
"World-Honored One!
What kind of sentient beings are there for whom the bodhisattva preaches the Dharma?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son! A bodhisattva preaches the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings:

Those who possess the faculty of faith, those who are capable of being matured, those who possess the vessel of the Dharma, those who have already planted roots of goodness under past Buddhas, those who are free from flattery and crookedness, those who are devoid of all deception, whose deportment is truly without hypocrisy, those who do not cling to worldly fame or gain, those endowed with faith, those sustained by virtuous friends, those who perform various wholesome deeds, those who are easily awakened, those sharp-witted beings who can understand the underlying intent of what is taught, those who, through diligent and courageous effort, are able to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and those who practice according to the teaching—O son of good family! [Such are the ones for whom this is intended.]
For such sentient beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma.
Son of good family!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is endowed with these ten directions, every word he utters may be trusted and accepted.
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas is well able to preach the Dharma.
What are these ten?
That is to say, he expounds the Dharma solely for the purpose of practicing all Buddha-dharmas, yet in this exposition of the Dharma, neither the Buddha nor the Dharma can be apprehended;
he expounds the Dharma solely with the desire to practice the various pāramitās, yet both this practice and the pāramitās cannot be apprehended;
he expounds the Dharma to bodhisattvas for the sake of the conduct of enlightenment, yet both that enlightenment and the conduct of enlightenment cannot be apprehended.
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing afflictions, yet he does not apprehend afflictions nor the extinction of afflictions;
he preaches the Dharma for the sake of cultivating revulsion and realizing cessation, yet the Bodhisattva does not apprehend revulsion nor cessation;

he preaches the Dharma for the sake of the Srotāpanna, the Sakṛdāgāmin, and the Anāgāmin attaining their respective fruits, yet he also does not apprehend these—neither the Srotāpanna, the Sakṛdāgāmin, nor the Anāgāmin, as all such states are ultimately unapprehendable.
The Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma for the sake of the fruit of Arhatship, yet neither the Arhat nor the fruit of Arhatship can be apprehended;
the Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma for the sake of attaining the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood, yet both the Pratyekabuddha and the fruit are unapprehendable;
the Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing attachment and all views of self, yet both the self and attachment are unapprehendable.
Although the Bodhisattva speaks of the existence of various karmic retributions, both karma and its retribution are unapprehendable. Why is this?
He reflects as follows:
"The Dharma that is taught relies upon names; yet, by searching for the Dharma through these names, it cannot be found. Why is this?
That which is called 'Dharma' is not the substance of letters."
Now, as for written characters, they likewise lack the essence of dharmas.
For this reason, relying upon conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) through provisional names, one establishes names for dharmas that are nameless; thus, all such names are illusory and not real.
That which is not real is not the ultimate truth;
being neither true reality, it is a deceptive dharma that deludes all infants and ordinary worldlings.
“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas is well able to preach the Dharma. Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, there is nothing they do not accord with. Good son! When a Bodhisattva accords with the Dharma, he does not depart from form;

when he accords with the Dharma, he does not depart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; when he accords with the Dharma, he does not depart from the desire realm; when he accords with the Dharma, he does not depart from the form realm; when he accords with the Dharma, he does not depart from the formless realm; when he accords with the Dharma, he does not depart from the Dharma itself; when he accords with the Dharma, he does not follow sentient beings; when he accords with the Dharma, he does not follow the view of annihilation; when he accords with the Dharma, he does not depart from the Path. Through wisdom and skillful means, he is in correspondence [with the Dharma] and does not fail to accord with it.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, there is nothing to which he does not accord. Good son!”
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they will skillfully understand the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

What are these ten? They are: being endowed with wisdom; being sustained by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); possessing courageous diligence; remaining far removed from all obstacles; being well able to purify [the mind]; generating a heart of profound respect toward instructions; frequently cultivating the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); remaining far removed from deviant views; skillfully practicing the noble path; and clearly perceiving reality. These are the ten dharmas.

"Good son! The Bodhisattva Jīvitendriya draws near to virtuous friends; upon seeing spiritual benefactors, he gives rise to a heart of joy, conceives of those virtuous friends as the World-Honored One, and dwells in reliance upon them."

Having relied upon a virtuous friend, one applies courageous diligence to extinguish all unwholesome dharmas and to bring all wholesome dharmas to fulfillment; through such courage, all obstacles are completely extinguished.

Being free from obstructions, one does not cease on the path and thus attains purity, remaining far removed from all evil of body, speech, and mind, as well as from the karma of violating the precepts.
Having attained purity, one develops a sense of earnest respect toward the instructions;
having been taught with earnestness, one extensively cultivates the characteristic of emptiness;
having cultivated the characteristic of emptiness, one does not give rise to inverted views.
“Having abandoned perverted views, one cultivates the Noble Path;
having cultivated the Noble Path, one perceives reality.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
“World-Honored One!
What is called ‘the reality’?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! That which is called ‘true reality’ is not a name that is inverted.
“World-Honored One!”
"What, then, is non-inversion?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
"That which is not false is called non-perverted.
"World-Honored One!
What is that which is not false?"
The Buddha said:
"It is precisely the dharma of suchness, which is without change or alteration. [The interlocutor asked:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is called 'suchness' (tathatā)?
The Buddha said:
"As for suchness, it refers to the Dharma realized within oneself, which cannot be displayed by means of words."

Why is this so? Because this Dharma transcends all paths of speech; it cannot be expressed by words, letters, or phrases. It surpasses the realm of sound, is free from all vocal karma, and cuts off all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). It neither increases nor decreases; it neither emerges nor enters; it neither unites nor disperses. It is not subject to calculation, nor can it be conceived. It transcends the sphere of arithmetic and is not the domain of mental activity. It is without obstruction and beyond the reach of thought, surpassing the realms of all infants and the places where no infant can go. It transcends the realms of all Māras, the realms of all afflictions (*kleśa*), and the realms of consciousness. It is a place of non-abiding, a state of tranquil stillness that is the domain of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

Thus it is, thus it is: that which is internally realized is stainless, undefiled, untainted, and pure; it is subtle and supreme, ultimately most excellent, eternally constant and serene, a dharma free from arising and ceasing. Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the dharmadhātu remains ever thus.

“Good son! For the sake of this Dharma, the bodhisattva practices with diligence and without slackening; he cultivates vigor and endures various sufferings. Through such ascetic practices, he realizes this Dharma-realm, and within this Dharma, he further establishes all sentient beings.”
Good son! This is called suchness;
this is called the limit of reality; this is called all-knowledge; this is called the knowledge of all modes; this is called the inconceivable realm; and this is called the non-dual realm.
The Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇavijaya said:
“World-Honored One,
how should one realize it?”
"How should it be attained?
Is this Dharma-realm described as that which is internally realized?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! By means of supramundane wisdom, you should internally realize it and internally attain it.
Bodhisattva Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is that which is realized through wisdom an internal realization?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! It is not so. Why is that?
"By means of wisdom, one sees dharmas as they truly are and realizes them with the body.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
“Good sons, if one attains realization of this Dharma through the wisdom of hearing or the wisdom of reflection, is this not called ‘internal realization’?
The Buddha said, “Good sons!”
It cannot be. Why?
Because this Dharma cannot be internally realized through the wisdom of hearing, nor can it be realized through the wisdom of reflection.
“Good son! I shall now speak a parable for you. Good son!”

It is like this: in the latter part of summer, within a vast wilderness forest, suppose there is one person traveling from the east toward the western regions, and another person traveling from the west toward the eastern regions.
Afflicted by the scorching heat and distressed by thirst and exhaustion, they encounter the traveler coming from the east on the road and ask him:
"O worthy one!..."
"I am now afflicted by burning distress, parched with thirst and agitated.
Could you show me the way to a pond or a lake where there is pure, cool, and unclouded water that might quench this thirst of mine?"

At that time, a man coming from the east, who was thoroughly familiar with the route and had previously traveled along it, well-versed in the characteristics of waterways and having himself once drunk and bathed in this water, replied to him, saying:
"O virtuous one!..."

Proceed directly along this path; if you encounter a fork in the road, avoid the left side and take the right path until you see a lush, verdant grove. Within that grove are three pools of water, pure, fragrant, and delicious, soft, light, and cool, endowed with the eight virtues.
“Good son! What do you think?
When a person is afflicted by heat and oppressed by thirst, would they not merely by hearing the name of water and thinking only of that water be able to eliminate their thirst?”
"Did you immediately realize that this water was cool and cold? He replied, "No."
"Bhagavān!
It is like one who is parched with thirst: they must reach a place of clear, cool water; only after drinking and bathing can their thirst be removed, and then they know it for themselves."
“Good son! It is likewise that the two types of wisdom—those of hearing and reflection—cannot attain internal realization.
Good son!”
What is called "the forest" is a name for birth-and-death;
those who suffer from the affliction of feverish distress are all sentient beings. Why is this so?
Because they are oppressed by the heat of the afflictions—the three obstructions—they are parched with thirst for the five desires.

That which is called "showing the way" is the name for a bodhisattva; it refers to one who skillfully understands the path of all-knowledge, has realized this Dharma through the scriptures, and has attained realization within.
That which is called "clear, cool water" is the name for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"Furthermore, good son!
I shall now speak another parable for you; you should listen to it. Good son!"
What do you think?

If the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, were to remain in the world for an eon and, before the people of Jambudvīpa, extol the flavor of ambrosia—described as being perfect in color, fragrance, delicious taste, and purity, and being soft and supple—would these sentient beings, upon hearing this praise of the food, be satisfied?
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! For this reason, you should know that the two types of wisdom—those of hearing and reflection—cannot internally realize such a Dharma.
Furthermore, good son!”
Listen attentively to this parable. Good son!

It is as if there were a person who, having eaten a sweet fruit, recognized its exquisite flavor and praised it before a great multitude, describing it as being fully endowed with color, fragrance, taste, and texture.
"Good son! What do you think?
When these people hear speak of the taste of the fruit, do they obtain the taste of the fruit?"
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Based on this meaning, you should know that the two types of wisdom—those of hearing and reflection—cannot internally realize such a Dharma.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin:
“Excellent, World-Honored One! Excellent!
It is well said.”
"Sugata! World-Honored One!
When shall these sentient beings be able to attain this Dharma?"
Because of hearing this account through the causal condition of reaching the ears. Why is that?
World-Honored One!
"These sentient beings, in order to attain this Dharma, have heard this Dharma without error.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said."
Having heard this Dharma, because it is non-perverted, one shall attain this Dharma as being no different from myself.
"Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas thoroughly understands the dharma-realm."
“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas practices the realm of emptiness.
What are these ten?

They thoroughly understand the emptiness of the powers, the emptiness of the fearlessnesses, the emptiness of the unique qualities of a Buddha, the emptiness of the treasury of ethical discipline, the emptiness of the treasury of meditative concentration, the emptiness of the treasury of wisdom, the emptiness of the treasury of liberation, the emptiness of the treasury of the knowledge and vision of liberation, the emptiness of all phenomena, and the emptiness of emptiness itself.

One does not attain the dharma of emptiness by means of these causes and conditions; nor is one attached to emptiness, nor does one hold a view of emptiness, nor does one rely upon emptiness, nor does one fall into the mark of annihilationism because of these causes and conditions.
"Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas practices the realm of emptiness. Good son!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they abide in the signless (*animitta*). What are these ten? They are: being free from external signs;

being free from internal signs; being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); being free from all discrimination (*vikalpa*); being free from all that is obtainable; being free from all movement and fluctuation; being free from all spheres of activity; being free from all objective domains; not apprehending consciousness (*vijñāna*); and not apprehending the phenomena that are objects of consciousness.
“Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas dwells in the signless.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Subduer of All Obstacles addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas observe this markless dharma?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! This matter is inconceivable, and its meaning is profound and subtle. Why is this so?
Because it transcends the sphere of the mental consciousness, all sentient beings become deranged and confused regarding this realm of phenomena.
Good son! This Dharma of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; no sentient beings are able to perceive it.
This Dharma of the Tathāgata is subtle and profound, beyond calculation and beyond exhausting the mind and consciousness.
Why is this so? Good son!

This Dharma is difficult to enter; it is exceedingly profound, exceedingly profound, and inconceivable. It is without "that" and without "this," equal to empty space, and lies beyond the domain of all masters of treatises; they cannot fathom it, nor can they calculate it.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to submit a further inquiry today; I pray that you will deign to grant me your hearing.”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, answer whatever you wish to ask; I shall respond to it.”
The Bodhisattva Subduer of All Obstructions then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has taught, all sentient beings are unable to perceive this markless Dharma."
"Who is able to believe this Dharma of the Tathāgata?
Since the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma, praises it himself, is this not arrogance or overweening pride?
Indeed, arrogance is not the mark of a Great Man."
The Buddha said:
"Good son! You have asked well. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Good son!

The Buddha is free from arrogance and conceit; he does not speak for the sake of fame, nor for the sake of gain and offerings, nor for the sake of acquaintances. He does not falsely praise himself, nor does he falsely exalt himself. Rather, it is solely for the benefit of all sentient beings and for the sake of attaining this Dharma that he speaks thus.

Why is this? Because these sentient beings, having heard what has been spoken from the presence of the Tathāgata, shall attain great joy and immeasurable purity; they shall obtain this Dharma no differently than today, becoming vessels for the Dharma to bring long-term benefit and peace, even unto the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Subduer of All Obstacles said,
“World-Honored One!
Will these sentient beings not recognize the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! These do not know."
Why is this? Because the mind is inferior. Good son!

In this buddha-field, there are many sentient beings who are small-minded and inferior, weak and base, possessing little wisdom and little faith, and having meager roots of goodness; for this reason, they do not know the majestic and divine virtue of the Tathāgata.
For the sake of these sentient beings, the Buddha praised himself so that they might develop faith in him, saying:
"Good son! It is like a king of physicians who is skillful in treating diseases."

At that time, many sentient beings were deeply mired in the suffering of illness; in this village, there was only this one physician—no second, no third—and among the multitude of sick people, not a single individual recognized that this physician was skilled in healing and possessed great majestic virtue.
At that time, the physician thought to himself:

"These patients are pitiable in their suffering and distress, oppressed by manifold afflictions; they do not recognize the nature of medicines, nor do they know how to increase or decrease them. I shall now treat these sentient beings so that they may be cured."
At that time, the King of Physicians sighed before the assembly of the sick, saying:
"You who are ill should know that I am the Great King of Physicians; I am skillful in treating illnesses, fully understand the origins of diseases, and am well-versed in diagnosis and medicine."
Having heard this, the patient comes to believe and recognize him as a physician and goes to rely upon him.
The Great King of Physicians then treats the patient, and various illnesses are cured in due time.
"Good son! What do you think?
Can this physician be said to be arrogant?"
“No, World-Honored One,” he replied.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise thus: they are great physicians who fully understand all the grave illnesses of affliction, as well as the root causes of these diseases of affliction, and universally bestow upon sentient beings the wondrous medicine of the Great Dharma.”

Those afflicted by the disease of the afflictions do not recognize this; having perceived this situation, the Tathāgata, the King of Physicians, proclaims his own merits before the assembly of the sick.
When all sentient beings hear the exposition of the Tathāgata’s true merits, they all give rise to faith and take refuge in the Tathāgata.

For the sake of such people, the Tathāgata, the Great Physician, employs the medicinal herbs of the Great Dharma and various subtle and wondrous treatments to cure the grave illnesses of all afflictions, so that they are entirely extinguished.
What is called the great medicinal medicine of the Dharma?
It refers to the contemplation of impurity, the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion, the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, and so forth. Good son!
The Buddha, seeing such immeasurable benefits, praised his own virtues out of his own accord;
this was not out of arrogance. "Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas remains far removed from all reliance on vows."
What are these ten? They are as follows:

although one vows to practice giving, one does not rely upon giving; likewise, although one vows [to practice] morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the three realms, awakening, and nirvana, one does not vow for any of them at all.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva has distanced himself from all vows; being without any vow, he wanders throughout the world.
O son of good family!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess these ten dharmas, they remain far removed from all reliance on vows. "Good son!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they take loving-kindness as their body."

What are the ten? They are: the perfection of compassion that is without partiality; the perfection of compassion that is without distinction between self and other; the perfection of compassion for the Dharma; the perfection of compassion that is tranquil; the perfection of compassion that does not dwell on past transgressions; the perfection of compassion that brings benefit; the perfection of compassion that is impartial toward all sentient beings; the perfection of compassion free from anger and resentment; the perfection of compassion that universally covers the realms of the ten directions; and the perfection of supramundane compassion.
“Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas takes compassion as his body. Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they take compassion as their body.
What are these ten? They are:
seeing that all sentient beings are suffering, distressed, without rescue, without protection, and without a place of refuge, they give rise to the bodhicitta.
Having generated this mind, they exert themselves in practice, practicing with courageous diligence in order to attain these dharmas;

having attained these dharmas, they bring benefit to all sentient beings—seeing those who are stingy, they exhort them to abide in generosity; seeing those who violate the precepts, they exhort them to maintain the precepts; seeing those who harbor anger and resentment, they exhort them to cultivate patience; seeing those who are indolent, they exhort them to cultivate diligence; seeing those who are distracted, they exhort them to cultivate mental concentration; seeing those who lack wisdom, they exhort them to cultivate wisdom. Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see that sentient beings are oppressed by intense suffering that is difficult to endure, they do not retreat from their bodhi-practice.
“Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas takes compassion as his body. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they abide in joy.
What are these ten? They are:
"I have already attained liberation from the prison of the fire-hut of the three realms of existence; therefore, I give rise to joy."
I have severed the net of birth and death and the beginningless entanglements; therefore, I give rise to joy.
I have successfully crossed over the various dragons of discursive thought that dwell in turmoil within the great ocean of birth and death; therefore, I give rise to joy.
For a long time I have upheld the banner of arrogance, but I have now cast it down; therefore, I give rise to joy.
I have shattered the high mountains of afflictions with the vajra-wisdom mallet, bringing them to ultimate exhaustion so that nothing remains; therefore, I give rise to joy.
I have found rest, and furthermore, I comfort those who have not yet rested so that they may attain gladness; therefore, I give rise to joy.

I have awakened, and for those who have not yet awakened—those long oppressed by the sleep of craving throughout beginningless worlds, whose eyes are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and delusion—I cause them to awaken; therefore, I give rise to joy.

I have already attained liberation from the various retributions of suffering within the six realms and evil paths; furthermore, I shall deliver all other sentient beings who have encountered these evil paths and are undergoing such retributive suffering, and for this reason I give rise to joy.

Since beginningless time, I was lost in the dense forest of the wilderness of birth and death, wandering alone without a companion, fleeing in panic and confusion, never having seen a path, not knowing the right way, and lacking a guide; today, I have suddenly encountered a teacher, and for this reason I give rise to joy.
Today I am gradually approaching the city of omniscience and am close to the seat of the Buddha, and for this reason I give rise to joy.
“Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he dwells in joy. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they abide in equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What are these ten? They are as follows:

regarding the objects of form perceived by visual consciousness, one relinquishes them within this state; one does not harm oneself through the realm of forms, nor does one allow them to become a festering sore.

He completely relinquishes all sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental objects cognized by the mind. He does not harm himself by cognizing phenomena with the mental consciousness, nor does he create sores or obstructions;

he dwells having relinquished the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). Within these three types of suffering, he does not harm himself, does not create sores, and has no obstructions, for his task is accomplished.
He dwells with a mind of equanimity toward the assembly of noble ones and gives rise to great joy toward them, further reflecting thus:
"These noble ones were originally on the stage of ordinary beings, whom I should have transformed and delivered.
Now that they have become sages, my vow has been fulfilled.
For this reason, he dwells in a mind of equanimity.
"Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas abides in the mind of equanimity. Good son!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*).

What are these ten? They are: descending from Tuṣita Heaven; entering the mother’s womb; manifesting birth; dwelling in the palace and enjoying pleasures; leaving the city to renounce the world; delighting in seclusion and practicing asceticism on the path; subduing the armies of Māra; sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and attaining perfect awakening; turning the wheel of Dharma; and manifesting *nirvāṇa*.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas manifest their descent from Tuṣita Heaven and even manifest their entry into parinirvāṇa?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Among the sentient beings in that Tuṣita Heaven Palace, there are those who cling to the notion of permanence."

At that time, seeing that the Bodhisattva—the most excellent in the world, the supreme and ultimate, the unsurpassed and boundless, untainted by sensual pleasures—had passed away from that state, their notion of permanence was extinguished and the notion of impermanence arose; relying on this notion of impermanence, they became heedful.

“Good son! Among those sentient beings in that celestial palace who are largely heedless, they give rise to a heart of joy toward the Bodhisattva; yet, being attached to sensual pleasures, they do not wish to go, nor do they cultivate the practice of visiting or serving the Bodhisattva. They think to themselves:
‘The Bodhisattva is always present, and we too are here; since the time is so vast and long, why worry about not being able to go and draw near to him?’”
Therefore, for the sake of eliminating the negligence of such sentient beings, the Bodhisattva manifests a retrogression and fall.
When those sentient beings suddenly see the Bodhisattva falling there, they experience great distress; they distance themselves from the five desires and no longer act with negligence.
Because they are free from negligence, they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Good son! There are sentient beings who are to be transformed while in the womb. When these beings behold the Bodhisattva’s majestic and sublime spiritual power within the womb, they immediately conceive a sense of wonder. For the sake of these beings, the Bodhisattva remains in the womb and preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate for them, ensuring that they will certainly and decisively attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

“Good son! There are sentient beings who should be brought to maturity when the Bodhisattva is an infant or while residing in the palace. For the sake of maturing those beings, and in order to accord with other inferior beings who delight in the Lesser Dharma, the Bodhisattvas manifest the appearance of an infant and dwell in the palace.”

“Good son! There are sentient beings for whom it is appropriate to see the Bodhisattva leave the city and renounce the world; for the sake of bringing those sentient beings to maturity, the Bodhisattva manifests such acts as leaving the city and renouncing the world.”

“Good son! There are devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others who delight in what is base and wretched; for their sake, I manifest ascetic practices. Furthermore, I manifest ascetic practices in order to subdue all those of other paths.”
"Good son! There are sentient beings who think:
'When the Bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, I shall go there and present various offerings.'"
It is for the sake of such beings that I manifest sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
These sentient beings, having approached the Bodhisattva and made offerings, will by virtue of these causes and conditions certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Good son! There are sentient beings who are arrogant and stubborn; for the sake of subduing them, the Bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment and conquers the armies of Māra.”

“Good son! There are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured; for the sake of their further cultivation of virtue and superior benefit, the Bodhisattva manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment.”

"At that time, when the Bodhisattva attained perfect enlightenment, all the various sounds throughout the trichiliocosm were completely stilled, and there was no part of the trichiliocosm that was not tranquil."
When these sentient beings see this matter, they give rise to great vows, saying:
"May I, in a future life, sit at the site of enlightenment and realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

“Good son! There are sentient beings who claim to be teachers of the world, yet they have not awakened to or realized the Dharma of ultimate liberation and purity; they will have no share in it in future lives. It is solely for the purpose of subduing such beings that [I speak thus].”

There are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured and who are capable of being vessels for the Dharma; for the sake of manifesting the Path to such assemblies, when this Bodhisattva attains the Way, he proceeds to the city of Kāśī to turn the Wheel of Dharma—a wheel of twelve aspects, complete with three revolutions—and therein he lets out a lion’s roar amidst the great multitude.
“Good son! There are sentient beings who should be taught and transformed through nirvana; in order to transform such as these, the bodhisattva manifests parinirvāṇa.”
“Good son! For these reasons, he manifests descending from Tuṣita Heaven to Jambudvīpa, and even manifests his entry into nirvana.”
“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas sports with supernatural powers. Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they remain far removed from the eight difficulties. What are these ten? They are: being far removed from all unwholesome karma;

not daring to intentionally transgress the prohibitory precepts established by the Tathāgatas; being far removed from stinginess and greed; having planted various roots of goodness under past Buddhas; being in accord with merit; being fully endowed with wisdom; possessing skillful means; making great vows; cultivating the perception of wearying detachment; and practicing with courageous diligence.
“Good son! A bodhisattva does not commit unwholesome karmas and thus does not experience rebirth in the hells.

There are sentient beings who fall into the hells and undergo various kinds of undesirable suffering; after enduring such suffering for a long time, they give rise to mutual anger toward one another among those beings in the hells.”
Furthermore, because this bodhisattva’s natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) are pure and the ten wholesome paths of action are fully perfected, the bodhisattva does not fall into hell. "Good son!

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dares not intentionally transgress any prohibitions established by the Tathāgatas, but rather receives and maintains them in accordance with them, he is not born in the evil realm of animals."
Why is this? Because these various animals undergo the sufferings of the animal realm. “Good son!

Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva has no mind of stinginess or greed— since it is due to the causes and conditions of stinginess and greed that one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts and undergoes the sufferings of a hungry ghost—
a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not born into a lowly family characterized by wrong views.
Why is this? Because sentient beings with wrong views are unable to draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
For what reason?

Because the Bodhisattva has planted various roots of goodness under the Tathāgatas of the past throughout many kalpas, by these causes and conditions, in birth after birth and life after life, he is born into families of right view, possesses abundant wealth, and is fully endowed with the causal factors for practicing the Way; thus, his merit and wisdom increase ever further.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains all faculties without exception; by this causal condition, the perfection of the faculties serves as a vessel for the Buddha-dharma.

Therefore, because the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of merit is in accord with the karma of blessings and virtue, they provide various offerings to the Buddha’s stūpas and temples, to the Dharma, and to the Saṃgha.
Through the causal conditions of these offerings, they cultivate wholesome karma, and by means of this, they attain the perfection of the faculties.
Because they possess all the sense faculties, they become vessels for the teachings of the Buddhas.
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are not born in borderlands. Why is this?

Sentient beings in the borderlands are dull-witted, ignorant, and obstinate; they are mute and unable to understand or comprehend speech. They are like sheep, incapable of hearing or receiving wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, and they fail to recognize the profound intent or the underlying principles. Thus, they are unfit vessels for the nectar of the Dharma, are not called śramaṇas, and are not called lay devotees (upāsakas). For this reason, the Bodhisattva is born in the Central Land.

The sentient beings of China possess sharp faculties and sagacious wisdom; their senses are clear and discerning, and they are praised by the wise. They are capable of receiving the teachings on wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, deeply understanding their underlying intent, and are worthy vessels for the nectar of the Buddhas; they are called śramaṇas and called faithful laymen (upāsakas).
Why is this? It is because of the power of past vows and the power of wisdom.

A bodhisattva is not born among the long-lived devas; for if they were to be born and dwell there, even though immeasurable Buddhas appear in the world, they would not receive the moisture of the Dharma nor obtain the benefits of the Dharma, and their ability to benefit sentient beings would thus be abandoned.
Therefore, Bodhisattvas are born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to teach and bring to maturity the sentient beings of the lower realms, encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Why is this? It is because such Bodhisattvas possess skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
“A Bodhisattva is not born in a place where no Buddha has appeared. Why is this?

Because in such places, sentient beings do not hear the name of the Buddha, do not hear the name of the Dharma, do not hear the name of the Sangha, and do not revere the Triple Gem; therefore, the Buddha-land in which a Bodhisattva is born possesses the Three Jewels, for it fulfills the vows he originally made in the past.”
“Sentient beings are stubborn, rigid, and difficult to transform;
Bodhisattvas are not so. Why is this?
Upon hearing of the suffering of the eight difficult conditions, there is none who does not feel weary of them and seek liberation from them.
Because of this weariness and desire for liberation, one applies oneself with courageous diligence, practicing right effort in order to extinguish such unwholesome dharmas.
“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas remains far removed from the eight difficulties. Good son!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they will not forget the bodhicitta.
What are these ten? They are:
being far removed from illusion, delusion, flattery, crookedness, and arrogance; being upright, honest, harmonious, and refined; and having pure faith.
Within the True Dharma, they sever doubt and regret; toward those sentient beings who delight in receiving the Dharma, they are not stingy and do not act as secretive teachers.
They distance themselves from all conditions that could harm the True Dharma and do not transgress them, practicing according to what is taught.

They uphold all the scriptures of the Mahāyāna; if they see someone upholding the Mahāyāna, they give rise to a heart of profound respect, bowing with reverence and regarding them as a fellow student. With single-minded devotion, they listen to and receive the Mahāyāna, and they conceive the thought of the Tathāgata toward the one who preaches the Dharma.
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas does not forget the bodhicitta. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they attain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).

What are these ten? They are: having already made extensive offerings to and served many Buddhas; having already received and upheld the true Dharma of the Buddhas; purity of the categories of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*); being far removed from restlessness and regret; being free from all hindrances; having a mind full of joy; cultivating the mind to make it straight; attaining entry into meditative concentration (*dhyānasamādhi*); constantly receiving birth through transformation (*upapāduka*); and having no mind of doubt or confusion.

“Good son! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have made extensive offerings to the Buddhas of the past, they revere the True Dharma and maintain a humble attitude toward those who uphold the Dharma. By these causes and conditions, they approach to listen to the True Dharma; they receive, uphold, read, recite, and master its phrases and sentences; they extensively explain and analyze it for others, propagating the True Dharma without begrudging their own bodies or lives.”

"Purity of restraint means that by upholding pure precepts regarding the three categories of conduct—namely, body, speech, and mind—one becomes free from agitation and regret and gives rise to reverence."

Why is this? Because through the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*), there is no agitation or regret; because there is no agitation or regret, one is free from hindrances; being free from hindrances, joy (*prāmodya*) arises; with abundant joy, one is able to endure the cultivation of the mind so that it becomes upright; through the cultivation of the mind, one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*); by attaining meditative concentration, the six realms (*ṣadgati*) are purified; because the six realms are purified, one receives transformational birth (*upapāduka*); receiving transformational birth, one is free from a doubting mind; being free from doubt, one attains the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), recollecting one life, two lives, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of births.
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas attains the knowledge of past lives. Good son!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they encounter virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). What are these ten? They are: not being separated from seeing the Buddha; not being separated from hearing the Dharma;

not being separated from making offerings to the Sangha, the field of merit; not being separated from reverently prostrating, humbly joining the palms, and serving all Buddhas and bodhisattvas; not being separated from those who are learned and who preach the Dharma; not being separated from hearing about the practices of the various *pāramitās*; not being separated from hearing about the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); not being separated from hearing about the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); not being separated from hearing about the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*); and not being separated from hearing about the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas encounters virtuous friends. Good son!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they remain far removed from evil associates (*pāpamitra*).

What are these ten? They are: being far removed from those who break the precepts—this should be known as being far removed from evil associates; being far removed from those with wrong views; being far removed from those who have lost dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*); being far removed from those who live by wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*); being far removed from dwelling amidst clamor and confusion; being far removed from those who are indolent and lazy; being far removed from those who delight in dwelling within birth and death (*saṃsāra*); being far removed from those who turn their backs on the practice of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*); being far removed from associating with householders; and being far removed from all afflictions (*kleśa*). These are what are called evil associates, and Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should remain far removed from them.
"Good son!

Although you have left that place, do not give rise to evil thoughts or anger toward sentient beings; let your mind be free from affliction and heat, and do not treat them with contempt. Regarding those beings before you, you should think:
'As the Buddha has taught, all sentient beings are a collection of karmic affinities; it is because they associate with evil friends that they lose their great benefit.'"
"Therefore, I shall now swiftly distance myself from all evil associates. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he is free from evil associates."
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas attains the Buddha-dharmakāya.
What are these ten?

That which is called the peerless body, the pure body, the body free from blemish, the body not attained through cultivation, the inconceivable body, the profoundly deep Dharma-body, the non-conceptual body, the tranquil body, the space-like body, and the Buddha-wisdom body.
“Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who possesses these ten dharmas attains the Buddha-dharmakāya.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In what place does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide so as to be able to attain such a dharma-body as that of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! In the first stage, one attains the body that is equal to the unequaled. Why is this?
Because they are far removed from all distinctions of body and accord with the equal Dharma of all bodhisattvas;
because bodhisattvas of the second stage attain a pure body through the purity of the category of ethical discipline (*śīla*);
and because bodhisattvas of the third stage attain a body free from sores, having distanced themselves from all malice and resentment.
Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage attain the body not acquired through cultivation, because they have already cultivated the Buddha-dharma;
Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage attain the inconceivable and incalculable body, because they have already attained thorough penetration of all dharmas;
Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage attain the profoundly deep dharma-body, because they have already cultivated the dharma that is beyond measure or thought.
Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage attain an inconceivable body because they have already cultivated skillful means;
Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage attain a tranquil body because they have distanced themselves from all conceptual proliferation and are free from afflictions;
Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage attain a body equal to space because their radiance is all-pervading.
Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage attain the body of wondrous wisdom. Why is this?
Because they have universally cultivated all objects of knowledge.
The Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇavijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there perhaps no difference between the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata and the Dharma-body of the Bodhisattva?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! While there is no distinction in obtaining various bodies, there is indeed a distinction in the clarity or obscurity of their merits.”
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that while there is no difference among their various bodies, there is a unique distinction in their merit, majestic power, and spiritual authority?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! That body and this body are without distinction."
Why is this? Because it is cultivated through a single body.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the majestic spiritual power of these merits possess distinct differences; one should contemplate them accordingly.
The Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇavijaya said:
“World-Honored One,
how should one contemplate the distinction between the two bodies?”
The Buddha said,
"Good son, listen attentively,
listen attentively! I shall provide you with a parable to establish this meaning."
"Good son!
Suppose there is a maṇi jewel that has been polished, refined, and adorned until its radiance is bright and pure because of this processing.
Compared to other maṇi jewels that have not yet been processed, can it be said that they are equal?"
"No, World-Honored One!
That which has been refined and tempered possesses a pure and penetrating luster, for it delights the minds of all."
"That which has not been purified cannot be considered a counterpart.
The Buddha said, "It is so.

Although the maṇi-jewel of the Bodhisattva’s body and the maṇi-jewel of the Tathāgata’s body are both the same pure *dharmakāya*, the *dharmakāya* of the Bodhisattva, compared to the body of the Tathāgata, is ultimately pure and cannot be compared to it."
Why is this so? Because the body of the Tathāgata is immeasurable; it is coextensive with the realm of sentient beings and penetrates the realm of empty space, abiding in all-pervading illumination.
For what reason?
It is supremely pure because it is far removed from all dust and defilements;
yet, the brilliance of the bodhisattva’s body, like a mani jewel, is not like that. Why is this?
"Because there are still remaining defilements. Good son!
It is like the new moon, whose light first appears and gradually increases until the fifteenth day, when it finally becomes full and bright."
Both receive the name "moon," yet this initial moon cannot be compared to the moon on the fifteenth night.
Why is this? Because it has attained its nature by way of *dharmatā*.

Although both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas equally receive the name "Dharmakāya," the body of a Bodhisattva cannot be compared to the body of a Tathāgata in terms of the pervasive illumination of its radiance.
"Good son!

In this way, the body of the Buddha and the body of the bodhisattva are identical in their physical characteristics; yet, as for the characteristics of the Buddha’s meritorious virtues and majestic spiritual power, they do not constitute a single characteristic."
“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, he attains a vajra-like body that is chaste, real, firm, and indestructible.
What are these ten?
That which cannot be destroyed by greed, hatred, and delusion;
that which cannot be destroyed by resentment, anger, malice, the hindrances, pride, arrogance, false views, and perversion;
and that which cannot be destroyed by the eight worldly winds.
The sufferings of the three evil realms cannot destroy it;
the various sufferings of sentient beings cannot destroy it;
birth, old age, sickness, and death cannot destroy it.
It cannot be destroyed by the various non-Brahmins or heterodox teachers outside;
it cannot be destroyed by any of the Māras or celestial Māras;
nor can it be destroyed by any of the pleasures desired by all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
“Good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he attains a body that is adamantine, chaste, real, firm, and indestructible. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten qualities, he acts as a great caravan leader.

What are these ten? They are: being worthy of congratulation; being worthy of veneration; being able to deliver others across [the ocean of existence]; being worthy of reliance; being able to establish others [in the Dharma]; possessing abundant provisions; being equipped with the tools for cultivation and practice; being free from weariness or satiety; being a preeminent guide; and being skillfully able to lead others into the city of omniscience.
“Good son! How is it that a bodhisattva is worthy of celebration and even becomes fully capable of entering the city of omniscience? Good son!”
Just as a great caravan leader is to be congratulated by kings, courtiers, and ministers;
so too is the Bodhisattva, the great caravan leader, to be congratulated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the same way.
“Good son! Just as a caravan leader is revered by kṣatriyas and commoners,
so too is the Bodhisattva, the Lord of the Multitude, revered by those in training and those beyond training, as well as by other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas.”
“Good son! Just as a great leader can deliver others from vast forests, wildernesses, and perilous difficulties, enabling them to attain peace and happiness without weariness;

so too is it with the Bodhisattva Leader who, amidst the dense forest and wilderness of birth and death, delivers the various classes of sentient beings when they are oppressed by the bandits of afflictions, enabling them to attain peace and happiness without weariness.”
“Good son! Just as merchants who are impoverished and destitute, by relying upon a great caravan leader, are able to emerge from the wilderness and dense forests;

so too do the Nirgranthas, Brahmins, and various followers of external paths, by relying upon the Bodhisattva—the great caravan leader—attain deliverance from the vast wilderness of birth and death and its many great perils.”
“Good son! Just as a caravan leader is able to provide security for those who rely upon him, such as the military and civil populations;
so too is the Bodhisattva leader able to provide security for sentient beings within birth and death.”

“Good son! Just as a caravan leader, setting out in a certain direction with a great multitude, braving the dangers of mountains, forests, and wildernesses in order to reach that city of peace and happiness, possesses sufficient provisions so that he may emerge safely from the perils of the wilderness without feeling fatigue, and eventually arrives at that place of abundance and joy;

so too is the Bodhisattva Leader. He follows the path traversed by the Buddhas of the past, leading this great multitude of sentient beings, desiring to enable them to cross over the great险难 (perilous difficulties) of birth and death, and desiring to cause them to swiftly reach the great city of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Thus, he cultivates various provisions of merit and virtue, which are abundant and limitless, and proceeds while showing the way.”

“Good son! Just as a great master of a household travels in various directions carrying many kinds of requisites for living, such as treasures of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, jade, coral, and so forth;
so too is the Bodhisattva master, who proceeds toward the great city of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), skillfully cultivating the various practices of the Buddha-dharma.”
“Good son! Just as a caravan leader seeks various goods and treasures without ever knowing satiety,
so too it is with the Bodhisattva leader who seeks the wealth of the noble Dharma without ever knowing satiety.”
“Good son! Just as a caravan leader is the foremost guide for all merchants. Why is this? Because—”
Because he possesses abundant wealth, because he is preeminent among the multitude, because he acts as a leader, and because his speech is purposeful;
in this way, the Bodhisattva, the great caravan leader, serves as a guide for all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because their merit is abundant, because their stages are superior, because they possess mastery over the Dharma, and because what they teach is free from error. "Good son!

Just as a skilled caravan leader can safely lead [traders] to a land of abundance and fertility, so too does the Bodhisattva, the great caravan leader, skillfully lead sentient beings to the realm of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
“Good son! Thus, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he becomes a great lord. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten qualities, they act as a great guide and thoroughly understands the correct path.

What are these ten? They are: knowing when the road is level; knowing when the road is obstructed and perilous; knowing when the road is fertile and rich; knowing when the road is secure and peaceful; knowing whether there is water on the road or not; knowing the places of rest along the road; knowing the characteristics of the road; knowing when the road is straight; knowing when the road is winding; and knowing how to exit the road swiftly.
"Good son!
In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he thoroughly understands the right path. Good son!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they are able to demonstrate and guide the correct path without error.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
if there are those who should be transformed by means of the Mahāyāna, they teach the path of the Mahāyāna to such individuals, and do not teach the Śrāvaka-yāna to them.
If there are sentient beings who are to be transformed by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, he teaches them the path of the Śrāvakas and does not teach them the Bodhisattva Vehicle;
if there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of All-Knowledge (sarvajñatā), he teaches them the path of All-Knowledge and does not teach them the paths of the two vehicles;
if there are sentient beings who are to be transformed by means of the Pratyekabuddha path, he teaches them the path of the Pratyekabuddhas and does not teach them the Mahāyāna path.

If there are sentient beings who cling to the view of a self and cling to all phenomena, for their sake I teach the path of non-self, emptiness, and signlessness, and do not speak of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
If there are sentient beings who adhere to the two extremes, for their sake I do not speak of those two extremes.
If there are sentient beings whose minds are distracted, for their sake I teach *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and do not speak of distraction.

If there are sentient beings who engage in much conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), for their sake I teach the path of suchness (*tathatā*), and do not teach the path of proliferating ordinary people;
if there are sentient beings who delight in dwelling within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), for their sake I teach the path of nirvāṇa, and do not speak of birth and death;
if there are sentient beings who travel upon deviant paths, for their sake I teach the level path, and do not teach the path of afflictions, thorns, and brambles.
"Good son!
In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he is able to show the true path without error. Good son!"

Now, for the sake of the peace and happiness of my fourfold assembly of disciples, I shall protect the body and mind of those who preach this sutra and those who listen to it, causing their eloquence to be clear, lucid, and inexhaustible. I shall cause the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings to guard this assembly, enabling them to obtain the four kinds of offerings, to be free from all ailments and afflictions, and to have the four hundred and four diseases extinguished without remainder. In birth after birth, they shall attain the knowledge of past lives; they shall see the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and encounter virtuous friends, progressing ever further until they attain Buddhahood, fully endowed with the ten powers and the fearlessnesses.
And he spoke the mantra, saying:
"Tadyathā dhakaṭe...

Kālañjaraṇa cica cica sarvasattvānāṃ vāraya me svāhā ajina gata raji.
Acināṇi dīrgha-svareṇa svasti-svareṇa ca.

*Pṛthivī-mātā ity-iti svāhā.* Whether there be danger from fire, danger from kings, danger from calamities, danger from bandits, danger from evil spirits, danger from two-legged beings, danger from four-legged beings, danger from many-legged beings, danger from legless beings, danger from those with form, danger from those without form, or danger from afflictions—regarding all such dangers, one should with single-minded devotion recollect, uphold, and recite this mantra. Thereupon, all dangers shall be eliminated and removed; one will immediately attain peace and happiness, be forever free from fear, and obtain whatever one has wished for.
The Mahāyāna Ratnamegha Sūtra, Scroll Four.
The Mahāyāna Ratnamegha Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Mandarasa of Funan together with Saṃghavarman during the Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Five: On Peaceful Conduct (5). Chapter Five: On Peaceful Conduct.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying: "Good son!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice ten dharmas, their minds remain constantly tranquil and they dwell in peace and happiness wherever they may be.

What are these ten? They are: skillfully cultivating mindfulness and observation of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena; skillfully cultivating mindfulness and observation of sensory objects and forest hermitages; skillfully cultivating mindfulness and observation of villages, kingdoms, cities, and capitals; skillfully cultivating mindfulness and observation of gain, honor, and fame; skillfully cultivating mindfulness and observation of the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgatas; and skillfully cultivating mindfulness and observation of all afflictions—whether superior, middling, or inferior—in relation to skin, flesh, and heart.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva observe the body and dwell in peace and happiness?

By means of wisdom, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes this body from the feet to the crown of the head, seeing it as merely a person formed by the provisional combination of thirty-six impure substances. He observes that it arises and perishes moment by moment, is impermanent and subject to decay, is held together by tendons and veins, is filled with impurities, and possesses nothing worthy of delight. Observing in this way, he gives rise to weary detachment.”
Because of this revulsion, bodily defilement, bodily craving, the view of a self in the body, and attachment to the body no longer arise.
By these causes and conditions, all unwholesome states associated with the body are completely abandoned, and all wholesome dharmas associated with the body fully increase.
"How does one dwell in happiness by skillfully cultivating mindfulness through the contemplation of feelings?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects thus:
'All feelings whatsoever are entirely suffering.'"
Why is this so? Because infants and ordinary worldlings are dull-witted and devoid of wisdom; due to their inverted views, they conceive the notion of pleasure within what is actually suffering.
All noble ones perceive only this as suffering, and furthermore, they are able to establish all sentient beings within this Dharma, causing them to attain accord with it.

Training in this way, one attains the contemplation of feelings and dwells well-established in the foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), neither feeling aversion toward painful feelings nor craving pleasant feelings.
