Therefore, I shall now, without contradicting his mind, receive and uphold the śramaṇa’s precepts, his virtuous deeds, his status as a field of merit for those who have left the household life, and all such meritorious matters.
Then he had this thought:

"I must deliver all beings from beginningless birth and death. Since I have now attained renunciation and entered the Way to practice the conduct of a śramaṇa, this is my first crossing over from birth and death;
I shall further cultivate the virtues and deeds of a śramaṇa, which will be my second crossing over from birth and death."
I am now courageous and dare not be indolent, solely for the sake of attaining this pure Dharma.
Thus, I must deliver myself from beginningless and immeasurable birth and death.
“Good son! In this way, when a bodhisattva performs such contemplation, they know their own body. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they thoroughly understand the world. What are these ten? They are: to give rise to humility toward those who are resentful;

to give rise to reverence toward those who are arrogant; to practice straightforwardness oneself toward those who are deceitful; to cultivate truthful speech oneself toward those who speak falsehoods; to speak pleasant words oneself toward those who use harsh language; to be gentle oneself toward those who are coarse and aggressive; to cultivate patience extensively toward those who are cruel and poisonous; to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness extensively toward those who are malicious and unreliable; to cultivate a mind of compassion extensively toward those who are distressed and suffering; and to cultivate joy and equanimity extensively toward those who are stingy and possessive.
"Noble son!
In this way, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they thoroughly understand the world. Noble son!"
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they are born in a pure Buddha-field.
What are these ten? They are:
the purity of the category of ethical discipline (śīla-skandha), being without gaps, without admixture, without blemish, and without flaw;
They give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
their application of effort is non-dual, and they possess great roots of goodness;
they remain far removed from gain, honor, and fame, with minds free from defilement.
Having perfected the faculty of faith, their minds are free from doubt;
they are courageous and diligent, never for a moment succumbing to indolence;
and being fully endowed with meditative concentration, their minds are not distracted.
One who is widely learned engages in discernment and does not practice heterodox doctrines;
being endowed with sharp wisdom, one does not give rise to dull faculties;
being naturally abundant in loving-kindness, one does not practice anger or malice.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
"World-Honored One,
are ten dharmas fulfilled for one to be born in a pure land?"
“Can one also be born [in that state] if they are not fully endowed with these?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
If one were to fully possess even a single one of these ten dharmas—without gaps, without admixture, without flaw, without blemish, pure and lucid—one would be fully possessed of all dharmas.
Why is this? One attains birth in the Pure Land by being fully endowed with ten dharmas, not by failing to be so endowed. "Good son!
In this way, a bodhisattva who is endowed with ten dharmas is born in a pure buddha-field. "Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas does not undergo birth from a womb, which is subject to defilement."

What are these ten? They are: creating images of the Tathāgata; repairing ruined and dilapidated stūpas; constantly offering fragrant ointments at the stūpas and temples; bathing the Buddha images; sweeping, sprinkling, and plastering the stūpas and temples; making offerings to one’s parents by washing, laundering, and polishing them; making offerings to preceptors, instructors, and fellow students with a mind free from expectation; and dedicating the roots of goodness thus cultivated while saying:
"By these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings not undergo birth from a womb, but attain pure births and undefiled births."
"Because of their profound resolve. Good son!
In this way, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they do not undergo birth from a womb."
Except by the power of his vows. "Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas leaves the household life."
What are these ten? They are:
being free from attachment;
and not dwelling in confusion.
Turning one's back on the objects of craving;
remaining far removed from thirsting desire and unstained by worldly toil;
and accordantly practicing and upholding the Buddha’s True Dharma.
Exert yourself with diligence and learn well to be content;
wear robes as appropriate, take food and drink as appropriate, use bedding as appropriate, and take medicinal requisites as appropriate;
do not store away alms bowls, Dharma robes, or articles for daily life.
They constantly give rise to fear toward all sensory objects;
they incline toward tranquility and do not abandon the cultivation of the Path. Good son!
In this way, a bodhisattva who is endowed with ten dharmas departs from the household life. "Good son!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas maintains a pure livelihood."

What are the ten? They are: being far removed from arrogance, flattery, and gain; being far removed from outward appearances; being far removed from hypocrisy; not seeking wealth through improper means; being free from unrighteous wealth; being free from impure wealth; not being attached to wealth; not being defiled by the pursuit of gain; not thirsting for or craving wealth; and even regarding wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma, giving rise to contentment.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from arrogance, flattery, and gain?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not, for the sake of gain, become arrogant in body, arrogant in speech, or arrogant in mind.”
What is meant by not being arrogant regarding the body?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva encounters a donor or benefactor, they do not manifest any extraordinary physical demeanor, nor do they walk with slow steps to display an appearance of tranquility, nor do they gaze a fathom ahead as if appearing sorrowful, nor do they act with effortless spontaneity as if it were not artificial; all such forms of bodily arrogance are entirely avoided.
What is the absence of verbal arrogance?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not speak with calm, gentle, or affectionate words, nor utter compliant speech, for the sake of gain and offerings; thus, they remain entirely free from such verbal arrogance.
What is mental arrogance?
It is when a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, if there is a donor who wishes to make an offering of material wealth, verbally displays few desires while inwardly wishing to take much.
"Good son!
This is what is called harboring inner heat—namely, to claim with one's mouth that there is no greed while the heart truly desires to obtain.
What are the characteristics of being free from this?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a donor, they do not manifest such signs as showing that their robes and bowl are much worn out or that they lack medicinal decoctions; nor do they display their deficiencies in order to solicit alms, remaining silent with their speech.
“What is meant by being far removed from flattery?
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a donor, he does not say:
‘This donor, so-and-so, gave me this object; I shall repay that gift with my own kindness and virtue.’”
He does not say: "I have accepted this gift from that donor out of compassion, so that he may know I am observant of the precepts, know I am learned, and know I have few desires."
He does not employ the expedient means of exaggeration or disparagement to incite others.
"How does a bodhisattva avoid seeking wealth through improper means?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks wealth without inflicting wounds upon his own body or wounds upon his own mind."

Regarding the "wound of the body," it refers to not shrinking from toil for the sake of wealth and property, subjecting one's body to labor in all directions, engaging in urgent and frantic affairs, and violating the precepts.
Regarding the "wound of the mind," it refers to giving rise to much envy toward fellow students who have diminished gains and offerings.
"How does a bodhisattva avoid unrighteous wealth?
They do not deceive others by using light scales or small measures, nor do they seek wealth through feigned intimacy or various forms of fraud."
"How does a bodhisattva remain free from impure wealth?

If a bodhisattva encounters property belonging to a stūpa, property belonging to the Dharma, or property belonging to the Saṃgha—provided it has not been given and they have not consented to its use—they do not partake of it at all."
"How does a bodhisattva not cling to wealth and profit?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva obtains wealth and goods, he does not conceive of them as 'mine,' does not regard them as 'wealth,' and does not accumulate them. He dedicates them for giving at the appropriate times, using them to make offerings to his parents, various relatives, and kinsmen; furthermore, he must use some for his own needs at the appropriate times."
"When obtaining this wealth, one does not give rise to attachment;
when not obtaining wealth, one neither becomes anxious nor yearning, nor does one harbor ill will toward the donor or seize upon their faults."

"Regarding wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma, shared with the community, praised by the Buddha, not disparaged by Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, extolled by celestial deities, and welcomed with joy by fellow students—one dwells with contentment through these riches."
“Good son, in this way, a bodhisattva who is endowed with ten dharmas maintains a pure livelihood.
Good son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas has a mind free from weariness.”
What are these ten? They are:
dwelling in the cycle of birth and death without feeling weary, solely for the sake of the wholesome causes and conditions that benefit sentient beings;
and undergoing the sufferings of birth and death without feeling weary, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
To exhort sentient beings to cultivate wholesome dharmas without becoming weary;
to engage in all the activities of sentient beings without becoming weary;
and to preach the path of the śrāvakas to those of the Hīnayāna without becoming weary.
One does not harbor hatred toward śrāvakas;
one practices the factors conducive to enlightenment without weariness;
and one does not give rise to fatigue while fulfilling the conduct for bodhi.
One aspires for nirvāṇa, yet does not grasp at nirvāṇa;
one practices the conduct of bodhi, with the mind never ceasing for even a moment. Good son!
In this way, a bodhisattva who possesses these ten dharmas does not become weary in mind. "Good son!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas carries out the Buddha's teachings."
What are these ten? They are:
being far removed from all negligence and dwelling in non-negligence;
guarding oneself well and refraining from committing evil physical karma;
Guard yourself well, so as not to commit evil karma of speech;
guard yourself well, so as not to commit evil karma of mind;
always stand in fear of the evil realms and remain far removed from all unwholesome dharmas.
They speak truthfully of the principles of the Way, remaining far removed from all unrighteous paths;
they constantly proclaim the True Dharma and censure all that is contrary to the Dharma;
they distance themselves from base deeds and accord with virtuous conduct.
They do not defile the Tathāgata’s true Dharma and precepts;
they remain far removed from the foul stench of all afflictions, extensively protecting the Buddha-dharma;
and regarding unwholesome dharmas, they constantly guard their own minds.
"Good son! In this way, a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these ten dharmas carries out the Buddha’s teachings. Good son!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten qualities, their countenance is radiant and joyful, and their face is free from frowning.

What are these ten? They are: the clarity and purity of the sense faculties; the purification of the sense faculties; the luminous penetration of the sense faculties; the absence of defilement in the sense faculties; the brilliant whiteness of the sense faculties; being far removed from anger and resentment; being far removed from the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); being free from further fetters and bonds; being free from hindrances and grievances; and being free from all forms of malice.
“Good son!
Thus, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, his countenance is radiant and joyful, and his face is free from frowning.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, because their faculties are pure, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have serene and joyful complexions;
because they are free from afflictions, their faces are without frowns.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is. Good son!"
As you have said, because their faculties are pure, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have a serene and joyful countenance;
because they are free from afflictions, their faces are without frowns.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they are fully possessed of extensive learning.
What are these ten?

Regarding what is called the blazing of birth and death: the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows as it truly is the fierce fire of lustful desire; he knows as it truly is the fierce fire of hatred; he knows as it truly is the confused mind of delusion; he knows as it truly is the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); he knows as it truly is that the three realms are all suffering; he knows as it truly is that the world is empty and void; he knows as it truly is that all dharmas are without self; he knows as it truly is that the world is deceptive and false, clinging to false imaginings and undergoing the discrimination of rebirth; he knows as it truly is that all dharmas arise dependent upon causes and conditions; and he knows as it truly is the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*.
Having realized these three natures through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation exactly as they are, one does not merely provide their names through vocal discrimination.

Although one knows them thus, one generates an expansive mind, arouses great compassion, and makes firm vows; for the sake of all sentient beings, one uproots the source of suffering and exerts oneself with right diligence and valor.
"Good son! In this way, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they are fully possessed of extensive learning. Good son!"
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they shall uphold the True Dharma.
What are these ten? They are as follows:

during the final age, in the last five hundred years when the True Dharma is about to perish, when disputes and contentions arise regarding the Tathāgata’s scriptural teachings; when immeasurable sentient beings practice false paths; when the lamp of wisdom is about to go out and there is no one to provide guidance; and yet, they are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, proclaim, and reverently make offerings to the subtle and profound Sūtras—those of vast meaning, great majestic power, and which are the *dharmamātṛkā* (the "Mother of Dharmas") of all phenomena.
They are also able to reveal its meaning to others, explain it extensively, and make it easy to understand;
they give rise to great joy toward those who practice the Dharma and protect them with skillful mindfulness;
their minds are free from expectation as they delight in hearing the True Dharma.
One should conceive the thought of a World-Honored One toward the teacher of the Dharma; conceive the thought of nectar and the thought of a wondrous medicine toward the True Dharma;
seek the True Dharma without begrudging body or life, and having attained the True Dharma, practice it with diligent effort.
“Good son! In this way, a bodhisattva who is endowed with these ten dharmas upholds the true Dharma. Good son!”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they are born as Dharma-Prince Heirs.

What are these ten? They are: adorning the body with marks and being fully possessed of the secondary signs; the subtle refinement of the faculties and their complete fulfillment; following the path practiced by the Tathāgatas; dwelling in the realm of the Tathāgatas; awakening to the non-retrogressive dharma of all Buddhas; being skillfully able to rescue sentient beings from suffering and hardship; being skillfully able to study and practice the rules of conduct of the various sages; being skillfully able to traverse and contemplate the four immeasurable minds; abiding in the Brahma-abodes where the Tathāgatas reside; and being able to follow and stabilize the city of omniscience.
“Good son! Thus, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he is born as a prince of the Dharma. Good son!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they are welcomed by Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings. What are these ten? They are: the non-retrogression of the mind of enlightenment;

being unable to be disturbed or confused by any māras; remaining unshakable and immovable within the Buddha’s true Dharma; entering deeply into the subtle and secret treasury of all dharmas; conforming to the wisdom of equality regarding all dharmas; not following the words of others regarding the Buddha’s Dharma; attaining unimpeded wisdom within the Buddha’s Dharma; not being the same as any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; standing at the head of all worldly beings; and dwelling securely in the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"Noble son!
In this way, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they are welcomed by Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings. Noble son!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they know the various dispositions of sentient beings.

What are these ten? They are: knowing as it truly is when sentient beings have a disposition of excessive lust; or a disposition of anger; or a disposition of delusion; or a disposition of stubbornness; or a disposition of mediocrity; or a disposition of gentleness; or a disposition of cruelty; or a disposition of impetuosity; or a disposition of sluggishness—knowing them as they truly are. Just as they know one person, so too do they know all throughout the realm of sentient beings.
"Good son! In this way, a bodhisattva who possesses these ten dharmas knows the various capacities and natures [of sentient beings]. Good son!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they skillfully know how to bring sentient beings to maturity.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
if there are those who should be delivered by means of the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya), he immediately manifests the form-body of the Tathāgata for them.
If there are those who should be delivered by means of a bodhisattva’s form-body, he manifests a bodhisattva’s form-body;
if there are those who should be delivered by means of a pratyekabuddha’s body, he manifests a pratyekabuddha’s body;
if there are those who should be delivered by means of a śrāvaka’s body, he manifests a śrāvaka’s body; and for those who should be delivered by means of the body of Śakra...
To those who should be delivered by the form of Śakra, he manifests as Śakra; to those who should be delivered by the form of Māra, he manifests as Māra;
to those who should be delivered by the form of Brahmā, he manifests as Brahmā; to those who should be delivered by the form of a Brahmin, he manifests as a Brahmin;
and to those who should be delivered by the form of a Kṣatriya king, he manifests as a Kṣatriya king.
To those who should be delivered, he manifests his body accordingly; if it is by means of the body of an elder or a householder that they should be delivered, he manifests himself as such. Good son!
According to causes and conditions, through various methods, whatever will bring sentient beings to maturity is manifested in accordance with their specific causes and conditions. Good son!
In this way, a bodhisattva who is endowed with ten dharmas brings sentient beings to maturity.
"Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas is capable of upholding the true Dharma."

What are these ten? They are: being upright and gentle; having a mind free from flattery and crookedness; having a well-tamed mind; having a mind free from defilement; having a pure inner mind; having a nature free from coarseness; having a mind free from anger; being far removed from rudeness; having a mind abundant in patience; and being fully endowed with the capacity for the station of a Dharma Prince.
“Good son! In this way, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, he is capable of upholding the True Dharma. Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they dwell in peace and harmony.

What are these ten? They are: being endowed with right view; being endowed with pure vision; being endowed with the categories of ethical discipline (*śīla*); purity of deportment; engaging in appropriate spheres of activity; dwelling without afflictions; subtlety and precision in movement and stillness; harmony among fellow students; sharing in all matters; and practicing the path of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) without relying on other teachers.
"Noble son!
In this way, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they dwell in peace and happiness together with others. Noble son!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they skillfully cultivate the dharmas of gathering [beings].

What are these ten? They are: gathering sentient beings through the gift of benefit; gathering sentient beings through the gift of happiness; gathering sentient beings through the inexhaustible gift; gathering sentient beings through beneficial speech; through speech of true meaning; through speech of the True Dharma; through speech of principle; through the matter of benefiting others; through the matter of providing the necessities of life; and through the matter of benefiting others with material wealth.
“Good son! The gift of benefit refers to the gift of the Dharma;
the gift of peace and happiness refers to the gift of material wealth.”
The inexhaustible gift is to demonstrate the correct principle;
the beneficial teaching is to exhort others to cultivate goodness;
and the teaching of true meaning refers to discourse that is non-erroneous.
The teaching of the True Dharma is that which accords with the teachings subsumed within the Buddha's instruction;
the teaching of principle is that which does not contradict actual reality;
and the matter of benefit is that which turns one away from the unwholesome and causes one to abide in the wholesome.
Regarding the matter of providing for livelihood: it refers to food and drink;
regarding the benefit of material wealth: it refers to gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, crystal, amber, coral, agate, elephants, horses, carriages, and all necessary articles.
“Good son! A bodhisattva who is endowed with ten dharmas skillfully cultivates the methods of gathering [beings]. Good son!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they are fully possessed of physical beauty.
What are these ten? They are: their deportment is dignified and orderly;

they are entirely free from hypocrisy in the four modes of deportment; they are lovely to behold, like the autumn moon; seeing them gives rise to joy; gazing upon them one never tires; they gladden the inner hearts of others; they harbor no hatred toward any sentient being; all who see them are without fail filled with delight; and all who see them give rise to a pure mind.
“Good son! In this way, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they are fully possessed of physical perfection. Good son!”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they are able to serve as a refuge for sentient beings.

What are these ten? They are: to protect sentient beings from the fear of afflictions; to lead sentient beings out of the dense forest and wilderness of birth and death; to deliver sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death; to act as kinsmen for those who are solitary and abandoned; to act as a king of physicians for sentient beings afflicted by the diseases of various afflictions; to act as a protector for those who have no protection; to provide care for those who have no one to care for them; to act as a refuge for those who have no refuge; to serve as an island for those who have neither island nor shore; and to show the way to those who have no direction in which to go.
“Good son!
In this way, a bodhisattva who is complete in ten dharmas can serve as a refuge for sentient beings. Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten qualities, they are like a great medicinal tree.
What are these ten? They are as follows:

they are like the great medicinal tree named Sudarśana (Good to Behold). For sentient beings afflicted by disease, it may be used according to their needs; whether its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, bark, pith, flowers, or fruit are seen, smelled, tasted, or touched, there is none who is not healed.
"Good son!

If it is so for a bodhisattva, then from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, seeing all sentient beings afflicted by the various diseases of the afflictions (*kleśa*), they provide treatment through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Whether they see or hear of the bodhisattva’s merits, whether they draw near to them, or whether they partake of their flavor, there is no illness that will not be cured."
“Good son!
In this way, a bodhisattva who possesses these ten dharmas is like a great medicinal tree. Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, their meritorious deeds are in accord with the Dharma.
What are these ten? They are:
to manage and maintain the Three Jewels according to one's ability;
To those among sentient beings who are afflicted by illness, he gives medicinal decoctions;
to those suffering from famine, he gives food and drink;
and to those sentient beings oppressed by cold or heat, he provides warmth or coolness as required.
They deeply serve, revere, and attend upon their preceptors and ācāryas;
they pay homage to, welcome, and escort their fellow students, greeting them with palms joined and acting as a source of harmony;
and in various places, they establish monasteries and groves, providing timely gifts of rice, grain, wealth, and storehouses.
He bestows food, drink, clothing, and medicine upon his slaves, servants, and subordinates, and protects them;
from time to time, he visits śramaṇas who maintain the precepts and possess great learning, approaching them to pay homage.
“Good son! Thus, when a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, their meritorious activity is in accord [with the Dharma]. Good son!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they are well able to perform transformations.
What are these ten? They are:
while remaining unmoved and unshaken in a single Buddha-field, they are able to travel throughout all Buddha-fields to consult and receive instruction from the Tathāgatas;
Without moving or wavering from a single buddha-field, they travel to immeasurable buddha-fields to listen to the Dharma there;
without moving or wavering from a single buddha-field, they travel to the immeasurable fields of all Buddhas to make offerings to and serve those Buddha-Bhagavāns;
and without moving or wavering from a single buddha-field, they travel to the immeasurable fields of all Buddhas to practice the conduct of enlightenment until it is fully perfected.

Without moving or wavering from a single buddha-field, they travel to the immeasurable buddha-fields of all Buddhas; when the bodhisattvas in those lands attain equal enlightenment, they go there to make offerings, pay homage, and prostrate.
Without moving or wavering from a single buddha-field, they travel to immeasurable buddha-fields to manifest their own attainment of Buddhahood.
Without moving or wavering from a single buddha-field, they travel to immeasurable buddha-fields to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma.
Without moving or wavering from a single buddha-field, they travel to immeasurable buddha-fields and manifest parinirvāṇa;

without moving or wavering from a single buddha-field, they travel to immeasurable buddha-fields where there are sentient beings who should be delivered, manifesting transformations for them all and performing various supernormal powers to bring them liberation. Although they perform these transformations, they have no conceptual thought and no discrimination.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva perform various transformations?”
"What is meant by 'not reflecting' and what is meant by 'non-conceptualization'?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! I shall now speak a parable for you.
Just as the sun and moon illuminate the four continents and bring benefit to sentient beings, yet the sun and moon have no thought or discrimination.”

It benefits sentient beings by means of its radiance; however, it is solely due to past karmic actions, causes and conditions, and the ripening of results that such beneficial functions as those of the sun and moon arise.
Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva:
although they manifest transformations to benefit sentient beings, all of these are without thought and entirely without discrimination; they do not exert effort to carry out such karmic activities.
Why is this so? Because these transformations are all accomplished through the causal conditions of the Bodhisattva’s virtuous karma.

When the Bodhisattva practices the path of a Bodhisattva during the stage of causes, he makes great vows; by the power of these original vows, various transformations arise without thought or discrimination, requiring no deliberate effort.
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with ten dharmas will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these ten?
What are called the "myriad practices" are fully as previously described.
As for the myriad practices, they consist of the perfection of giving and the perfection of the categories of precepts.

Regarding the categories of precepts, they are without gaps, without admixture, without flaws, and without blemishes; they surpass the categories of precepts of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, being pure and lucid.

He is fully endowed with the aggregate of ethical discipline, fully endowed with patience, fully endowed with diligence, fully endowed with meditative concentration, fully endowed with excellent wisdom, fully endowed with skillful means, fully endowed with excellent vows, fully endowed with the various powers, fully endowed with subtle, profound, and correct knowledge, and fully endowed with the sublime wisdom he has cultivated.
It is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, as it transcends their sphere; from the first bodhisattva stage up to the ninth, it transcends their sphere.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with ten dharmas, they will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
*Mahāyāna-ratnamegha-sūtra*, Scroll Six.
The Mahāyāna Ratnamegha Sūtra, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Mandarasa from Funan, together with Saṃghavarman and others, during the Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: The Accumulation of Jewels (7). Chapter Seven: The Accumulation of Jewels.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, saying: "Good son,
there are four kinds of dharmas that cause one to fall away from the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
What are these four? They are:
lacking a mind of reverence for the Buddha’s true Dharma and failing to show respect to those who preach it;
being stingy and envious regarding the true Dharma, such that one does not explain it to others even when they come seeking it; [and so forth].
They create obstacles for those who delight in the Dharma, shielding and concealing it while giving rise to arrogance;
furthermore, they slander those who preach the True Dharma.
Ratnākara!
"These four dharmas cause the loss of wisdom. 'Good son!
There are four kinds of dharmas that increase the vast wisdom of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.'"
What are these four? They are:
first, to revere and honor the true Dharma and those who preach it;

second, to extensively analyze and explain for others the subtle and sublime true Dharma as one has heard and received it, preaching the Dharma without seeking fame or renown and with a mind free from expectations; [and so forth].
One should diligently seek the True Dharma as if one’s head were on fire;
whatever one hears and learns, one should firmly uphold and practice in accordance with the Dharma, rather than merely reciting its names.
"Noble son!
These four dharmas increase the vast wisdom of a bodhisattva. Noble son!"
If one possesses four qualities, one will completely forget the great bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
What are these four? They are:

failing to accord with one’s preceptors, ācāryas, and all fields of merit; causing others who have no doubt to harbor doubt; seeing those who practice the Mahāyāna and slandering them; and deceiving one's own mind while further deceiving others.
"Noble son!
These four dharmas cause one to lose the bodhicitta. Noble son!"

There are four dharmas by which the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s great bodhicitta naturally manifests in birth after birth throughout all lifetimes, without being lost in the interim, until he sits at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
What are the four? They are:
even at the cost of one’s own life, never to speak falsely, even in jest;
and knowing the truth, not to utter words of falsehood.
They give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; their minds are free from deceit and they do not deceive others;
and they conceive the thought of the Bodhisattvas as World-Honored Ones because they take no pleasure in the Lesser Vehicle.
"Good son!
Through these four dharmas, in birth after birth and life after life, the great bodhicitta will manifest spontaneously, never being lost until one sits at the site of enlightenment."
“Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses four qualities, none of his roots of goodness will grow or flourish.
What are these four?

They give rise to arrogance within themselves, diligently seeking worldly literature and incantations; they strive for gain and offerings, craving fame and reputation, and deceive others with a mind of fraudulence.
“Good son! Possessing these four dharmas, the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva will never increase. Good son!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses four qualities, their roots of goodness will increase in life after life, becoming ever more excellent, clear, and pure, never again to decline or be lost.
What are these four?

Abandoning all impure dharmas, one should diligently seek all pure and correct dharmas; for that which is called the "correct dharma" refers to the treasury of the Bodhisattva-dharmas, namely the six pāramitās.
Toward all sentient beings, one should have no pride in one's heart, remaining like a domestic dog.

Receiving offerings in accordance with the Dharma, one should know one's own measure, abandon all forms of false pride and arrogance, and dwell in the noble lineages with a mind at peace and contented.
One does not speak of the faults or virtues—whether real or unreal—of others, nor does one seek out the shortcomings of others.

Even if one’s mind has not yet attained thorough penetration regarding all phenomena, one will continue to increase one's roots of goodness from lifetime to lifetime, becoming increasingly superior, clear, and pure, never again falling back or losing them.
“Good son! There are four kinds of deceitful and crooked minds that a bodhisattva should always abandon.
What are these four?
Regarding the various teachings of the Buddha, if one gives rise to doubt, regret, or indecision, one should reflect upon those things that are not to be disparaged, thinking:
"Only the Buddha is my witness."
"The Buddha-dharma is immeasurable; it is taught according to the capacities of all sentient beings.
It is profoundly deep and difficult to understand, known only by the Buddha himself, and is not within the scope of my understanding.
For this reason, one does not give rise to a mind of opposition.
"Good son!

These are called the four dharmas that cause sentient beings to give rise to arrogance, anger, resentment, and affliction; to conceive envy toward the gains and offerings of others; and to revile Bodhisattvas and spread their ill repute."
“Good son! These are called the four kinds of deceitful and crooked minds; a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should always abandon them. Good son!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess four characteristics of reality.
What are these four? They are:
never concealing any committed offenses, but instead confessing and repenting them before others, reforming their past ways, and having a mind free from the entanglements of afflictions.
If, by speaking the truth, one were to lose one’s kingdom, life, or wealth, even in such urgent matters, one does not abandon truthful speech nor utter other words based on different circumstances;

when encountering all manner of evil deeds—insults, slanders, beatings, bindings, and various forms of injury—and while undergoing such suffering, one only reproaches oneself and attributes it to past karma, feeling no resentment toward others and harboring no ill will, remaining well-established in the power of faith because of the purity of one’s own mind;
and if, regarding the profound teachings of the Buddhas—which are difficult to believe and difficult to understand—one is able to fully believe in them, accept them, recite them, and uphold them.
"Good son! These are called the four marks of a bodhisattva’s true and straightforward nature. Good son!"
There are four qualities that constitute the characteristics of being stubborn, difficult to discipline, and difficult to subdue. What are these four?

Reciting the scriptures while treating them as mere frivolous discourse; though speaking the Dharma with one's mouth, failing to act in accordance with it; and being rebellious toward and disbelieving of all instructions.
They are unable to follow, respectfully serve, or make offerings to their preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), and various fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) so as to gladden their hearts;
they squander the faithful offerings and respectful services of others, violating their own original vows while accepting such offerings;
and upon seeing various taming Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, they treat them with contempt and give rise to arrogance rather than showing respect.
“Good son! These are called the four kinds of dharmas that constitute the characteristics of a bodhisattva who is stubborn, difficult to discipline, and difficult to subdue. Good son!”
Bodhisattvas have four signs of being well-disciplined and compliant. What are these four?
They skillfully expound the Dharma according to what they have heard; they act in accordance with their words; they rely upon the Dharma rather than relying upon mere verbal expression.
Receiving and honoring the teacher’s instructions, they are able to understand their intent; they are easy to converse with, and all that they do is wholesome, never failing the teacher’s purpose.
They do not regress from ethical discipline or meditative concentration, receiving offerings with a mind of harmony and compliance.

Seeing those who are well-disciplined, faithful, compliant, and great beings (mahāsattvas), they feel reverence and affection; following along with virtuous instruction, they receive and uphold moral conduct.
"Good son! These are called the four marks of a bodhisattva’s discipline and docility. Good son!"
Bodhisattvas have four kinds of deviant errors. What are these four? To agree with those who are untrustworthy is a bodhisattva’s error;

to preach the profound Dharma to sentient beings who are not vessels for it is a bodhisattva’s error; to preach the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to those who delight in the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is a bodhisattva’s error; and when practicing giving, to give only to those who maintain the precepts and honor the virtuous while not giving to those who are evil is a bodhisattva’s error.
“Good son! These are called the four kinds of deviant errors of a bodhisattva. Good son!”
Bodhisattvas have four right paths.
What are these four? They are:

generating a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; universally believing that all sentient beings are equal by means of the Buddha’s wisdom; preaching the Dharma with equanimity to all sentient beings; and causing all sentient beings to equally abide in right practice.
"Good son! These are called the four right paths of a bodhisattva. Good son!"
Bodhisattvas have four who are not good spiritual friends and not good companions.
What are these four?
Those who seek the state of a śrāvaka desire only their own benefit.
Those who seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha delight their minds in few activities;
they praise external scriptures, Lokāyata, and ornate compositions;
those whom they associate with only increase worldly gain and do not aspire to the gain of the Dharma.
"Good son! These are called the four types of individuals who are not spiritual friends and not virtuous companions for a bodhisattva. Good son!"
A bodhisattva has four kinds of spiritual friends and four kinds of virtuous companions.
What are these four?
Those who come to beg are spiritual friends, because they serve as the causal conditions for the Path.
Those who can expound the Dharma are spiritual friends, for they increase one's roots of goodness;
those who encourage one to leave the household life are spiritual friends, for they lead one out of the suffering of the triple world;
all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are spiritual friends, for they increase all the right and wondrous Dharmas.
"Good son! These are called the four virtuous spiritual friends and the four virtuous companions of a bodhisattva. Good son!"
There are four types of individuals who are not bodhisattvas in reality, yet resemble bodhisattvas.
What are these four? They are:

those who crave gain and offerings rather than seeking the Dharma; those who crave reputation rather than seeking merit; those who crave their own pleasure rather than rescuing sentient beings; and those who delight in gathering followers through the teaching of methods for extinguishing suffering, rather than delighting in solitude.
“Good son! These are called the four who are not bodhisattvas but resemble bodhisattvas. Good son!”
There are four kinds of true bodhisattvas.
What are these four? They are:

those who can believe in emptiness while also believing in karmic retribution; those who know that all phenomena are without self yet give rise to great compassion for sentient beings; those who deeply delight in nirvana yet roam within the cycle of birth and death; and those whose acts of giving are all for the sake of sentient beings, seeking no reward for themselves.
“Good son! These are the four kinds of true bodhisattva merits. Good son!”
Bodhisattvas have four great treasuries. What are these four?

If there is a bodhisattva who encounters a Buddha appearing in the world, thereby hearing the six pāramitās and their underlying meanings; who serves the Dharma-preacher with an unimpeded mind, never departing for even a moment; whose mind is free from indolence; and who dwells in an araṇya without negligence.
"Good son! These are called the four great treasuries of a bodhisattva. Good son!"
Bodhisattvas possess four dharmas that can destroy the works of Māra.
What are these four? They are:
never abandoning the bodhicitta; having a mind free from hindrance toward all sentient beings; being fully aware of all attachments; and not disparaging any sentient beings.
“Good son! These are called the four dharmas of a bodhisattva that can destroy the works of Māra. Good son!”
Bodhisattvas have four kinds of inconceivable meritorious deeds.
What are these four? They are:

practicing the gift of Dharma with a pure mind; generating great compassion for those who break the precepts; praising and extolling the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) among all sentient beings; and cultivating patience toward those who are weak.
“Good son! These are called the four inconceivable meritorious karmas of a bodhisattva. Good son!”
Bodhisattvas have four kinds of dharmas that shatter the afflictions and the ground of abiding ignorance.
What are these four? They are:

purity of the category of precepts—neither minor nor major transgressions being committed; upholding the True Dharma without shrinking from toil; offering lamps as illumination to the fields of merit; and giving away wealth and goods without partiality toward kin or strangers. These are called the four dharmas that shatter the afflictions and the ground of abiding ignorance.
“Good son! There are four kinds of dharmas by which one attains unobstructed wisdom. What are these four?

To constantly practice the gift of Dharma with a mind free of expectation; to uphold the true Dharma in accordance with principle; to feel no envy toward the gains and offerings of others; and to always restrain one's own mind so as not to give rise to arrogance—these four dharmas are called the means by which one attains unimpeded wisdom.

“Good son! It is not merely by name that one is called a bodhisattva; one who can practice wholesome dharmas and cultivate a mind of equanimity is called a bodhisattva. If one can accomplish thirty-two qualities, then one is named a bodhisattva.”
What are the thirty-two dharmas?
Constantly seeking profound peace and happiness for all sentient beings so that they may all dwell within omniscience;
constantly assessing oneself as a supreme vessel for the Dharma; not harboring hatred toward the wisdom of others; and destroying arrogance.
Deeply delighting in the Buddha-way, their mental ground is firm and steadfast; they are respectful without hypocrisy, and through their spiritual kinship, they ultimately attain Buddhahood.
Toward both friends and non-friends, their mind is always equal;

their speech is always accompanied by a smile, they know moderation in their words, they always offer greetings before speaking, and their face is never furrowed with frowns. Whatever deeds they undertake, they never abandon them midway.
With tranquility, he universally practices great compassion for all sentient beings with a tireless mind;
he is insatiable in his extensive learning, reproaches his own faults, and does not deride the shortcomings of others; he reprimands those who have committed offenses out of compassion;
he performs all formal dignities with the bodhicitta; and in the practice of giving, he seeks no recompense nor...
Practicing the precepts wherever one is born; giving rise to unimpeded patience toward all sentient beings;

exerting diligent effort for the sake of cultivating all roots of goodness; dispelling attachment to the formless realm within meditative concentration; practicing the wisdom of skillful means in accordance with the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);
maintaining equanimity of compassionate heart whether others uphold or violate the precepts; and listening with a sincere mind.
Regarding the Dharma, their minds delight in seclusion; they dwell in *āraṇya* hermitages without taking pleasure in or becoming attached to the various worldly splendors.
Within the Mahāyāna, they perceive great benefit; they distance themselves from evil associates and draw near to virtuous friends.
They constantly exercise equanimity through the four types of *brahmavihāra*, sport with the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and always rely upon [the Dharma].
True wisdom neither abandons nor rejects sentient beings, whether they engage in wrong or right conduct;
it always maintains a firm resolve to honor the Dharma of reality, and takes the bodhicitta as the foremost of all roots of goodness.
If a person is endowed with these thirty-two qualities, they may be designated as holding the rank of a bodhisattva.
"Good son! The merits of a bodhisattva are immeasurable and boundless; one should know them through the causes and conditions of parables."
"Good son! Just as the great earth accommodates all sentient beings without a discriminating mind and without seeking repayment for its kindness, so too is the Bodhisattva:

from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until sitting at the site of awakening, all sentient beings receive benefit, yet the Bodhisattva’s mind remains free of discrimination and seeks no repayment."
“Good son! Just as all waters moisten and give birth to a hundred kinds of rice, medicinal herbs, thickets, and trees, causing them all to grow;
so too is the Bodhisattva: because his own mind is pure, he universally covers and moistens all sentient beings with compassion, causing them all to increase in all wholesome dharmas.”
“Good son! For example, just as the seeds of fire can bring to maturity a hundred kinds of grain, medicinal herbs, flowers, and fruits;
so too is the wisdom of a bodhisattva, for it can accomplish all roots of goodness.”
“Good son! Just as the wind-circle can establish all worlds and all Buddha-fields,
so too is the skillful means of a bodhisattva, for it can establish all wholesome dharmas.”
“Good son! Just as when the moon first appears, its radiance and color increase day by day;
so too is it with the bodhisattva’s pure mind—every wholesome dharma increases day by day.”
“Good son! Just as when the sun first rises, it emits light all at once to universally illuminate all sentient beings;
so too is the bodhisattva, who emits the light of wisdom to universally illumine all sentient beings all at once.”
“Good son! Just as the lion king is neither startled nor afraid wherever he goes, so too is the bodhisattva:
with pure ethical discipline and true wisdom, he is neither startled nor afraid wherever he dwells.”
“Good son! Just as a well-trained great dragon-elephant king carries heavy burdens without his body becoming exhausted, so too is the bodhisattva:
because he has well trained his mind, he carries the burden of all classes of sentient beings, performing great benefit without weariness.”
“Good son! Just as a lotus flower grows in water yet is not defiled by it, so too is the Bodhisattva:
though born into the world, he is not defiled by any worldly dharmas.”
“Good son! Just as when a person cuts down a tree, it grows back again if the roots remain;

so it is with the bodhisattva. By the power of skillful means, although they have severed the fetters and proclivities, because of their roots of goodness and craving, they are reborn within the triple world.”
“Good son! Just as the flowing waters from all directions enter the great ocean and become of one single taste, so it is with the Bodhisattva:
by practicing various roots of goodness through manifold gateways and dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all become of one single taste.”
“Good son! Just as the king of mountains, Sumeru, is the dwelling place upon which the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and the Four Heavenly Kings all rely;
so too is the Bodhisattva’s great bodhicitta, for it is that upon which sarvajñatā relies and dwells.”
“Good son! Just as a great king is able to accomplish state affairs through the power of his ministers, so too is the wisdom of a bodhisattva:
through the power of skillful means, it is able to accomplish all buddha-works.”
“Good son! For example, when the heavens are pure, clear, and bright, and there are no clouds or vapors, there will certainly be no signs of rain;
likewise, it is the same for a bodhisattva of little learning who lacks knowledge and understanding and is not moistened by the rain of the Dharma.”
“Good son! For example, when the heavens are overcast and clouds arise, rain will surely fall, sufficiently nourishing the sprouts and shoots that grow for all living beings;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva, who from the clouds of great compassion raises the great rain of Dharma to benefit sentient beings.”
“Good son! Just as wherever a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears, the seven treasures are present;
so it is with the Bodhisattva: wherever he appears, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment manifest in the world.”
“Good son! Just as wherever a maṇi jewel is located, there will be immeasurable gold, silver, and precious treasures;
likewise, wherever a bodhisattva appears, there will be immeasurable hundreds of thousands of jewels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
“Good son! Just as when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the Caitraratha Garden, everything they desire for their use is found therein;
so it is with the Bodhisattva: because of his truly pure mind, he teaches and transforms all sentient beings with impartiality.”
“Good son! Just as poison cannot cause harm through the power of mantras or medicinal herbs, so it is with the fetters (saṃyojana) of a bodhisattva:
by the power of wisdom, they do not fall into the evil realms.”
“Good son! Just as the discarded filth in a great city becomes beneficial if placed within fields of sugarcane or grapes;
so too it is with the fetters of a bodhisattva—the remaining habitual tendencies serve as the causal conditions for all-knowledge.”
“Good son! For example, if a person has never practiced the arts of the spear and halberd, they will have no martial utility;
so it is with the Bodhisattva: if they have not practiced all dharmas, they are unable to calculate, select, discern, uphold, and practice them.”
“Good son! It is like a potter’s unbaked earthenware; while it is not yet dry, it cannot withstand a great fire.

So it is with the Bodhisattva: because his wisdom regarding sentient beings is still weak, he cannot withstand hearing the Great Dharma of the Buddhas and therefore it is not preached to him; were he to hear it, he would fall into madness.”
“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to study the subtle *Ratnamegha Sūtra* should constantly practice the correct contemplation of the true dharma.
What is correct contemplation?

What is called "true contemplation" is the correct observation of phenomena; not observing a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span—this is termed the Middle Way, the true correct observation.
“Good son! As for true contemplation:

one contemplates that form is neither permanent nor impermanent; likewise, one contemplates that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor impermanent. This is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of dharmas.”

Why is this so? "Permanence" is one extreme, and "impermanence" is another extreme. Between these two extremes—permanence and impermanence—there is no form, no shape, no life, and no cognition; this is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.

"Self" is one extreme, and "non-self" is another extreme. Between these two extremes—self and non-self—there is no form, no shape, no life, and no cognition; this is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.

“Good son! If the mind exists as something real, this is one extreme; if the mind does not exist as something real, this is another extreme. That which is without mind-consciousness and also without the mental factors (caitta) and the universal mental states (mahābhūmika-dharma), is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.”

In this same way, it is with wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, mundane and supramundane dharmas, blameworthy and blameless dharmas, outflowing and non-outflowing, conditioned and unconditioned, and even with those that are defiled and undefiled: they are likewise free from the two extremes, neither graspable nor expressible. This is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all dharmas.
"Good son!

'Existence' is one extreme; 'non-existence' is another extreme. That which lies between existence and non-existence—without form, without shape, without life, and without cognition—is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of the Dharma."
“Good son! That which I have taught as the twelve links of dependent origination is as follows:

ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. Thus, through these causal conditions, this great mass of suffering is summoned and accumulated.”

If ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, thus do aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, and the entire mass of suffering and affliction cease.
Luminosity and ignorance are non-dual and undifferentiated; if one knows them thus, this is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Likewise, formations and the absence of formations, consciousness and the object of consciousness, name-and-form and the visible and invisible, the six sense bases and that which is not the six sense bases, contact and the contacted, sensation and the cessation of sensation, craving and the cessation of craving, grasping and the cessation of grasping, existence and the cessation of existence, birth and the cessation of birth, and old age and death and the cessation of old age and death—all these are non-dual and undifferentiated. If one knows them thus, this is called the Middle Way, the true contemplation of all phenomena.
"Furthermore, good son! As for true contemplation:
it is not by means of emptiness that all phenomena are made empty, for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is itself empty;
it is not by means of signlessness that phenomena are made signless, for the essence of the nature of phenomena is fundamentally signless from the beginning."
One does not make dharmas wishless by means of wishlessness; rather, the nature of all dharmas is inherently wishless from the very beginning.

One does not make dharmas unarisen, unborn, selfless, ungraspable, or without intrinsic nature by means of non-arising, non-birth, selflessness, non-grasping, or the absence of intrinsic nature; rather, dharmas are inherently, from the very beginning, unarisen, ungraspable, and without intrinsic nature.
If one contemplates in this manner, it is called true contemplation.
"Furthermore, good son, it is not because there is no person that it is called empty; rather, emptiness is itself empty."
The past, the future, and the present are also empty; it is simply that phenomena are empty by their own nature.
It is not that emptiness arises from the cessation of form; you should rely upon emptiness, and not rely upon persons.
If one attains emptiness and yet relies upon emptiness, the Buddha says that such a person has fallen into decline. "Good son!
It would be better to give rise to a view of self as vast as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to overweening pride through a view of emptiness."
Why is this? All views are liberated through emptiness; however, if one gives rise to the view of emptiness, it cannot be cured. "Good son!
Suppose a physician prescribes medicine to treat a certain illness, yet that medicine remains within and does not emerge.
What do you think?
Would such a patient be able to recover?
"No, World-Honored One!
If this medicine does not come forth, that illness will only increase further."
“Good son! Such views can only be extinguished by emptiness (*śūnyatā*); however, if one gives rise to a view of emptiness, it cannot be cured.
It is like a person who fears empty space, wailing and beating their breast, saying these words:”
"Set aside this empty space.
What do you think?
Can such empty space be removed or set aside?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Good son!"
Thus, if one fears the dharma of emptiness, I say that such a person is deranged and has lost their mind. Why is this?
Because they constantly practice within emptiness yet fear emptiness itself.
"It is like an artist who, with his own hand, paints the image of a yakṣa demon; upon seeing it, he becomes terrified, faints, and falls to the ground.

All ordinary worldlings are just the same: because they themselves create forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, they wander through birth and death, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction without realizing it."
“Good son! It is like a magician who conjures a fierce tiger by illusion; once the illusory tiger has been created, it turns around and devours the magician.
So too it is with the śramaṇa who practices the Way: whatever dharmas he contemplates are all empty, all quiescent, and there is no one who sees them; this contemplation itself is also empty.”
“Good son! It is like two pieces of wood that originally possess no quality of fire; yet, by rubbing them together, fire is produced from within them and subsequently burns those very pieces of wood.
Good son!”
Because one contemplates thus with reality, noble wisdom arises;
once noble wisdom has arisen, the contemplation of reality is then extinguished. "Good son!

It is like lighting a lamp: all darkness naturally vanishes; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. It does not come from the east, nor does it go there; it does not come from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below, nor does it go there.
Furthermore, this lamp-light has no such thought as,
"I am able to extinguish darkness"; rather,
it is simply because of the lamp-light that, by the nature of things, there is no longer darkness.
Both light and darkness are empty; there is no action and no grasping.
Son of good family!
In this way, when true wisdom arises, ignorance naturally ceases; both wisdom and ignorance are empty of dual characteristics, with neither action nor grasping.
“Good son! It is like a dark room that has been so for a thousand years, where light has never been seen; suppose someone were to light a lamp within it.
What do you think?”
Aṇḍa thought to himself:
"I have lived here for a long time; I do not wish to leave.
[The Buddha said: "No."
“World-Honored One!
When a lamp is lit, this darkness is powerless and must necessarily be extinguished. “Good son!”
In this way, the karmic bonds accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas can all be extinguished by a single wisdom of contemplation.
That which is the light of the lamp is the faculty of noble wisdom;
that which is darkness is the various karmic bonds.
“Good son! It is like planting seeds in the air; it is impossible for them to grow.
The realization of a bodhisattva is likewise: it is impossible for the Buddha-dharma to grow [from such a basis].”
“Good son! For example, it is possible for seeds planted in fertile soil to grow;
likewise, it is possible for a bodhisattva to have various fetters and worldly defilements yet still cause the Buddha-dharma to grow.”
“Good son! For example, just as lotus flowers do not grow upon the high plains and dry land, so too it is with the bodhisattva:
within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the Buddha-dharmas do not arise.”
“Good son! Just as lotus flowers grow from low-lying, damp mud, so too it is with Bodhisattvas:
from the mud of birth and death, and from sentient beings fixed in wrong views, they can give rise to the Buddha-dharma.”
“Good son! For example, it is as if the four great oceans were filled with clarified butter;
likewise, the conditioned roots of goodness of a bodhisattva are exceedingly many and immeasurable.”
“Good son! It is like this:
suppose one were to split a single hair into a hundred parts and take a single drop of ocean water with one of those parts;
the conditioned roots of goodness of all śrāvakas are likewise so.
“Good son! For example, it is like the space within a hole made by an insect in a mustard seed;
the conditioned wisdom of all śrāvakas is likewise so.”
“Good son! For example,
just as the empty space of the ten directions is immeasurable and boundless,
so too is the conditioned wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
“Good son! It is like this:

suppose the chief queen of a wheel-turning sage king has been pregnant for seven days, and the child she bears possesses the marks of a wheel-turning king; the devas hold him in greater esteem than all other sons who possess physical strength.”
Why is this so? This prince in the womb will surely succeed to the sovereign position and continue the lineage of the holy kings.
O son of good family!

A bodhisattva at the stage of initial resolve is also like this: although they have not yet fully perfected the characteristics of all bodhisattvas, they are deeply respected by devas, spirits, and kings, just as a prince in the womb is.
Why is this? Such a bodhisattva will surely succeed to the position of honor and shall not sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
"O son of good family!
For example, a single lapis lazuli gem surpasses crystal;
likewise, a bodhisattva, from the very first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, surpasses all classes of sentient beings. "Good son!
For example, on the day the queen of a great king gives birth to a son, the subordinate kings and the ministers all come to pay their respects;
so it is with the Bodhisattva: at the moment they first resolve their mind [on enlightenment], they are worthy of being venerated by all devas and people of the world.
“Good son! It is like the King of Snowy Mountains, where all medicinal herbs grow without partiality or discrimination, yet are able to treat every illness according to its nature;
so too is the Bodhisattva, whose accumulated medicine of wisdom is without discrimination, universally providing equal protection and salvation for all sentient beings.”
“Good son! Just as when the moon first appears, all people love and revere it even more than when it is full. Good son!”
In this way, those sentient beings who place their trust in my words love and revere the bodhisattvas even more than they do the Tathāgata. Why is this?
It is because it is from the bodhisattvas that the Tathāgatas are born.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnākara, saying:

"Good son! A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly cultivates and accumulates the pure conduct, pure merits, and unsurpassed roots of goodness for the benefit of all sentient beings. With a mind of equanimity, he bestows these upon sentient beings; the medicinal wisdom thus obtained reaches throughout the ten directions to treat the sicknesses of affliction and suffering, causing them all to reach ultimate cessation so they never arise again."

"What is called the medicinal medicine of the bodhisattva’s wisdom? It is as follows: the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) treats greed; the cultivation of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) treats anger; the contemplation of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) treats delusion; the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) treats all false views; the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*) treats the objective realms of conceptualization and discrimination; the contemplation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vipaśyanā*) treats all aspirations for birth within the three realms; the four non-perversions treat the four perversions; the contemplation of impermanence treats the perversion of conceiving permanence within the impermanent; the cultivation of the contemplation of suffering treats the perversion of conceiving pleasure within suffering; the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) treats the perversion of conceiving a self within the selfless; and the quiescent extinction of nirvāṇa treats the perversion of conceiving purity within the impure."

"The contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness—body, feeling, mind, and phenomena—is the antidote to the four kinds of inversion: by contemplating the characteristics of the body, one does not fall into the view of self; by contemplating the characteristics of feeling, one does not fall into the view of self; by contemplating the characteristics of the mind, one does not fall into the view of self; and by contemplating the characteristics of phenomena, one does not fall into the view of self. These four foundations of mindfulness can cure all [delusions regarding] body, feeling, mind, and phenomena, and open the gate to Nirvana."

"By means of the four right efforts, one can abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen, prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising, cause wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise, and cause wholesome states that have already arisen to increase."
To state the essentials: it is able to sever all unwholesome dharmas and accomplish all wholesome dharmas.
The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) remedy the mark of the body and mind being conjoined, enabling the attainment of sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

By means of these five faculties, one cures all sentient beings who lack faith, are indolent, have lost mindfulness, possess distracted minds, or lack wisdom; by means of these five powers, one subdues all afflictions; by means of the seven factors of enlightenment, one cures doubts, regrets, and delusions regarding all phenomena; and by means of the eightfold noble path, one cures all teachers of heterodox paths.
“Good son! This is the wondrous medicine of ultimate wisdom; a bodhisattva should constantly cultivate and gather it, and practice it with earnest diligence. Good son!”
Within Jambudvīpa, the physician-king Jīvaka is the foremost.

Even if all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm were made like Jīvaka, if someone were to ask about the medicine for the diseases of mental fetters, afflictions, false views, and doubt and regret, they would still be unable to answer, let alone treat them.
Within this, the bodhisattva should form this thought:
"I shall never consider worldly medicines sufficient; I must cultivate the medicine of supramundane wisdom and also cultivate all roots of goodness and merit."

"In this way, having obtained the medicinal herbs of wisdom, the bodhisattva travels throughout the ten directions to ultimately treat the diseases of afflictions and other ailments of all sentient beings.
What is called the 'transcendent medicinal herb of wisdom' of a bodhisattva?"

One comes to know with faith that all phenomena arise from the convergence of conditions; one believes that all phenomena are without self and without person, and likewise lack the notions of a sentient being or a life-span; one believes that there is neither an agent nor an experiencer, and through faith and understanding, one penetrates the realization that there is no self and nothing belonging to a self.

Thus, within this emptiness where nothing can be apprehended, one is neither startled nor afraid, but exerts diligent effort to seek the characteristics of the mind; in this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks the mind.
“What is this mind? Is it desire?
Or is it hatred?”
Is it delusion?
Is it past, future, or present?
If the mind is past, it has already ceased.
If the mind is in the future, the future has not yet arrived;
if the mind is in the present, the present does not abide.
This mind is neither internal, nor external, nor in between. This mind is without form, without consciousness, without shape, without visibility, without cognition, and without a place of abiding.
A mind such as this has never been seen by all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; it is not being seen now, nor will it be seen in the future.
If that which has not been seen by all Buddhas of the past, present, and future does not exist, how could it possibly be?
It is solely due to the conditions of inverted false conceptualization that the mind gives rise to the various distinctions among all phenomena. "Good son!
This mind is like an illusion; through recollection, thought, and discrimination, it gives rise to various karmas and undergoes various bodies."
“Good son! The mind moves like the wind; when it wanders far into realms that are not its own domain, it is difficult to restrain.
The mind is like a flowing stream, arising and ceasing without ever remaining still.”
The mind is like the flame of a lamp, existing due to a multitude of conditions;
this mind is like lightning, ceasing without stopping for even a single moment;
the mind is like space, obscured by adventitious afflictions.
The mind is like a monkey, grasping at one thing and letting go of another as it roams through all sensory objects;
the mind is like a painter, for it is able to create the various causes and conditions of karma;
the mind is never momentarily settled, as it pursues and follows after all manner of afflictions.
The mind is solely singular, for there is no second;
the mind is like a great king, for it is the sovereign lord over all phenomena;
the mind always travels alone, for it has no companion.
The mind is like an enemy, for it is capable of producing all manner of suffering and affliction;
the mind is like a mad elephant trampling the mud huts of small children, for it is capable of destroying all roots of goodness;
this mind is greedily attached like a fish swallowing a hook, for it conceives the notion of pleasure within the experience of suffering.
This mind is like a dream, for it gives rise to the notion of a self within that which is selfless;
the mind is like a blue fly, for it conceives of purity amidst the impure;
the mind is like a creditor, for it produces suffering and torment.
The mind is like a malevolent spirit, for it seeks out the vulnerabilities of others;
the mind is constantly fluctuating between high and low, for it is oppressed by greed and hatred;
the mind is like a thief or a robber, for it plunders the roots of goodness.
The mind constantly craves forms, like a moth throwing itself into a flame;
the mind constantly craves sounds, like the resonance of a battle drum;
the mind constantly craves fragrances, like a pig delighting in a latrine.
"The mind constantly craves flavors, like a camel that loves honey;
the mind constantly craves tactile sensations, like a fly clinging to oil. Good son!"
In this way, the bodhisattva seeks the characteristics of the mind but cannot find them; if they cannot be found, they are neither past, present, nor future;
if they are neither past, present, nor future, they transcend the three periods of time;
and if they transcend the three periods of time, they are neither existent nor non-existent.
If it is neither existent nor non-existent, then it does not arise;
that which does not arise is without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva);
and that which is without intrinsic nature is without birth.
If there is no arising, then there is no cessation;
if there is no cessation, then there is nothing to be relinquished;
if there is no relinquishing, then there is no coming, no going, no retreating, and no arising.
If there is no coming or going, no passing away, and no arising, then there are no conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
If there are no conditioned phenomena, this is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That which is unconditioned is the root of all the noble ones; therein, there is neither the observance of precepts nor the breaking of precepts.
If there were neither those who maintain the precepts nor those who violate them, then there would be neither practice nor non-practice;
if there were neither practice nor non-practice, then there would be neither mind nor mental factors;
if there were neither mind nor mental factors, then there would be neither karma nor the retribution of karma.
If there were no karma and no retribution for karma, then there would be neither suffering nor pleasure;

if there were neither suffering nor pleasure, that would be the nature of the noble ones (āryatva). Within this, there is no karma and no agent of karma; there is no bodily action and no mental action, and within this, there is no distinction between superior and inferior.
"The nature of the noble ones is equal, just like space;
this nature is equal, without superiority or inferiority, for all dharmas are of one single flavor;
this nature is equal, for it is far removed from all marks of body and mind."
This nature is detached from all phenomena because it accords with nirvāṇa;
this nature is pure because it is free from the defilements of all afflictions;
this nature is selfless because it is devoid of the notion of "mine."
This nature is true and real, for it accords with suchness;
this nature is quiescent, for it is eternally peaceful and blissful;
this nature has no high or low, for it emerges from equality.
This nature is true and real, because it is the ultimate truth;
this nature is inexhaustible, because it is ultimately unarisen;
this nature is eternally abiding, because all phenomena are always thus.
This nature is peaceful and blissful, for it is the foremost of all things, nirvāṇa;
this nature is pure, for it is free from all marks;
this nature is selfless, for it cannot be found upon seeking.
“Good sons! You should examine well within yourselves; do not let your minds run outward. Good sons!”
In the future, śramaṇas will be like dogs chasing clods of earth.
What is meant by "like a dog chasing a clod"?
It is, for example, as when someone throws a clod at a dog; the dog immediately abandons the person and runs to chase after the clod.

In this way, noble son, there are śramaṇas, laymen, and laywomen who, out of fear of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, dwell in forest hermitages and secluded places, alone and without companions, far removed from the clamor of crowds; though their bodies are detached from the five desires, their minds do not renounce them.

This person dwells on thoughts of forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles; with a mind greedily attached to them, they do not examine within and do not know how they should detach from the five sensory objects.
Because of this ignorance, at times they enter cities, towns, and villages, and even amidst crowds of people, they are again bound by the five desires.
